an-examination-of-phrenology-in-two-lect: An Examination of Phrenology, 1838. The two lectures. This book preserves that examination. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
anderson-constitutions-1738:
James Anderson, a Scottish minister in London, rewrote his Constitutions of the Free-Masons for this second edition of 1738. The first edition of 1723 had founded modern Freemasonry on paper. The New Book of Constitutions recasts that work substantially, with a fuller legendary history and revised charges and regulations for the Grand Lodge.

Anderson's history carries Masonry from Adam through the builders of Scripture and the kings of Britain. His charges set the Craft's famous rules on God, government, and conduct. The library holds the 1723 first edition; this 1738 text shows the founding document growing. Every later Masonic constitution descends from Anderson's pages in one of their two forms.
arxiv-2511-20338:
Adamson, Mertzios, and Spirakis price the chore of keeping a changing network two-colored. Their 2025 paper studies bipartite colorings on temporal graphs. Temporal graphs rewire themselves step by step. A proper two-coloring must survive every snapshot. Recoloring vertices fixes clashes but costs effort.

The budget question asks if few enough recolorings suffice. Static bipartite coloring is trivially easy by contrast. On temporal graphs the problem turns NP-hard. Worse, no constant-factor approximation exists in general. That hardness holds unless the Unique Games Conjecture fails. A positive result exploits snapshot structure instead. Few connected components per snapshot make it tractable. An exact algorithm runs in time exponential only in components. An approximation algorithm achieves a root-log factor guarantee. It runs in roughly cubic time in problem size. Longer palettes are the natural next question. Matching-only snapshots leave approximation open. Time-varying networks inherit deep coloring complexity.
arxiv-2511-20538:
Colombo rebuilds plasma physics inside one geometric structure. His 2025 paper recasts the Maxwell-Vlasov system, the core equations of collisionless plasma. Particles and fields usually get separate treatments. The Skinner-Rusk scheme handles both on a single space. A constraint algorithm then pulls out the full equations.

Gauss's law, Faraday's law, and gauge structure emerge naturally. Vlasov advection joins the same chain of constraints. Shrinking the system by its relabeling symmetry transforms the picture. The reduced system recovers the known Euler-Poincaré form. It also yields the classic Lie-Poisson Hamiltonian form. States that partly break the symmetry get a shifted version. That version clarifies Goldstone-type neutral modes in plasmas. The energy-Casimir stability method gains firm geometric ground. Antenna fields enter as controls on the Hamiltonian. Shaping conserved quantities suggests a route to stability.
arxiv-2511-20738:
Dmitry V. Fedorov and colleagues work in 2025 on a weak force with outsized influence: van der Waals attraction, the faint pull between molecules arising from correlated flickers in their electron clouds. In molecular crystals these feeble forces are the main glue between building blocks, so predicting a crystal's structure means computing them well. The standard tool, density functional theory, fixes this with van der Waals density functionals, recipes that add the missing attraction.

The team analysed the formalism behind the two functional families, DF1 and DF2, and built a scheme combining them into one optimisable tool. They proved the scheme on the X23 dataset, the standard set of 23 molecular crystals. Their combined functional beat existing approaches on unit cell volumes and lattice energies, the two numbers crystal predictions are judged by. Accuracy matched the many-body dispersion method, a respected but heavier technique, at far lower cost.
arxiv-2511-21038:
Anantha Padmanaban Krishna Kumar tests in 2025 whether examples shown in a prompt can teach small language models to use words against their learned meanings. He ran eight classification tasks across eight open-source models of 1 to 12 billion parameters, from the LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and Gemma families. Demonstrations came in two flavours: natural labels, and inverted labels that systematically flip meanings, such as tagging positive reviews as negative.

With natural labels, in-context learning improved accuracy while predictions stayed aligned with the models' prior instincts. With inverted labels, no model learned a coherent anti-semantic classifier. The semantic override rate, correctness under the flipped scheme, stayed at exactly zero in every few-shot run. Prompt alignment rose only by sacrificing accuracy. Kumar concludes that in-context learning re-aims inputs onto stable semantic directions from pretraining rather than remapping them, so flipping label meanings at this scale needs interventions beyond prompting.
arxiv-2511-21338:
Julianna Piskorz and five coauthors at Cambridge and Qualcomm probe a new kind of language model and find old habits, in 2025. Masked diffusion language models generate text by unmasking tokens in parallel, reading context from both sides, unlike standard models that write left to right. That global view should make them use distant context evenly, but the team shows it does not.

Piskorz and her coauthors find a strong locality bias: answers depend heavily on where the key information sits, favoring nearby text. They also show that the many mask tokens the model must carry during generation act as distractors, measurably degrading comprehension. Their fix is a mask-agnostic loss, training the model to give the same predictions regardless of mask count. Fine-tuning with it substantially restores robustness, and the authors urge benchmarks to report mask counts and test mask sensitivity routinely.
arxiv-2511-21538:
Finnian Gray, David Kubizňák, Hryhorii Ovcharenko, and Jiří Podolský probe the hidden symmetries of a new family of black holes, in 2025. The Ovcharenko–Podolský spacetimes describe black holes bathed in an electromagnetic field that is not aligned with the geometry, a class beyond the classic Plebański–Demiański family. Hidden symmetries, encoded in mathematical objects called Killing–Yano forms, are what make motion around rotating black holes exactly solvable.

Gray and his coauthors prove the whole class carries a non-degenerate conformal Killing–Yano 2-form, the seed of hidden symmetry. One wrinkle: unlike the aligned family, this seed does not grow the full tower of symmetries, thanks to the field's non-alignment. It still does heavy lifting, separating variables in the massless Hamilton–Jacobi, conformal wave, and Dirac equations, and making perturbations tractable. The spacetimes also test Penrose charges, quantities tied to hidden symmetries.
arxiv-2511-21638:
Daniel Jiang, Jalaj Bhandari, Yukai Yang, Rémi Munos, and Tyler Lu reduce a hard alignment problem to a solved one, in a 2025 technical note. Training chatbots for multi-turn outcomes, like a sales agent closing a deal over many messages, suffers from sparse, delayed rewards. Direct multi-turn reinforcement learning is unstable and tooling-poor.

Their Iterative PPO reframes the task: learn a multi-turn Q-function, a value estimate for conversation states, and use it as the reward model for an ordinary single-turn RLHF problem. They prove that solving that single-turn problem with standard token-level PPO is exactly a policy improvement step in the original multi-turn problem. The algorithm alternates between fitting the Q-function on logged trajectories and improving the policy with off-the-shelf tools. It sits between fully online and fully offline training, keeping adaptability with offline stability.
arxiv-2511-21738:
Single author Luke Tonon rethinks circuit complexity, the study of how large a circuit a computation needs, through information theory, in 2025. Since Claude Shannon introduced them in the 1930s, Boolean circuits have been viewed as machines that transform inputs into outputs through logic gates. Tonon proposes viewing them instead as descriptions.

On this reframing, a circuit's size measures how compactly the function it computes can be described. The paper draws analogies to Kolmogorov complexity, the theory of shortest descriptions, and develops the title's idea: truth, embodied in a function's full table of outputs, resists compression. Circuits become a special case of a general description problem, letting information-theoretic limits speak to computation limits. The framework aims to give fresh purchase on the field's fundamental open questions about efficient computation. Rather than counting gates mechanically, it asks what a function's structure permits any description to achieve.
arxiv-2512-00238:
Spinors describe particles with spin, and their duals are a subtle part of quantum field theory. Cavalcanti and Hoff da Silva present a unified approach to spinor duals in 2025, built on Clifford algebras and related symmetry groups. Recent work has revealed several distinct algebraic formulations of generalized Dirac duals.

Different dual constructions can lead to different physical models, so a unified view helps theorists compare them safely. The authors locate these formulations inside the structure of a complex Clifford algebra. The work is mathematical physics, aimed at readers who build field theory models from algebraic first principles. Clifford algebras unify rotations and reflections, which is why spinor theory leans on them.
arxiv-2512-00538:
Large optimization problems often exist at several resolutions at once, from coarse grids to fine ones. Robert Baraldi, Michael Hintermüller, and Qi Wang present a multilevel proximal trust-region method for nonsmooth optimization in 2025, with applications. Multilevel methods exploit that hierarchy to converge faster.

Combining coarse and fine information has proved highly effective for partial differential equations and related problems. Trust-region methods control step sizes, while proximal terms handle nonsmooth structure that gradients alone cannot. The method targets science and engineering problems whose scale defeats single-level algorithms. Nonsmooth problems include contact and friction, where gradients jump or fail to exist. Proximal methods are the standard toolkit for exactly that structure.
arxiv-2512-00738:
Paul Oamen, Robert Wesley, and Pius Onobhayedo wrote a 2025 paper on loyalty programs in the age of smart commerce. Reward schemes have grown from copper tokens to complex digital systems. Yet most programs stay closed, with one brand controlling the points, rules, and rewards.

Coalition programs let points work across brands, which should help everyone. Still, the authors note that many such coalitions fail within ten years, despite the network gains theory predicts. Their paper asks how rewards should be orchestrated so partners share value fairly. The lessons matter for retailers building joint programs that last.
arxiv-2512-00838:
Md Muzakkir Quamar, Ali Nasir, and Sami ELFerik present a planning framework for drones in a 2025 paper. Unmanned aerial vehicles must plan missions in complex, uncertain settings, from shifting weather to failing parts. Good plans are often computed with Markov decision processes, which weigh actions, chances, and rewards together.

Those processes grow too large to solve directly as missions scale up. The team's two-stage decomposition breaks the big problem into smaller pieces that can be solved and recombined. The framework is built to be scalable and fault-tolerant. Faster, sturdier planning would let drone fleets take on bigger jobs.
arxiv-2512-01038:
Hetvi Shastri and four coauthors present FMTK in a 2025 paper on time series tools. Foundation models adapt to new tasks with little or no extra training, and time-series foundation models do the same for data that unfolds over time. They have shown strong results on classification, regression, and filling missing values.

FMTK is a modular toolkit for building composable pipelines from such models. Users can mix and match stages instead of rebuilding a whole system for each job. Modularity matters because time series work spans forecasting, monitoring, and health signals, each with its own steps. A shared toolkit lowers the cost of trying foundation models on real problems.
arxiv-2512-01138:
Search tasks that always have an answer sit at the heart of this study. Some can be solved fast by a chance-based method. The work starts a close study of that class of tasks. It groups tasks that a fast random method can always solve.

Examples include finding a prime in a fixed range. They also include tasks that test claims about circuit limits. The study maps what sits in the class and how its parts link. A clear map helps show which hard search tasks may yield to fast random methods and which may not.
arxiv-2512-01338:
Sanjeeda Sultana, Chayan Ranjit, and Surajit Chattopadhyay rebuild a dark energy model. The model mixes a Chaplygin gas with holographic dark energy in the Barrow frame. That frame tweaks how entropy works at the edge of space. Such models try to explain why the cosmos grows faster over time.

The team checks if the rebuilt model obeys the broad law of thermodynamics. They also bound its values with fresh data from space probes. A model that passes both checks stays in the race. One that fails helps rule out paths for dark energy theory.
arxiv-2512-01538:
Marco Romanelli, Gabriel Gil, and Stefano Corni quantize light modes of metal nanoparticles. Tiny metal bits can trap light as plasmons. Their shape can be any form, not just spheres. The metal's response shifts with light tone in ways set by real data.

Their method handles odd shapes with that real response built in. Quantized modes let scholars compute quantum effects of plasmons. Those effects matter for sensors and light tools at tiny scales. A general method frees the work from shape-by-shape hand math. Experimental dielectric data anchor the modes, so predicted resonances can be checked against measured spectra for real metals, not ideal ones.
arxiv-2512-01638:
Zvirzdin searches for ultra-high-energy photons with the Telescope Array. Such photons can test astrophysics models and new physics. The array's surface detector has run for many years. Its data holds a vast set of air shower events.

A neural network sorts showers by their likely source particle. Photon showers differ in shape from proton showers. The sort yields updated caps on the diffuse photon flux. Tight caps rule out models that would flood the sky with such photons. They also bound exotic ideas about dark matter decay. Fourteen years of data give the caps weight, since rare photon showers need huge exposure before a null result means anything at all.
arxiv-2512-01738:
Pedro Curvo, Jan-Willem van de Meent, and Maksim Zhdanov scale neural solvers to industrial physics. Large simulations must capture fine local acts and long-range links at once. Millions of spatial elements make both hard. Attention over all elements is too costly.

Their Multi-Scale Patch Transformer splits the task. Local attention works inside patches of elements. Global attention works on coarse patch summaries. That split keeps fine detail without full cost. Industrial users could run larger, truer physics models with learned speed. Patch summaries carry the far field cheaply, much as multigrid solvers do, which is why the design scales near linearly in tests.
arxiv-2512-02138:
Networks of machines, from drone swarms to power grids, are often built from parts that are individually easy to control. Fengjun Yang, Jake Welde, and Nikolai Matni study in 2025 what happens when those parts are coupled: the whole network can lose the flatness property that made each part simple.

Differential flatness lets engineers plan motion and design controllers with unusual ease for a single subsystem. The authors seek distributed control that survives coupling designed to preserve flatness across the network. Their results matter wherever many nonlinear units must cooperate, because a control scheme that only works in isolation fails exactly when the system becomes interesting.
arxiv-2512-02238:
Roger Penrose held that time's arrow is writ in the shape of space. As things form, one kind of curve in that shape, Weyl curvature, should come to dwarf the other kind. Four authors led by R. A. Sussman take a fresh look in 2025 at what they call a long-held false take on this Weyl claim.

A claimed counter-case by Bonnor used exact math for hot spheres that fall inward in a Vaidya setting. The team rechecks that case and what the claim in fact says. The stakes are high. The claim ties the smooth start of the cosmos to the rule that disorder must grow.
arxiv-2512-02538:
Nathanaël Berestycki gives a concise tour of the hidden sound spectrum of Liouville quantum gravity. That theory describes a random, fractal like geometry meant to model quantum space. On it runs Liouville Brownian motion, the natural random walk for such a strange landscape.

Berestycki lays out how the motion's eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are built, forming the spectrum of the geometry. He also summarizes a recently proved Weyl law, which counts those tones at high frequency. Work in progress on the heat trace is reported too, linking the spectrum to how heat would spread on quantum geometry. The talk also serves as a map for those who want to learn this young field from the ground up.
arxiv-2512-02738:
Joel Nyholm, Wojciech Mostowski, and Christoph Reichenbach profile energy use down to single lines of code. Energy demand grows from phones to huge data centers, and developers need detail to fix waste. Older profilers blame whole programs or single functions, which is too coarse to act on.

Their probabilistic profiler targets statically typed JVM based languages, including Java. It estimates energy per source statement, with uncertainty stated openly. Line level feedback could help teams cut the energy cost of common software, a growing share of global electricity use. Line by line costs show staff the exact line that eats the watts, not just the app as a whole blob.
arxiv-2512-02838:
Ridha Horchani drafts an experiment to tell two explanations of the classical world apart. Quantum theory allows macroscopic superpositions, yet daily life never shows them. Either the environment steadily erases them, a process called decoherence, or the wave function collapses on its own.

Both stories predict similar everyday behavior, so telling them apart takes care. Horchani's blueprint lays out how a real experiment could distinguish the two mechanisms. A working test would strike at one of the deepest open questions in physics, the border between quantum and classical. Two tales that match on all past tests can still split on the next one, and this plan names that next test in full.
arxiv-2512-02938:
Maksymilian Kuna and seven co-authors show that a weak magnetic field brightens valley control in a tungsten diselenide sheet. The monolayer was grown by molecular beam epitaxy on hexagonal boron nitride. Valley polarization measures which of two electron valleys the light emission favors.

Circularly polarized photoluminescence measurements track that balance as a field is applied. A field on the order of a tenth of a tesla already enhances the polarization, the authors report. Easy valley control in grown monolayers supports valleytronic devices, which store information in electron valleys. Weak fields are cheap to add and safe for the flake. So a boost at low field is worth more than one that needs a huge rig to run.
arxiv-2512-03038:
Giulio Fabbian and six co-authors remeasure a faint distortion in the cosmic microwave background's spectrum. The y type distortion records the pressure of hot gas trapped in galaxy groups and clusters. Archival data from the FIRAS instrument still holds untapped signal for this measurement.

With improved cleaning of astrophysical foregrounds, the team extracts a new mean distortion value. The result carries implications for feedback models in galaxy formation and for cosmic shear measurements. Old satellite data, reanalyzed well, can still sharpen how we model gas in the universe. Old tapes with new eyes is a cheap trick with real yield. This yield is a mark that gas rich clumps must match in their own tales of growth.
arxiv-2512-03238:
Synthetic data can train AI without exposing real records. Natalia Ponomareva and a large team offer a practical guide in this 2025 work. They focus on making such data with differential privacy, which bounds what can be learned about any one person.

Good data are vital for AI, yet fresh human data are getting scarce. The guide, called how to DP-fy your data, walks through the process step by step. Clear guidance helps firms share and use data safely. It also helps meet privacy rules while still training useful models. Step-by-step guidance lowers the barrier for teams with data but no privacy experts.
arxiv-2512-03438:
Rewarding only final answers can starve agent training. Reuben Tan and a large team address that in this 2025 work on multimodal reinforcement learning. Agentic models are capable, yet sparse outcome rewards dominate their training.

Rewards computed from reasoning tokens give finer guidance during learning. The authors add an agentic verifier to supply those richer rewards. Finer feedback can teach agents to plan and check their work. That may raise reliability in tasks that mix text, images, and tools. Reasoning-token rewards teach process, not just outcomes, which may curb lucky but flawed answers in multimodal agent training.
arxiv-2512-03738:
Doctors predicting how long a patient will survive need honest uncertainty ranges, especially when a wrong call is costly. Jaeyoung Shin, Chi Hyun Lee, and Sangwook Kang work on that problem in a 2025 statistics preprint. They use conformal prediction, a model-agnostic method that promises correct coverage in finite samples, and extend it to survival data where many outcomes are cut short by censoring.

Earlier conformal methods for censored data either assumed narrow settings or demanded heavy computation. One recent approach builds censoring-adjusted p-values, but its coverage depends on heuristic tuning and it breaks when the patient population shifts. Shin and colleagues supply the missing theory for how its prediction sets are built, then extend the method to handle such covariate shift. Simulations and a real dataset show robust coverage and sensible interval shapes across censoring levels and shift strengths.
arxiv-2512-03838:
Medical prediction models can be accurate yet untrusted, because doctors need reasoning they can check, not just a score. Michael Staniek, Artem Sokolov, and Stefan Riezler teach language models to reason from clinical consensus guidelines step by step. Their 2025 preprint turns written guidelines into training data by applying the rules to real electronic health records.

Because the rules are explicit, the model's reasoning can be graded automatically, checking conclusions against premises and values against measurements. The team demonstrates the approach on the complex Sepsis-3 definition. Small fine-tuned models beat much larger models that were merely shown the definition, and nearly perfect rule-following appeared on unseen patients from the same area. The remaining bottleneck is forecasting sparse clinical variables into the future. Adding a time-series model's output to the language model improved that part as well.
arxiv-2512-04138:
When a dataset contains errors, fixing them well depends on knowing how they got there, yet most monitoring tools only flag that something looks wrong. Philipp Jung and colleagues present MechDetect in a 2025 preprint, a simple algorithm investigating how the errors were generated. It builds on the statistics literature about missing values, where mechanism has long mattered.

Given a table of data and a mask marking which entries are erroneous, MechDetect trains models to test whether the errors depend on the data itself. That distinction, data-dependent versus data-independent corruption, guides very different repairs. The method generalises classic missing-data tests and applies to other error types whenever an error mask exists. Experiments on benchmark datasets show the approach identifies mechanisms effectively. The authors pitch mechanism detection as the missing diagnostic step between noticing dirty data and cleaning it correctly.
arxiv-2512-04238:
Vision-language models are entering clinical workflows, yet their benchmarks mostly show them typical anatomy. Leon Mayer and colleagues probe the blind spot in a 2025 medical imaging preprint. Rare anatomical variants, such as six fingers or a single kidney, act as natural adversarial examples. They violate the expectations the models have learned.

The team introduces AdversarialAnatomyBench, the first benchmark of naturally occurring rare variants across modalities and body regions. Testing twenty-five state-of-the-art models brought three findings. Mean accuracy on perception tasks collapsed, from about seventy-one percent on typical anatomy to twenty-eight percent on atypical anatomy. Even the strongest models lost between roughly two-fifths and half their accuracy. Their errors mirrored anatomical biases, and neither scaling nor bias-aware prompting or test-time reasoning fixed the problem. The benchmark gives the field a systematic way to measure and mitigate anatomical bias.
arxiv-2512-04338:
Biagio Montaruli, Luca Compagna, Serena Elisa Ponta, and Davide Balzarotti present one detector for harmful Python packages that fits both public stores and company systems. Malicious packages are a rising path for supply chain attacks. Current tools miss two things: tricks that rewrite code to dodge scans, and the distinct false-alarm limits that distinct users can accept. A public store needs very few false alarms; a firm can accept more. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles both gaps.

The team built a method that crafts sneaky package variants with fine code scrambling. Training on such variants made the detector far harder to fool. They then tested it on a huge daily haul of real packages from PyPI, gathered over eighty days. The tests show the hardening works but needs care, since it can shift false alarms. The result is a single tool that adapts to each setting's risk line.
arxiv-2512-04438:
Tu Nguyen, Tuan Nguyen, and Vu Le give an explicit algorithm that reads off the type of a Lie algebra from a single invariant. Lie algebras encode the local rules of continuous symmetry groups. Sorting them into types is a basic step in algebra and physics. The invariant they use, named Jordan-Kronecker, packages the algebra's structure into data that a computer can check. Their 2025 arXiv paper turns that package into a decision method.

The algorithm takes the invariant of any finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra as input. It then walks through fixed steps to name the algebra's type. The authors built the method into a working Matlab program. Such a tool lets researchers sort new algebras without hand proofs for each case. It also gives students a concrete way to test how the invariant reflects structure, and it supports wider computer algebra work on symmetry.
arxiv-2512-04638:
Kei Beauduin presents a new formula for umbral operators, a tool from a quirky corner of algebra that treats sequences as if they were powers. Umbral calculus has long given shortcuts for handling polynomial families. The new formula does three things at once. Its 2025 arXiv paper ties the field to iteration theory, the study of repeated function application. It also gives a natural meaning to fractional powers of umbral operators, which had lacked a clean definition.

The proof gathers a wide spread of older results in operational calculus and shows their combined force. As a sample payoff, Beauduin extends the classic Laguerre polynomials in a new and natural way. Fractional exponents could let researchers interpolate between known operators, opening paths that integer steps cannot reach. The work renews a classical subject by linking it to modern dynamics.
arxiv-2512-04738:
Zhuoyue Wan, Wentao Hu, Chen Jason Zhang, and co-authors present OsmT, an open model that turns plain questions into queries for OpenStreetMap. The map's data answers through OverpassQL, a structured language few casual users can write. Big closed models can translate, but they cost much, hide their workings, and resist small deployments. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a lean, open alternative tuned for map tags.

A mechanism called Tag Retrieval Augmentation feeds the model relevant tag knowledge while it writes a query. Tags are the map's vocabulary, arranged in layers from broad classes to fine details. With the right tags in context, generated queries stay valid and precise. The team reports gains over generic open models on their tests. A trustworthy translator could open the world's largest open map to journalists, planners, and aid workers who think in words, not code.
arxiv-2512-04838:
L. D. M. S. Sai Teja, N. Siva Gopala Krishna, Ufaq Khan, and co-authors present DAMASHA, a framework for finding the seams where a text switches between human and machine authorship. Mixed-authorship documents now appear in classrooms, newsrooms, and courts, and knowing who wrote which span matters for trust and oversight. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a detector, called Info-Mask, that segments such texts at their transition points.

Info-Mask blends three signal kinds: stylometric cues from writing style, perplexity signals that flag machine-like smoothness, and structured boundary modeling. To stress the system, the team built and released an adversarial benchmark of mixed texts with deliberate perturbations. The framework also exposes human-interpretable attributes behind each call, so users can see why a seam was drawn. Reliable segmentation could help editors and teachers judge collaborative writing fairly.
arxiv-2512-04938:
Raquel Norel, Michele Merler, Pavitra Modi, and co-authors propose watching the brain through the voice: continuous cognitive monitoring from smartphone speech, fused with other records by a relational graph transformer. Patients with rare neurological diseases report brain fog that standard tests cannot see. Clinic visits are snapshots months apart. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests the idea in phenylketonuria, a metabolic condition where blood chemistry swings affect thinking.

A speech measure, Proficiency in Verbal Discourse, tracked blood phenylalanine levels with a clear correlation. Standard cognitive tests showed no such link. The authors argue a graph transformer can weave speech, lab values, and assessments into one model, dodging the bottlenecks of mixed medical data. The prize is alerts weeks before a patient crashes. Validation across diseases and languages remains the hard road ahead.
arxiv-2512-05038:
Cassandra Goldberg, Chaehyeon Kim, Adam Stein, and Eric Wong uncover a quirk in how transformers handle concepts. Concept vectors are directions inside a model that stand for human ideas, a tool for reading what the model is thinking, but their signals are often noisy. The authors find that transformers systematically sharpen the signal instead of spreading it evenly across many tokens.

Attention heads tuned to a concept multiply the gap between matching and non-matching inputs, so the already-strong activations grow fastest and the best evidence piles into a few tokens they call SuperActivators. In large models those tokens stand out from the noise, appear reliably whenever the concept is present, and are few — a small slice of the top activations does the job. Detection built on them beats standard scoring across images and text, and the tokens carry sharper, more local meaning than global concept vectors.
arxiv-2512-05138:
Sakshi Agarwal, Wei Xiong, and Rampi Ramprasad present polyRETRO, a language-model tool that works backward from a target polymer to how it could be made. Machine learning now designs promising polymers quickly, but deciding how to actually synthesize one still rests on expert intuition, and automated retrosynthesis — routine for small molecules — barely exists for polymers. That gap slows the move from computer designs to real materials.

Given only the target's chemical string, polyRETRO first predicts which class of polymerization reaction most likely built it, then identifies the reaction template and the starting monomers, working largely in natural language. Framing the problem for a large language model makes the reasoning readable to chemists rather than a black box. The authors present it as a first step toward polymer retrosynthesis tools that scale — and toward lab validation at the speed designs are proposed.
arxiv-2512-06138:
N. T. Nguyen-Dang and twenty co-authors stack faint X-ray signals to weigh galaxy clusters that optics found and X-rays barely see. eROSITA supplies X-rays; Subaru supplies the optical catalogue. Nearly a thousand clusters are stacked into measurable profiles. Weak lensing calibrates the mass scaling relations.

The luminosity relation runs slightly steeper than self similar prediction. No extra evolution is required. Detected clusters are a biased subset, with brighter centers. Optical and X-ray samples are different populations; cosmology depends on knowing it. Combining deep surveys is the value shown.
arxiv-2512-06238:
Yuping Zheng and Andrew Lamperski study how to measure cause and effect flowing between two streams of data. Their tool of choice, directed information, gauges how much one stream helps predict the next step of another, step by step in time. Labs must guess this value from a finite run of data, so they need to know how far off the guess might be.

Work on error bounds had covered data drawn from a fixed set of symbols, but not smooth real valued data. The authors fill that gap for data that follows a bell curve pattern. They write the target rate as a clean formula built on best guesses of the next value, then build an estimator from it. They prove its error shrinks at a known rate as more data comes in. Such bounds help engineers trust causal measures drawn from real sensors.
arxiv-2512-06438:
Ramazan Fazylov and four co authors present AGORA, a system that creates moving three dimensional head avatars that can be driven in real time. Such avatars serve virtual reality, remote presence, and film. Older methods were slow to render or stiff in motion, while fast splatting methods, which paint a scene with soft three dimensional blobs, mostly made still heads with no control over expression.

AGORA grows splatting inside a generative contest setup, where one network makes avatars and another grades them. A light branch, steered by a standard face model, nudges each blob so the face can change expression while keeping its identity. Two graders, fed with synthetic renders of the face mesh, police realism and expression alike. The avatars render at high speed on a graphics card and, notably, at a usable rate on a plain processor alone. On expression accuracy the system beat leading rivals.
arxiv-2512-06638:
Isha Karn and David Jensen show that two favorite data sets for testing fake news detectors cannot judge the very thing they are used to judge. Graph neural networks detect fake news by modeling both article content and how stories spread between accounts. The benchmarks, GossipCop and PolitiFact, pair articles with their spread graphs, so they look ideal for grading such models.

The authors benchmark five graph architectures against a plain network that ignores spread entirely and reads only article features. The plain network matched or nearly matched the graph models, with gaps inside the noise. Shuffling the article features wrecked performance, while randomizing the spread links changed almost nothing, a sign the graphs carry no useful signal. Most nodes sit one hop from the root, so the graphs are shallow fans with little structure. On synthetic data where spread truly informs, graph models pulled clearly ahead.
arxiv-2512-06738:
M Yashwanth and four co authors adapt image models across sites that cannot share their data or even reveal their labels. In federated source free domain adaptation, each client holds unlabeled images from its own world, and the only starting point is a model pretrained elsewhere. The source data itself is off limits. Clients' worlds differ sharply from each other and from the source, so local training drifts, and the guessed labels that guide it go unreliable.

Their framework, FedSCAl, steadies clients by aligning their predictions with the server model's predictions, a mechanism they call server client alignment. After alignment, the clients' guessed labels measurably improved, which cuts the drift at its root. Across benchmark vision data sets, FedSCAl consistently beat leading federated methods in this strict setup. The work matters wherever privacy or ownership bars data pooling, from hospitals to fleets of cameras.
arxiv-2512-06938:
Ivanhoé Botcazou and co-authors work on a mundane but stubborn problem: making a language model write a text of exactly the requested length. A recent method counts down the tokens left to write, but the authors show it wobbles badly when asked for lengths outside its training range. Tying control to an absolute remaining count, they argue, is the weak point.

Their fix replaces the countdown with a progress ratio, the share of the target length already written. That ratio feeds the model as a smooth signal built from wave-like functions, which the authors liken to a sense of impatience. The method slots into standard transformer designs without fuss. In tests on two news-summarization benchmarks, length was held steady and text quality did not drop. It also worked for target lengths the model had never seen in training, the very case that broke the older approach.
arxiv-2512-07138:
Emi Cora Valmai Hughes, Avinash Upadhya, and Kishan Dholakia survey a detector technology that counts single particles of light, and its promise for seeing inside living tissue. Superconducting nanowire detectors offer extreme sensitivity, timing precise to trillionths of a second, and reach across a broad range of wavelengths. This perspective weighs them against established photon-counting devices for the biomedical imaging tasks where light is scarce and every photon counts.

The advantages are concrete: better signal against noise, sharper timing, and wider bandwidth enable deeper tissue imaging and exact measurements of how long fluorescence lingers, a signature of tissue state. Quantum-enhanced imaging schemes also come into reach. Barriers remain at the system level, since the detectors need deep cooling and careful collection optics. Arrays are scaling up and cryogenics are shrinking, lowering those barriers.
arxiv-2512-07638:
Mohammad Farhoudi, Masoud Shokrnezhad, and Tarik Taleb wrote this 2025 survey paper on future mobile networks. Sixth-generation networks will fuse edge and cloud computing with very fast links. Services will multiply, shift, and surge in ways today's systems cannot handle.

Four tasks sit at the heart of running such services. They must be registered, indexed, discovered, and selected, a chain the authors call SRIDS. The survey first lays out the theory and the end-to-end workflow. It lists design goals from reliability and scale to privacy and trust. A broad review then exposes gaps that block a unified approach. The authors sort known mechanisms into centralized, distributed, decentralized, and hybrid kinds. Each study is graded against the design goals they set out. Their own proposal is a hybrid architecture for the field. Central data management keeps consistency, while distributed coordination supplies scale. Generative AI is woven in as support.
arxiv-2512-07738:
Dengjia Zhang and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 report from Johns Hopkins' HLTCOE team. They entered the TREC 2025 track on video question answering. The task, answer generation, asks a model to answer questions about a video.

Their approach works in two stages built around ranking. A base multimodal model first drafts several candidate answers. A second model then reranks those candidates into a final order. The reranker trains on a new loss designed for this listwise job. That loss mixes pointer-based selection with weights that depend on rank. A masked cross-entropy term, restricted to a set vocabulary, completes it. The blend gives stable and interpretable training for the reranker. Generative fluency and discriminative ranking thus pull together. Experiments show steady gains in accuracy and ranking stability. Questions needing temporal reasoning benefit most from the design. Semantic disambiguation, another hard case, improves as well.
arxiv-2512-08038:
Elifnur Sunger, Tales Imbiriba, Peter Campbell, Deniz Erdogmus, and colleagues, researchers in machine learning and medicine, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is retinopathy of prematurity, an eye disease of premature infants that neural networks can help classify from fundus images. Doctors, however, need explanations they can trust before acting on a model output.

Their method, called SSplain, explains a classifier pixel by pixel while keeping the explanation smooth and sparse. Earlier explainers often broke up the natural structure of the image, producing unrealistic maps. SSplain poses the task as an optimization problem with combined constraints and solves it with a standard splitting method. In experiments it beat common explainers on accuracy and smoothness checks. It also highlighted features that match what clinicians themselves treat as signs of the disease, and it carried over to other public datasets.
arxiv-2512-08138:
Kyriakos Lotidis, Panayotis Mertikopoulos, Nicholas Bambos, and Jose Blanchet, researchers in game theory and learning, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the Nash equilibrium, the standard solution idea for games, and whether equilibria survive when conditions shift. They examine robustness in two senses: against small changes to game payoffs, and against noise in the learning process that leads players to an outcome.

The authors define robust equilibria as those unchanged by any small payoff disturbance, and describe them geometrically. They then study a learning rule called follow the regularized leader, asking which equilibria it settles on under randomness. Despite their different origins, the two robustness notions match: strategic robustness implies dynamic robustness, and weakening the first breaks the second. They also show how fast learning converges to robust equilibria, with entropy based regularization giving geometric speed in many games.
arxiv-2512-08238:
Mahathir Monjur and Shahriar Nirjon, computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about judging speech quality with a language model. Phone, voice over internet, and streaming services must monitor huge amounts of degraded audio. Classic measures mimic human opinion scores but need controlled tests, while learning based scorers give numbers without explaining themselves or answering questions.

Their system, SpeechQualityLLM, pairs an audio encoder with a language model trained on the NISQA corpus. Training uses question and answer pairs about overall quality and four traits: noisiness, coloration, discontinuity, and loudness. The model writes textual answers, from which numeric scores are read back. On held out clips, its error on overall quality was small and its ranking matched human ratings well. Users can also ask free form questions and request the ear of different listener types, cutting the need for costly listening panels.
arxiv-2512-08438:
J Maes, Gavin J Pringle, and Hannah P Menke, earth scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They simulate fluid flow through rocks using full resolution scans, with no shrinking of the images to fit the computer. Their two rock samples, a sandstone and a carbonate, were imaged by micro CT at billions of voxels each, the carbonate full of fine porous patches.

Running on the United Kingdom ARCHER2 supercomputer, their solver treats the rock surface through a simple volume indicator rather than a complex fitted mesh. That choice allows plain grid meshes built in parallel, scaling cleanly as the machine grows. Scaling tests show full resolution flow simulations are now feasible on such giant images, opening true scale modeling for geology and engineering.
arxiv-2512-08638:
Anthony Manni and coauthors study a variant of the Michelson interferometer designed to sense tiny strains, such as those from gravitational waves. In place of normal beam splitters, the design uses special four port scatterers called Grover coins, which are unbiased in direction. That change is meant to sharpen phase readings.

The team works out the noise to signal ratio for sideband tones created when a gravitational wave shifts the phase. They explain how the Grover setup boosts the signal, and how adding light recycling can improve it further. The work is a careful quantitative case for the design. It shows where the gains come from and what limits remain, giving builders a clearer path to more sensitive detectors.
arxiv-2512-08738:
Samuel Johnny, Blessed Guda, Emmanuel Aaron, and Assane Gueye define a new task called Sign Language Spotting. Automatic sign recognition helps bridge deaf and hearing communities, but finding one specific sign inside a longer signed sequence has barely been studied. Their task asks whether a query sign appears in a sentence level target video.

Instead of using raw video frames or gloss text, their model works directly on pose keypoints taken from the videos. An encoder only design with a binary head decides whether the query sign is present. Pose input cuts compute cost and reduces visual noise. On a shared task data set for word presence, the system reaches moderate accuracy and F scores. The authors present the result as a first step toward full sign retrieval and verification tools.
arxiv-2512-09538:
Ekaterina Fadeeva leads a team improving how the uncertainty of a language model's answers is measured. Consistency-based methods sample answers to the same question and gauge how much they agree; disagreement signals uncertainty. In short-answer tasks, random sampling often produces duplicate answers because the model's distribution is peaked, and its randomness makes uncertainty estimates vary from run to run.

Their alternative uses beam search, a deterministic decoding method, to generate the answers instead. The resulting family of methods performs better and with less variance than sampling-based ones. The authors also prove a lower bound on the probability mass a beam set captures, under which beam search is guaranteed smaller error than random sampling. Across six question-answering datasets, the beam-based approach improved on multinomial sampling and reached uncertainty quantification performance. The message is in the title: do not throw away the beams a model computes.
arxiv-2512-09638:
Cristiano Longarini and Cathie Clarke investigate a bottleneck in how stars gain mass from their protoplanetary discs. They work with a sample of discs where the star's mass, the disc's mass, and the disc's size have all been measured dynamically. From those data they infer each disc's viscosity, the parameter summarizing how fast material spirals inward.

The inferred viscosities span a broad range, over a thousandfold. That spread tracks the star's rotation period: systems whose stars spin faster show lower accretion rates, as if their inflow is choked. The authors interpret this within magnetospheric accretion models. The balance is between the co-rotation radius, where the star's magnetic field rotates with the disc, and the magnetospheric radius, where the field takes over. It decides whether material accretes steadily or is held back in the propeller regime. They conclude stellar spin is a key regulator of disc-to-star transfer.
arxiv-2512-09738:
Tanja Amerstorfer leads a team testing whether heliospheric imagers watching from the L5 Lagrange point can improve forecasts of coronal mass ejection arrivals at Earth. These solar eruptions drive space weather that can damage satellites and power grids, so arrival time and speed predictions matter. The study prepares for the European Space Agency's Vigil mission, which will observe from L5.

Using the ELEvoHI model, they feed in imager data from the STEREO mission, adding observations progressively as would happen in real time, and measure how forecast accuracy changes. They also test human factors: predictions based on tracking by three scientists expose how manual choices bias results. Direction estimates from imager methods are compared with coronagraph-based ones. The findings show imager data improves forecasting when combined with other observing platforms, especially once data extend beyond an elongation from the Sun, laying groundwork for Vigil-era prediction methods.
arxiv-2512-10138:
Raymond Chu, Inwon Kim, and Sebastian Munoz analyze the supercooled Stefan problem, the mathematics of water freezing below its melting point. Supercooled liquid can freeze in jagged ways, with ice nucleating suddenly at scattered points. The authors first study general solutions, proving with a new Markovian gluing technique that fractal freezing and nucleation are the generic pattern. They then single out maximal solutions, obtained by maximizing a suitable average freezing time, and prove this marked class is far better behaved.

For maximal solutions, the transition zone between liquid and solid is open except for a low dimensional leftover set, letting obstacle problem methods deliver finer regularity. Maximal solutions are generally not universal: unlike constructions can give unlike answers. Yet sharp stability under perturbations holds for each. In radial and one dimensional settings, the picture cleans up fully: the maximal solution is universal and minimizes nucleation, matching what physicists observe.
arxiv-2512-10238:
Antu Saha surveys a research program on resolving software issues with artificial intelligence. Fixing reported bugs is central to software quality, yet developers struggle with poor quality issue reports, limited knowledge of real workflows, and little automated help. The program attacks on three fronts. First, it improves the reports themselves, using language model reasoning enriched with application specific information. Second, it studies how developers actually resolve issues, in both traditional and AI augmented teams, to ground the tools in real practice rather than assumptions.

Third, it automates the cognitively hardest resolution tasks: locating the buggy user interface element behind a report, and identifying the right solution. Machine learning, deep learning, and language model methods are all brought to bear. The document is a compact three page research overview rather than a single study. It presents empirical findings, practical tools, and automated methods as one agenda.
arxiv-2512-10438:
Jacob Fox, Benny Sudakov, and Yuval Wigderson work on a Ramsey theory question about tournaments, round-robin style directed graphs where every pair of vertices has exactly one arrow between them. Colour the arrows with many colours, and the question is how long a directed path can be guaranteed that avoids one chosen colour entirely. Questions of this shape feed into vector sequences, convex geometry, and hypergraph theory.

The authors prove a clean threshold result. Once the number of colours is large enough, any coloured tournament holds a colour-avoiding directed path nearly as long as the whole tournament. It misses the full length only by a small power. That settles a question of Gowers and Long, strengthens several of their results, and extends earlier work by Loh.
arxiv-2512-10538:
Shubham Ghatul and co-authors present NUTEx, a small near-ultraviolet telescope riding on a CubeSat platform to watch the sky for brief, flashing events. CubeSats are cheap and compact, and this payload is built for a micro-satellite bus. Its Ritchey-Chrétien telescope feeds a photon-counting detector that is blind to sunlight, giving a wide field of view in the near-ultraviolet band.

The instrument aims to catch transient phenomena such as supernova remnants and flaring M-dwarf stars, events that unfold too fast for slow survey schedules. The paper lays out the optical design, the home-built readout electronics, and the mechanical structure with its analysis. Sensitivity reaches faint magnitudes in a twenty-minute exposure, and launch is scheduled for the second quarter of 2026, making the paper a full design report for a mission still under development.
arxiv-2512-10638:
Sepideh Adamiat, Wouter Kouw, and Bert de Vries ask whether spikes can do statistics. Bayesian inference gives a principled account of how natural agents process information, but how neurons might carry out its steps is unknown. The team tests a concrete hypothesis: that belief propagation, the message-passing algorithm on factor graphs, can run inside a network of spiking neurons.

They encode each incoming message to a factor node as a spike-based signal, pass it through leaky integrate-and-fire neurons, and decode the result as the outgoing message. Three core operations, branching, addition, and multiplication, are each realised in such networks. Checked against the standard sum-product algorithm, the message updates come out accurate. And the framework handles Kalman filtering and Bayesian linear regression, covering both still and moving inference problems on the road to neuromorphic reasoning hardware.
arxiv-2512-11438:
Tariq Berrada Ifriqi and colleagues present Flowception, a video generation method that builds films by inserting frames rather than predicting them one after another. Autoregressive generators extend a video step by step, so errors accumulate and long clips drift. Generating the whole sequence at once avoids drift but costs far more computation and cannot decide how long a video should be.

Flowception learns a probability path that mixes two operations: dropping new discrete frames into the sequence and continuously cleaning up frames already there. Insertions compress long term context efficiently, cutting training computation roughly threefold compared with full sequence flows. The model learns video length jointly with content. Scores on standard quality benchmarks beat both autoregressive and full sequence baselines. The same machinery handles image to video generation and filling in missing frames between two known ones.
arxiv-2512-11538:
Gergely Bérczi and Felix Minddal introduce a non associative model for the Hilbert scheme of points, a central object in algebraic shape that parametrises clusters of points on a space. Nested versions of these schemes, tracking clusters inside clusters, are notoriously singular, which blocks the building of virtual invariants, the corrected counts modern shape relies on. Their idea is to embed the problem in a smoother, larger space.

In the non associative Hilbert scheme, the standard nested scheme appears exactly where an explicit associativity condition holds, cut out by a section of a purpose built bundle. That description yields canonical obstruction theories and virtual fundamental classes in every dimension and for every cluster pattern. Virtual localisation then produces closed formulas as sums over admissible nested partitions. Over the most singular locus, these collapse into a single iterated residue formula. That formula governs all the virtual integrals at once.
arxiv-2601-06638:
J. J. Segura finds an exact rule for how grain sizes change as they break, in 2026. Breakage rules track how the spread of grain sizes shifts over time. Bits from each break are shared out to new, smaller sizes.

From a self-similar class of breaks, he derives an exact move rule. The rule works on the log of size, for the share of mass at each size. It takes the form of a pure-jump master rule, as he shows. Mass moves in jumps in log size, not in a smooth drift at all. From it he draws drift and spread limits for large scales. The frame also helps infer the size spread from test data. Those who model mills get exact form first, not rough fits.
arxiv-2601-06938:
Heng Xu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with forgetting similar samples. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Machine unlearning, a process enabling pre-trained models to remove the influence of specific training samples, has attracted significant attention in recent years. Although extensive research has focused on developing efficient machine unlearning strategies.

We argue that these methods mainly aim at removing samples rather than removing samples’ influence on the model. Thus overlooking the fundamental definition of machine unlearning. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07038:
Emma Rafkin and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers task arithmetic with support languages for Low-Resource ASR. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. The development of resource-constrained approaches to automatic speech recognition (ASR) is of great interest due to its broad applicability to many low-resource languages.

For which there is scant usable data. Existing approaches to many low-resource natural language processing tasks leverage additional data from higher-resource languages that are closely related to a target low-resource language. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07238:
Hanbin Wang and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers group pattern selection optimization. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Large reasoning models (LRMs) exhibit diverse high-level reasoning patterns (e.g., direct solution, reflection-and-verification, and exploring multiple solutions). Yet prevailing training recipes implicitly bias models toward a limited set of dominant patterns.

Through a systematic analysis, we identify substantial accuracy variance across these patterns on mathematics and science benchmarks. Revealing that a model’s default reasoning pattern is often sub-optimal for a given problem. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07338:
An arXiv preprint from 2026 covers beyond literal mapping. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced Machine Translation (MT), applying them to linguistically complex domains—such as Social Network Services, literature etc.

In these scenarios, translations often require handling non-literal expressions, leading to the inaccuracy of MT metrics. To systematically investigate the reliability of MT metrics, we first curate a meta-evaluation dataset focused on non-literal translations, namely MENT . The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07638:
Isaiah Onando Mulang' and colleagues build a benchmark for learning from business tables with meaning attached. SALT-KG extends the earlier SALT benchmark for relational prediction. The new version links multi-table transaction data to a structured knowledge graph of operational business knowledge. That graph records field-level descriptions, relations between fields, and business object types. Their 2026 preprint defines the resource.

Most table benchmarks give models numbers without the business context behind them. Semantics-aware learning tests whether models can use that context to predict better. Enterprise data is exactly where such context exists but is rarely shared. A public benchmark lets teams compare methods fairly. The paper targets machine learning scholars who work with relational and enterprise data.
arxiv-2601-08238: Jia-Wei Ying and co-authors design quantum secure direct communication that ignores reference frame drift. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that current protocols check photon error rates in two bases. Those checks assume the two parties first calibrate a shared reference frame. In mobile settings, keeping that calibration continuous and accurate is hard. A reference-frame-independent protocol removes the prerequisite entirely. The work targets secure links on moving platforms, where alignment shifts constantly. Quantum direct communication sends the message itself, so frame freedom could widen its practical reach.
arxiv-2601-08938:
Michael Weber, Barbara Ercolano, and Giovanni Picogna ask if star light alone can carve gaps in young disks of gas and dust. Such disks form round new stars, and planets grow in them. Light from the star can boil gas off the disk face. That boil off is called photoevaporation. Some claim it can open a clean gap, as a planet can.

The team runs 2D sims that tie disk growth to the boil off flow. They find a catch. Once a dip forms, the boil off rate there drops fast. That drop stops the gap from deep growth. A reader in planet birth work gets a bound on what star light can do alone.
arxiv-2601-09138:
Sahas Kamat and five co-authors report a vast zone of shakes in a heavy superconductor named UTe2. A superconductor bears charge with no loss under a set heat. In most such stuffs, shakes near the shift heat span a thin band. Past that band, a plain mean law holds well. In UTe2 the shake band is as wide as the shift heat itself.

That width is the large known for a stuff of this type, the team says. It hints that pairs of charge bits form across bands, not in one band. Such cross band pairs would break the plain law in just this way. A reader in new stuffs gets a case that may force a fresh take on how pairs form.
arxiv-2601-09238:
Jackie Alex and Justin Petter grow fake flaw shots of power sub station meters from a few real ones. Such meters watch grid health. Cracks and flaws on them must be caught. Marked real shots of flaws are rare, so a spot tool starves for train data. A grow tool can fill that gap, if its fakes look true and can be set by type.

Their frame adds fact codes and a hyper net guide to a spread based grow tool. The guide steers flaw type, place, and size from few cases. A reader in grid work gets train shots for a rare flaw hunt, with a hand on what each fake shows.
arxiv-2601-09338:
Yao Sun and four co-authors chart all study work on OpenStreetMap from its start to 2024. OSM is a free world map built by vol hands. It grew from a bold side task to a base for work in maps, towns, aid, and nets. The team runs a count and theme scan of that study set to see who built it, and what they asked.

They track how themes shifted as the map grew. Early work asked if vol maps could be true. Late work uses the map as firm data for hard asks. A reader in map work gets a guide to a vast field, and a view of where it may go next.
arxiv-2601-09638:
A. Rigoulet, S. Nanos, I. K. Kominis, and D. Antypas hunt for axion-like dark matter with a tabletop magnetometer. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports a broadband search using a radio-frequency rubidium-87 atomic magnetometer. Axion-like particles could form the dark matter that fills the galaxy.

If such a field couples to the spins inside atoms, it would act like a tiny oscillating magnetic field. The magnetometer covers a wide band of frequencies with high sensitivity. A null result still trims the space of allowed couplings. Tabletop searches like this one complement huge detectors at modest cost.
arxiv-2601-09738:
Haley Stone and eleven co-authors link landscape ecology to the risk of wildlife disease outbreaks. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a heterogeneous graph network for epidemiological reasoning. Estimating how common a pathogen is, and how it spreads, is hard when surveillance data is sparse.

Field data on wildlife disease is detection-driven and unevenly sequenced. The authors build a graph that joins ecological connectivity with case data across space and time. Graph reasoning can fill gaps that raw counts cannot. Better prevalence estimates help agencies target testing and protect both wildlife and people.
arxiv-2601-09838:
Leonie Dyck and a large team describe a robot built to help children recover through play. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Mobirobot, a socially assistive robot for pediatric therapy. It supports mobilization in children healing from trauma, fractures, or depressive disorders, through personalized exercise programs.

Socially assistive robots can raise engagement in therapy. Success needs more than sound engineering: the design must fit clinics and therapy rooms. Clinicians, therapists, and engineers built it together in short agile cycles. Co-design across settings aims at a robot that busy ward staff will actually use each day.
arxiv-2601-10238:
Stijn Cambie, Andrea Freschi, Patryk Morawski, Kalina Petrova, and Alexey Pokrovskiy bound a Ramsey count. Ramsey counts ask how large a graph must be to force a set shape. Here the shapes are a cycle and a graph of set size. Size is read as the count of edges.

The team prove a clean bound. For each cycle length and each graph with no lone nodes, the count is at most twice the edge count plus half the cycle length. The bound needs the graph to be large next to the cycle. Such bounds pin down how fast forced shapes must show.
arxiv-2601-10338:
Yi Liu and co authors map flaws in add on skills for AI agents. A skill is a pack of rules and code. It can be loaded to give an agent new powers. Such packs run with deep trust. Few checks vet them before use.

That trust gap is a fresh attack field. Bad code in a skill can harm the host. The team ran a large scale test of skills in the wild. They sort the flaws they found by type and risk. The work is a first map of this field. It shows why skill stores need vet steps like app stores.
arxiv-2601-10938:
Xingyu Guo, Cheng Gui, and Zhenbin Wang benchmark universal machine learning potentials for battery kinetics. Faster alkali-ion battery discovery needs accurate models of atomic-scale motion. Shared potentials promise one model for many materials. How far they can be trusted on steep energy landscapes, the terrain of kinetics, is still unsure. The authors test that trust head on.

They compare M3GNet, CHGNet, MACE, SevenNet, GRACE, and Orb against DFT baselines. The test materials are cathodes and solid electrolytes. Kinetics governs charging speed and lifetime, so errors there mislead design the most. The benchmark tells battery modelers which shared tools are ready for kinetic work and which still lag.
arxiv-2601-11238:
David Otero and Javier Parapar work on search quality in this 2026 preprint. Their topic is feedback from first search results, a classic trick. Search fails at times when query words miss the words in texts. Added terms from top hits can close that gap for users.

The classic method, RM3, builds the new query from top-ranked texts. It can drift off topic when early hits are noisy. New work asks large language models to write the added terms. Otero and Parapar test that LLM-assisted path for feedback. The goal is growth of the query with less drift. Good feedback lifts weak first searches at low cost to the user.
arxiv-2601-11438:
Qiaosen Zhang, Matteo Nerini, and Bruno Clerckx solve channel estimation for analog-aided MIMO. Their 2026 letter deals with microwave linear analog computers. Such computers, called MiLACs, aid beamforming in vast MIMO systems. They cut hardware and compute cost by a large share.

Channel estimation for MiLAC systems was an open problem. Classic least squares and MMSE schemes lean on digital math. Heavy digital work would undo the analog gains of MiLACs. The team gives LS and MMSE schemes that fit the hardware. Their schemes keep the estimation light and efficient. That keeps the cost edge of analog beamforming intact. The work clears a key block for gigantic MIMO design.
arxiv-2601-11638:
Josafat Ribeiro Leal Filho and Antonio Augusto Frohlich verify PINN fidelity. Their 2026 preprint uses classical Fisher information for the check. Physics-informed neural networks solve differential equations by learning. They embed physical laws into the training process itself.

Judging how fully a PINN captures dynamics is still hard. Trajectory prediction alone says little about full behavior. The team draws Fisher information from a differentiable system. That quantity can measure sensitivity in the model's fit. A differentiable dynamical system supplies the needed gradients. The method aims at rigorous fidelity scores for PINNs. Such scores matter where PINNs guide real engineering.
arxiv-2601-11838:
Hao Lyu, Jingzheng Wu, Xiang Ling, and their co-authors test a way to find bugs in RISC-V chips. RISC-V is an open design for computer cores. Its open use speeds new chips, but also brings risk of hidden flaws in how cores run code.

Fuzzing feeds odd inputs to a chip to trip flaws. Their tool, named SimFuzz in the work, guides its changes by how alike code blocks are. Smart guidance can reach deep code paths that random tests miss. The work aims to catch flaws before chips ship.
arxiv-2601-12038:
Beishui Liao adds subargument links to a classic frame for argument. Dung's frame judges arguments by attack links alone. It sets aside the inner form of each argument on purpose. That choice made the maths rich, but hides how arguments are built.

Many formal systems need those inner links, most of all when one argument sits inside a larger one. Liao's frame keeps attack links and adds subargument links. That lets the frame track built form while it judges which claims stand. The work links two strands of argument theory.
arxiv-2601-12138:
Abhishek Kumar, Riya Tapwal, and Carsten Maple build a risk taxonomy for language model driving aides. Such aides now sit in cars, where bad or vague advice can cause real harm. It can also breach law or ethics on the road.

Past safety lists are too broad to catch driving risks. Their DriveSafe taxonomy sorts risks by the driving case. A clear list helps teams test aides on road cases before launch. It also helps map which faults are most grave in a car.  A shared list helps car firms test aides the same way.
arxiv-2601-12238:
Sharan Sahu, Cameron J. Hogan, and Martin T. Wells prove that momentum SGD can be shown to be suboptimal for nonstationary problems. They study SGD and its Polyak and Nesterov momentum forms. The task is to track optima that move with time, under strong convexity and smoothness.

Their finite-time bounds split tracking error into three parts. One is transient, one is noise-led, and one is drift-led. That split shows where momentum hurts in a moving task. The result guides choice of optimizer for live systems.  Drift terms grow as the tracked optimum moves more.
arxiv-2601-12438:
Simone Taioli, Francesca Triggiani, and Stefano Simonucci revisit a mismatch in early universe physics. Standard Big Bang theory predicts how much lithium 7 should exist. Old, metal poor stars suggest a far lower value, by a factor of about three to four. This gap is the primordial lithium problem, and it has lasted for years.

Most early lithium 7 was first made as beryllium 7. That beryllium later turned into lithium by electron capture. So the rates of weak and radiative moves for beryllium set the final count. The team recheck those rates with fresh care. If the rates shift, the predicted lithium count shifts too. Their work tests whether nuclear physics alone can close the gap.
arxiv-2601-12538:
Tianxin Wei and a large team survey agentic reasoning in large language models. Reasoning sits under inference, problem solving, and decision making in human thought. Language models reason well in closed worlds, like standard math and code tests. They struggle more in open ended, changing environments where the ground shifts.

The survey tracks the field in three parts named in its title. It covers foundations of agentic reasoning, how the area has evolved, and how agents collaborate. Agentic systems plan, act, and check their own work over many steps. A map of this fast moving field helps builders see what is settled and what is not. It also frames open problems for the next wave of work.
arxiv-2601-12738:
Ba Khiet Le, Zakaria Mazgouri, and Michel Thera study monotonicity for pairs of operators. Monotonicity of a single operator is a classic tool in analysis and optimization. Extending it to pairs helps solve non monotone inclusions, a harder class of problems. Monotone pairs have become an important new tool for such inclusions in recent work.

A key open challenge is how to design the mappings that form a monotone pair. The team also work with a generalized inertial proximal method. Inertial methods add momentum like terms to speed convergence. Pairing the two ideas may yield algorithms for problems once out of reach. The work serves variational analysis and applied optimization.
arxiv-2601-13238:
Chengyin Hu and co-authors craft a rain based attack to test vision language models. Such models train on image and text pairs shot in fair light and clear air. They score well on fair tasks. Their grip in real bad weather is far less known. So is the calm of their image to text match when rain warps a scene.

The attack splits sense parts of a scene, then adds rain in two stages. It aims to show where the match breaks. Weak spots found this way can guide more sound train sets. For teams that ship such models for road or watch use, rain is not a rare edge case. It is a core test.
arxiv-2601-13338:
Ziyi Liu and a large team set out a space where people and many robots talk in plain words first. As homes gain more than one robot, plain speech may be the main way for person to robot and robot to robot talk. Past rigs lean on screens, code, or set commands.

Their space is called a Natural Language Environment. In it, folks and mixed robots plan and act through speech as the shared stream. The paper lays out what such a space needs and how acts flow in it. For home robot teams, a speech first space could cut the learn load for users and let mixed fleets mesh with ease.
arxiv-2601-13538:
Han W. G. and co-authors unscramble weak lens mass maps with a deep net of nested U shapes. Weak lensing bends light from far galaxies by the mass it passes. From that bend, teams map where dark matter lies. True mass maps need a sound inversion of the bend field, a hard step.

Their net is called MIU2Net. It stacks U shaped nets in nests, a form apt for maps at many scales. Next lens surveys will flood teams with bend data. A fast learnt inversion can keep pace where slow rules lag. For dark matter teams, map speed and grade set how much of that flood can be used.
arxiv-2601-14038:
Alexandre Justo Miro and co-authors fix errors in the 3D boxes used to train driverless cars in 2026. Accurate ground truth annotations are critical to supervised learning for vehicles. Cars use active sensors like LiDAR, which scan the surroundings in set patterns. In dynamic scenes, objects are observed at different timestamps and positions.

That timing spread makes 3D box annotation challenging and error-prone. The team works on correcting and quantifying systematic errors in these boxes. Known error sizes let teams judge how much to trust a dataset. Safer self-driving needs labels that match the real world.
arxiv-2601-14538:
Robert L. Bray studies revenue management in this 2026 paper. His model is the simplest one with reusable resources: admission control of two customer classes into a loss queue. A loss queue turns away arrivals when all resources are busy. The model's long-run average collected reward has two natural upper bounds. One is the deterministic relaxation. The other is the full-information offline problem.

Bray's title states his result in formula form. A lookahead of order log N over N is sufficient to bound costs in the overloaded loss network. In plain terms, a short peek ahead nearly matches far costlier schemes. Readers get a sharp limit on how much foresight is worth.
arxiv-2601-14838:
Maram Alwohaibi and four co-authors study a stochastic diffusion equation in this 2026 paper. The equation is a time-space nonlocal diffusion equation driven by additive time-space white noise. Its time derivative is the Caputo derivative of order alpha between zero and two. Fractional derivatives give the process memory: the past keeps weight in the present.

The model couples local diffusion with a nonlocal convolution operator generated by a radial probability density. That coupling incorporates memory effects and long-range spatial interactions. The team studies mild solutions, the weakest solution form that still makes the equation meaningful. The math is hard. It is built for experts who work on noise, chance, and change in one frame. The work stays in the realm of proof. It shows the mild form can be solved, and how. Readers get existence theory for diffusion that remembers and reaches far.
arxiv-2601-14938:
Virginia Falcone, Eleni Prountzou, and co-authors at ETH Zurich build light guides from barium titanate. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with photonic chips, tiny circuits that steer light. Such chips serve in modulators and in sources of paired photons.

Metal oxides suit this work well. They react strongly to electric fields and stay clear across a wide range of colors. Barium titanate stands out for its large Pockels coefficient, a gauge of that response. The team makes its waveguides from a solution-based, liquid route, aimed at compact, efficient on-chip light control.
arxiv-2601-15538:
Himanshu Mishra and Kanwal Mehreen study a clash between two model-editing tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Machine unlearning removes specific knowledge from a trained model. Targets include copyrighted text and private data. Done well, it avoids the cost of full retraining. Quantization is a separate trick. It shrinks models, often to 4-bit form, so they run cheaply.

The authors find a nasty interaction between the two. Quantization can bring back knowledge that unlearning removed. They describe the effect as catastrophic restoration of forgotten content. Their method, QUAIL, is quantization-aware unlearning, per the title. It aims to keep removals in place after shrinking. For teams that ship small models, the warning is direct. A privacy fix is not done until it survives compression.
arxiv-2601-15838:
Toan Gian and four co-authors compress Wi-Fi sensing data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Wi-Fi sensing estimates human poses without cameras or wearables. It is device-free and privacy-preserving, which makes it attractive. The raw data are channel state information, or CSI. Existing methods process vast amounts of it directly. That volume strains networking resources. Their framework is called TinySense.

TinySense compresses CSI while keeping sensing accurate. The title promises scalability along with accuracy. Human pose estimation is the target task named in the abstract. Homes and clinics could use pose sensing for fall detection and rehab. A compression layer that cuts traffic makes such systems cheaper to run at scale.
