The work speaks to the wireless sensing community.
arxiv-2601-15938:
Julia Müller and a large team report running a giant xenon detector in a 2026 arXiv paper. Future observatories like XLZD will hunt rare processes in liquid xenon. They need large parts tested in cryogenic xenon first. The PANCAKE facility hosts such tests without shielding. The team operated a shallow dual-phase liquid xenon TPC there. Its inner diameter is 133.4 centimeters, and the chamber is shallow in height.

Stable operation is the headline result. A time projection chamber of this width had to hold steady in liquid xenon. Rare-event searches demand that stability at scale. Every component proven now lowers risk for the full observatories. The paper serves the dark matter and neutrino communities that build these giant detectors.
arxiv-2601-16138:
Zainab Alhathloul and Irfan Ahmad sort Arabic texts by the age they came from. Their 2026 preprint notes how Arabic has changed through time. New words came in, old words fell out, and word use shifted. Those shifts mark old texts from new texts in clear ways. Past work oft splits texts to just old and new age groups.

The pair build a sort tool for texts by time age. Word and style cues guide the sort to the right age. A fine sort helps teams tag large text sets by era. It also aids study of how the tongue changed. The work serves search and care of Arabic text hoards.
arxiv-2601-16438:
Ziwei Zhao, Xiaoni Du and Xingbin Qiao build LCD codes from bent Reed Solomon codes. Their 2026 preprint deals with codes that meet their dual in a null way. LCD means the code and its dual share no word but zero. Such codes guard bits and have clean maths form. The base codes are a bent form of the known GRS codes.

From that base, the team builds two new LCD code sets. Each set rests on a choice of point sets in the base. New sets widen the pool of LCD codes teams can pick. Pool breadth helps match code terms to real links. The work is a build note in code theory.
arxiv-2601-16838:
Emily Hunt and a team of seven co-authors launch a web home for space fans and pros. Space work thrives on talk among peers and with the public. Yet big social sites serve that talk less and less well. Their 2026 preprint sets out Astrosky, a free platform built for this crowd. It stands apart from the big ad-driven sites.

Astrosky joins chat, posts, and outreach in one place. It aims to give space folks a calm, apt home. Pros can share work and news there. Fans can learn and ask in the same halls. The team hopes it keeps the field's talk in its own hands.
arxiv-2601-17238:
Rishi Vanukuru and eight co-authors compare two ways to work with far-off partners. One way is mobile video calls. Calls show real places and objects in real time. The other way is augmented reality, which adds digital content to a live view. The team studies joint work in space across both tools.

They note that calls lose much of the feel of shared space. Moving around and pointing at things is harder on a call. The study looks at how people cope with those limits. It also tests what augmented reality adds or fails to add. The findings can guide tools for remote teams. Good design should keep the sense of place strong.
arxiv-2601-17338:
Hiroshi Onuki, Yukihiro Uchida, and Ryo Yoshizumi build modular polynomials with level structures. The classic modular polynomial links two elliptic curves joined by an isogeny. It has wide use in computational number theory. Point counting on curves is one such use. Computing the polynomial itself is a hard task in its own right.

The authors give a geometric construction for the level case. Level structures add data that many modern algorithms need. A clean construction can make those algorithms faster and safer. Curve-based cryptography rests on such tools. So does research on curve families. The work adds a firm base for both.
arxiv-2601-17638:
Nitin Choudhury and three co-authors present FOCA for malware classification. FOCA fuses audio and visual views of malware data. Most fusion methods work in flat Euclidean space. FOCA works in hyperbolic space instead. That curved space fits hierarchical links between the two views well. Cross-attention joins the streams inside that space.

The authors claim FOCA is first to use that structure for this task. Hierarchy is natural in malware families, which branch like trees. A space that matches that shape can sort samples with more care. Security teams face new malware daily. Better classification speeds response and cuts harm. The work adds a new geometry to the defender's toolkit.
arxiv-2601-18438:
Wei Wang and many colleagues build a tool that grades the sound of made-up speech the way a human ear would. Tests by human ears are slow, dear, and hard to scale, yet new speech tools need grades to grow. Most past tools learned from a thin stock of human grades. That thin stock makes them weak when new kinds of speech show up.

Their tool learns from more than one kind of grade at once. It blends set scores with side by side picks, where a judge says which of two clips sounds best. More kinds of truth make the grades more firm across new data sets. A firm auto grade could let labs test new speech tools fast, with less cost and less wait for human ears.
arxiv-2601-18638:
Tingkai Xue and seven colleagues add doubt counts to the smart design of parts that pick which waves may pass. Such parts, used in chips and in light tools, let some tones through and block the rest. Past smart design was fast but blind to its own doubt. In zones with few past facts, its guesses could be far off, and the search would chase a false peak.

Their plan tracks doubt as it designs, and it steers the search away from zones where doubt is high. Physics rules guide the doubt count, so it stays true to how waves act. A search that knows its doubt should land on parts that work in the lab, not just on screen. That gain counts for parts that are dear to make and test.
arxiv-2601-18738:
Yifan Jing, Cosmin Pohoata, and Max Wenqiang Xu study when a sparse set of whole counts must still hold a neat pattern. The set is banned from a graph shape: no group in it may form a full web of a set size in two parts. Sets that shun such webs can still be quite thick by count. The team ask if a thick set of that kind must hold a full solve of a plain sum task.

The task must stay the same when all its counts are shifted by one step. The team show that a thick banned set holds such a solve for each sum task of five or more counts. That is a strong claim: a ban on one shape can't kill all neat sum forms. It ties the maths of graphs to the maths of sums in a fresh way.
arxiv-2601-18938:
Xin Qiao and seven co-authors fill in missing node features in graphs when most data is gone. Graphs store facts as node features, but real graphs often lose many of them. Older methods, built on hidden features or broad spread, give shaky guesses and can pass errors along the graph.

Their method, FSD-CAP, works in two stages to lift the quality of the filled in values. It spreads facts across parts of the graph while staying aware of each node's class. Better fills under extreme sparsity matter wherever graphs are built from patchy records, from social data to molecule sets.
arxiv-2601-19038:
Long Chen and four co-authors speed up mirror descent, a method that bends downhill search around a space's shape. A mirror function encodes the shape and the limits of the space, which keeps steps valid while they converge. Speeded up forms of the method exist, drawn from a system of differential equations.

The team derives their version by splitting the work into a variable part and an operator part. Splitting lets each piece be handled by the tool that fits it best. The result is a faster method with the same kind of guarantees, aimed at large problems where shape and limits matter.
arxiv-2601-19738:
Daniele Lizzio Bosco and three colleagues work on making quantum circuits cheaper to run. Fault-tolerant quantum computers build circuits from Clifford gates plus T gates. The T gates dominate the cost, so cutting their number can decide whether a circuit runs at all. Compiling a circuit into this gate set with few T gates is a central task.

The authors propose pre-synthesis: learning small local edits to a circuit before the main compilation. Local edits that lower the T-count are found by learning, then applied across the circuit. Even modest savings multiply over large computations. The approach sits before standard synthesis in the toolchain. It offers a new lever for the resource problem in fault-tolerant computing.
arxiv-2601-20138:
Richard Csaky scales up next-token prediction for MEG, a method that records magnetic fields from brain activity. His model works in source space, on signals mapped to locations in the brain. It is trained on a corpus of over five hundred hours and thousands of sessions, drawn from the three largest MEG datasets.

A modified vector quantizer turns the many channels of MEG into a flat stream of tokens. A Qwen2-based model then learns to predict the next token across long contexts and across scanners. Large models of brain signals could support tools that read neural activity and compare recordings between labs.
arxiv-2601-20238:
Gavin Wang and four colleagues study how the release of ChatGPT changed political talk on Reddit's largest political forum. They examine ideological and emotional patterns across millions of comments. Their analysis shows that ideological polarization grew after the release: liberal-leaning authors posted still more liberal comments, and conservative-leaning authors posted still more conservative ones.

The title states the paired finding: models polarize users ideologically but moderate them affectively, in tone. That split matters for how platforms judge AI's effect on public debate. A tool can calm the mood of a thread while quietly pushing its sides further apart.
arxiv-2601-20338:
Nam V. Tran builds a neural network method for solving generalized monotone inclusion problems, a broad class in optimization and equilibrium theory. The method rests on a forward-backward splitting dynamical framework. It is designed so that solutions are reached within a predefined time, a property called predefined-time stability.

The problems are set in Hilbert spaces, with one maximal set-valued operator and one single-valued mapping. Guarantees of arrival by a chosen time are rare and valuable in control, where deadlines are real. The paper adds applications that show where such timed solvers can be used.
arxiv-2601-20438:
Ailsa Keating, Ivan Smith, and Michael Wemyss survey examples where symplectic monodromy splits off the symplectic mapping class group. Symplectic geometry studies spaces with a structure that tracks area, and monodromy describes how that structure twists around a family of spaces. In some cases the twist separates cleanly from the rest of the mapping class group.

The authors use the examples to display different techniques and inputs for such arguments. Along the way they state several open questions and conjectures. A survey of this kind gives researchers a map of a subtle corner of geometry, and of where its proofs still run out.
arxiv-2601-20538:
Ling Tang and six colleagues study how to interpret extreme events that emerge in systems of interacting language model agents. Such multi-agent systems can simulate complex human-like behavior. Their interactions sometimes produce extreme events whose origins stay hidden inside the black box of emergence.

Interpreting those events is critical for system safety, the authors argue. If a simulation of markets or crowds suddenly tips into a crash or a panic, operators need to know which interactions drove it. Their work aims at tracing emergence back to causes that can be checked and governed.
arxiv-2601-20738:
Dawit Kiros Redie, Reza Arablouei, and Stefan Werner work on making federated learning cheaper to run. Their 2026 paper concerns training shared across many devices. Each device trains locally and sends updates, not raw data. To cut traffic, updates are compressed. Error feedback stores what compression dropped and adds it back later.

The catch appears when data differ across devices, the non-IID case. The stored error can decay too slowly. That leaves a gradient mismatch and stalls progress in the early rounds. The authors propose SA-PEF, which joins step-ahead correction with partial error feedback. The method aims to keep early training moving despite compression. It speaks to teams training models across split data sources that do not match.
arxiv-2601-20838:
Brian Christian and six co-authors show that the judges of AI carry biases from their own upbringing. Their 2026 paper studies reward models, the scorers at the heart of AI alignment. Reward models are central to aligning large language models with human values. Yet they have received less attention than the models they guide. A reward model starts life as a pretrained language model. It therefore inherits representations that shape its behavior.

The authors ask how deep that inheritance runs. Values absorbed during pretraining may tilt what the reward model favors. That tilt then steers every model trained under its scores. The paper examines the nature and extent of this influence. Its findings matter for anyone who treats reward models as neutral judges. They begin biased, and the study measures the bias.
arxiv-2601-21038:
Barbara Kaltenbacher proves that solutions of a slow diffusion equation settle to a steady state. Her 2026 paper studies a nonlinear subdiffusion equation with two counteracting terms. Subdiffusion spreads more slowly than normal diffusion. The equation pairs that slow spread with a spatial operator and two rival effects. One term pushes growth; the other pulls it back. A source term completes the balance.

The result gives decay rates to equilibrium as time grows. Rates matter: they tell how fast a system forgets its start. The proof handles the fractional time derivative that makes subdiffusion hard. Such equations model transport in crowded, sticky media. Knowing the pull toward equilibrium helps predict long-run behavior. The paper is a rigorous analysis aimed at specialists in partial differential equations.
arxiv-2601-21138:
Noah Dasanaike builds a record linkage method that needs no labeled training data. The 2026 paper presents EnsembleLink. Record linkage matches records that refer to the same entity across datasets. It is essential to empirical social science. Yet it remains methodologically underdeveloped. Researchers often treat it as a preprocessing step. They apply ad hoc rules and never quantify the uncertainty that linkage errors add downstream.

Existing methods force a bad choice. They either achieve low accuracy or demand substantial labeled training data. An ensemble approach can sidestep that trade-off. Combining several weak linkers can yield a strong one. EnsembleLink aims for accuracy without the labeling burden. Cleaner linkage means cleaner conclusions in studies that merge records. The paper upgrades a quiet but vital step of data work.
arxiv-2601-21238:
Xuewen Liu, Zhikai Li, Jing Zhang, Mengjuan Chen, and Qingyi Gu study how to shrink a class of image-making models without ruining them. These models build pictures step by step, much like language models build text. Shrinking a model by using fewer bits per number cuts its size and speeds it up.

That trick is well tested on other networks but barely tried here. The authors show that standard shrinking methods do not carry over well to this model type. Their method adapts the process to how these models actually generate images. The goal is smaller, faster models that still produce output of the same quality.
arxiv-2601-21338:
Ji-Xuan He and five co-authors improve the sharpening of hyperspectral images. These images record many narrow color bands, which reveal material details normal photos miss. Raising the spatial detail while keeping the colors true is the core challenge.

Recent methods lean on spatial patterns and often neglect how bands relate to each other. That neglect can cause false wiggles in the spectra and results that break physics. Their plug-in module refines the spectra inside existing models. Any current method can adopt it without a rebuild. Truer spectra matter for farming, geology, and environmental checks from aircraft and satellites.
arxiv-2601-21538:
Ruifeng Zheng and Yanqing Xu study how primordial black holes could form from the early universe's inflation. Such holes need very large density bumps to collapse under their own gravity. Those same bumps would also stir gravitational waves that detectors might hear.

The authors join two known inflation models with a local coupling of a special shape. The coupling briefly breaks the slow roll that keeps inflation smooth. That break is what lets the bumps grow large enough. The study links black hole births to a wave signal, giving observers a paired prediction to test.
arxiv-2601-21638:
Mingji Deng, Cuihua Du, Jian Zhang, HaoYang Liu, and ZhongCheng Li build a lighter model of the Milky Way that explains its warped disk. Warps, where the disk bends like a hat brim, can grow out of galaxy mergers. Recent work also shows the galaxy's rotation curve dropping off in a way heavier models do not predict.

The authors construct a merger model based on the known Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus event. That ancient merger is a prime suspect for stirring our galaxy. A low-mass model that matches both the warp and the rotation curve would revise estimates of the galaxy's dark matter. It also sharpens the story of how the Milky Way was assembled.
arxiv-2601-21838:
Weizhou Cai and co-authors report progress on protecting quantum information with bosonic codes. Quantum error correction is the foundation of any future fault-tolerant quantum computer. Yet corrected logical qubits so far live only about twice as long as their best physical parts, a disappointingly small gain.

The team argues that the main barrier is not the coherence of the cavities that hold the information. Instead, errors introduced by the ancilla, a helper system used during operations, do the damage. Their 2026 preprint presents error-detectable universal control aimed at high-gain bosonic correction. If operational errors can be caught and curbed, bosonic codes could finally deliver the large gains their theory has long promised.
arxiv-2601-22038:
Vitalii Aksenov, Martin Eigel, and Mathias Oster speed up sums that deal with chance curves. Many tasks in stats can be cast as fixed-point sums. You run the same step again and again till the result stops moving. One key use is to find the mean of a set of chance curves, in a sense set by the Wasserstein gap.

Plain runs of such steps can be slow. The team tries a speed-up trick called Anderson mixing. They test it in the space of bell-shaped curves, where gaps and means have neat closed forms. Fast solvers of this kind help in Bayes work and in training AI models. In both, these sums run deep in the loop, and their cost is paid on each run.
arxiv-2601-22238:
Erik Aver and a large team present a fresh value for how much helium the Big Bang left behind. Their 2026 preprint is part four of a project built on the Large Binocular Telescope. The team took clean new data from a set of gas clouds poor in heavy elements.

All clouds were watched and worked through in the same way. The team also updated key steps, such as the glow rates used for helium. A firm early value tests the standard story of the cosmos. It also guides work on how the first elements formed. The clouds act as near time capsules.
arxiv-2601-22438:
Shangshu Qian and four co-authors make model serving bounce back fast when hardware fails. Their 2026 preprint, KevlarFlow, notes that big clusters fail often, and one fault can down a whole service. Old recovery can take ten minutes, as gear restarts and huge weights reload.

KevlarFlow aims to cut that dead time to a small part of the old span. Fast recovery keeps chat and search tools live for users. It also saves the vast cost of idle chips. The work is a shield for the serving layer. It treats faults as routine, not rare.
arxiv-2601-22538:
Yannis Montreuil and four co-authors study when a forecaster should hand a call to a human expert as conditions drift. Their 2026 preprint works on non-stationary time series, where the pattern shifts over time. Feedback is partial: the router sees only the picked expert's call, and the pool of experts changes.

They model signed expert errors with a switching state-space model. That model tracks who is hot as regimes change. Smart hand-offs can lift accuracy while saving expert time. The work fits streams like energy, health, and finance. That saving can be large at scale.
arxiv-2601-22638:
Palash Goyal and a team built ScholarPeer, a multi-agent system that reviews papers with context, not in a vacuum. Auto review has grown from sorting text to writing structured feedback. Their 2026 preprint notes that top systems still give surface notes, and miss novelty and deep method flaws.

ScholarPeer checks a paper against its field, so praise and blame rest on what is truly new. Deeper reviews could ease the load on human referees. They must still be watched for error and bias. The work aims at review that reads like a peer.
arxiv-2601-22738:
Han Wang and four co-authors built StreamSense, a live monitor that reads social cues in streams and calls in a big model only when needed. Live platforms must react to social signals in real time, from partial video, text, and audio that arrive out of sync. Their 2026 preprint pairs a light streaming encoder with selective routing.

Hard cases go to a vision-language expert; easy ones stay cheap. That split keeps the watch both fast and sharp. The work serves safety and community teams on live platforms. It spends big-model effort where it counts.
arxiv-2601-23138:
Duván Cardona, William Obeng-Denteh, and Frederick Opoku study hyperbolic equations with complex characteristics on Fourier Lebesgue spaces. These spaces measure functions through their frequency content, with flexible integrability. Well-posedness asks whether solutions exist, are unique, and depend steadily on the data.

Their harmonic analysis approach first bounds Fourier integral operators with complex phase on several function spaces. Those bounds then carry over to the differential equations. Such results support models of wave motion in settings beyond the classical theory. Besov and Triebel-Lizorkin spaces are included alongside Fourier Lebesgue spaces, widening the result's reach in harmonic analysis.
arxiv-2603-01638:
Virtual reality apps gather fine details on body motion and biometrics, yet few users read the privacy terms. Vincent Freiberger, Moritz Dresch, Florian Alt, and colleagues test AI helpers that explain those terms in this 2026 study. The helper sits inside a VR app store, right where users pick which apps to install.

Users meet the helper in two forms: a text chat box and a speaking avatar in the scene. In a small study, each person browsed work apps with no help and with each helper form. Early findings suggest both forms help users choose with more care than no help at all. The work probes how the form of an explanation shapes informed consent at the moment of choice.
arxiv-2603-02238:
Andy Yang, Pascal Bergsträßer, Georg Zetzsche, and colleagues settle an open question about transformers in this 2026 paper. A model shows length generalization if it handles inputs of any length after finite training. For trust, one needs a bound past which success is guaranteed. The authors ask whether such bounds can be computed for a language class tied to transformers.

For the full class, already at two layers, no computable bound exists. That negative answer covers transformers themselves. For a positive fragment of the class, a bound can be computed. That fragment matches fixed-precision transformers, models with limited numeric detail. Its length cost grows exponentially, and the authors prove that growth cannot be improved in general.
arxiv-2603-02338:
Lorenzo Gotta, Filiberto Ares, and Sara Murciano study symmetry breaking in fragmented quantum systems in this 2026 paper. Entanglement asymmetry measures how much a quantum state breaks a symmetry. They focus on uneven charges, like dipole and higher multipole moments. Typical asymmetry stays below a fixed share of its maximum, they show.

Random matrix product states confirm that bound across several settings. Bond size in those states plays a role much like time in random circuits. That match hints at a universal pattern for charge asymmetry in local systems. Multipole charges also arise when dynamics split into countless disconnected sectors, called fragmentation. The authors extend asymmetry to that fragmented case and bound it. There it can grow with system size, offering a probe of quantum fragmentation.
arxiv-2603-02638:
Wilfried Wiedner, Lukas Eller, Mariam Mussbah, and colleagues release a city-scale mobile network data set in this 2026 paper. Machine learning for network planning is starved of large, real-world measurements. Their Vienna data set records 4G and 5G signals across the whole city. Passive scanner readings pair with active handset logs for network-side and user-side views.

Measurements span varied urban and suburban settings, aligned by time and place. For a subset of base stations, inferred locations, sector directions, and antenna heights are included. Detailed building and terrain models support geometry-aware learning and ray-tracing calibration. Data are organized into scanner, handset, cell information, and city-model parts. Documented joins between parts ease practical reuse. Reproducible benchmarking for coverage and propagation modeling is the goal.
arxiv-2603-03238:
Mikhail Osipov tests four ways to tidy the hidden space of a learned simulator, and most of them backfire. His 2026 paper studies reduced models built on an autoencoder, which squeezes a system's state so a small model can step it forward. The test case is a spread-and-react equation, with the hidden state stepped by a learned rate law.

Three smoothing penalties, applied while the squeezer trains, often made later training harder. Long forecasts suffered most, even when local smoothness scores improved. The fourth approach, forcing the decoder's first layer into a well-shaped set, steadily helped both diagnostics and forecasts. Osipov argues that a mismatch between hidden shape and dynamics costs more than rough decoding does.
arxiv-2603-03338:
Severin Field, Raymond Douglas, and David Krueger interview leading artificial intelligence researchers about automating research itself. Many expect such automation to open a feedback loop, sometimes called an intelligence explosion, where systems improve themselves ever faster. In late summer 2025 the authors interviewed twenty-five researchers from frontier labs and top universities to record how the people closest to the work see that prospect.

Twenty of the twenty-five named automating research among the most severe and urgent risks, and most expected capable systems to be kept inside companies or governments, out of public view. Lab and academic researchers split on how explosive growth could get, and on timelines and governance. Power concentration and progress accelerating behind closed doors were the most common worries. Nearly everyone favored transparency measures, while set red lines divided the group.
arxiv-2603-03438:
Rajath Radhakrishnan and a colleague study how exotic symmetries act on local operators in quantum field theory. Non-invertible symmetries extend the usual symmetry idea: applying them cannot always be undone. Most known cases in three and four spacetime dimensions still act in a usual, reversible way on local operators, with coset symmetries the known exception. Their 2026 paper settles the question for a general finite non-invertible symmetry in four dimensions.

They prove that a non-invertible symmetry with no topological line operators must act in a reversible way on local operators. More broadly, any such symmetry's action splits into a reversible part composed with a gauging interface. That split then drives an anomaly study. The authors find a necessary condition for the symmetry to be anomaly-free. They show that anomaly-free cases lacking line operators are never non-invertible at their core.
arxiv-2603-03838:
Erik Larsson and others introduce Climate Downscaling with Stochastic Interpolants, or CDSI, a data-driven method for turning coarse global climate output into fine local projections. Global climate projections come from Earth System Models, which are costly to run and so work at coarse spatial resolution. Regional Climate Models refine them for areas of interest, but they are expensive too and limit how many runs can be done at once.

The authors build the method on stochastic interpolants, recent chance-based machine learning tools. They show that CDSI converts coarse model output into accurate detailed regional forecasts at a fraction of the cost of standard regional models. Extensive checking produces accurate regional ensembles, which sharpens uncertainty estimates and widens access to detailed climate information for regional impact work.

Johann Joachim Becher's Physica Subterranea appears here in Georg Ernst Stahl's 1738 edition. Becher, a German physician and adviser on trade, wrote on what lies beneath the earth. Stahl, who edited and praised the work, built his own theory of burning on Becher's ideas.

cia-0000135838: Central American Situation, dated 4 September 1952, is a declassified CIA paper surveying the region as a whole. The early 1950s were tense years in Central America, with reform governments and their opponents drawing close attention from Washington. The catalog title is broad and names no single country or crisis, so the paper is best described as a regional situation report of its date. It was written two years before the 1954 Guatemala coup reshaped the region's politics, and it now reads as a baseline from before that break.
cia-0000136138: The CIA cable of 2 April 1954 is about destroying rail targets, cutting the lines that moved the government's troops and goods, and it survives in declassified form. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136338: Proceed with the present plan, LINCOLN advises in this late June 1954 cable, while admitting it is not optimistic about forthcoming peace talks. The station has no confidence in the enemy junta's sincerity and notes 6,000 tons of arms in enemy hands. Circumstances permitting, it would push back the Beta H-hour to ensure a vessel arrives to serve as floating artillery and communications center, with signal plans prepared for both vessels.
cia-0000136638: Dated 2 February 1961, this Spanish-language document comes from the declassified records of Brigade 2506. The brigade's own paperwork was kept in Spanish, the language of its members. That winter the force was training for the landing in Cuba. The catalog names no subject for this item. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, a dated piece of the exile archive.
cia-0000136738: Another Spanish text in the 2506 Brigade papers carries an estimated date of 1 January 1961, the estimate noted in the catalog. The brigade was then in winter training for Cuba under CIA direction. The record names no subject for this item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, one of the many brigade documents the reviewers placed at the opening of 1961.
cia-0000136938: Eight fighter planes at about 25,000 dollars each are on offer in this April 1954 cable to LINCOLN, signed under Frank Wisner. Another component has been given official opportunity to purchase them but is not yet certain it will; it may dicker for better terms. If the development becomes current talk, the moment is ripe for CALLIGERIS to approach the seller offering part of the purchase price for two planes, made available on request for his use. A rental deal would make even better cover.
cia-0000139038: The Greek junta wants Andreas Papandreou out of politics. This assessment concludes he probably will not be executed, though. Government members gave assurances on prisoners. Andreas would not be harmed, they said. None of the four main ASPIDA defendants would be executed. The defense minister pledged Andreas would not be executed even if sentenced to death. The regime may still deport him regardless of the trial. The interior minister asked the embassy about his American citizenship. Note: the file dates from after the April 1967 coup, not January 1966 as cataloged.
cia-0000141138: Personnel strength in the Guatemala station is listed in this September 1960 cable. Names and job titles appear throughout. The station was then supporting the coming Cuba operation. The surviving excerpt shows two entries. Richard Blehar is a United States Air Force operations officer. Edward Sirota is an Air Force pilot. Other names in the roster fall outside this sample. Strength reports were the agency's staffing audits. This one preserves the human roster behind a pivotal station.
cia-03153738: May 7, 1959: this bulletin briefed the leadership. The analysts' global roundup for decision-makers. The Cold War's spring memo. Such papers rarely see the light of day. This declassified bulletin is kept. The text is preserved.
cia-06040638: THE PROSPECTS FOR THE GOVERNMENT OF THE REPUBLIC OF CHINA, a CIA assessment. The Taiwan outlook. This file preserves that declassified paper. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The paper lived through the years and remains here.
cia-06628538: ALLEGED RIFT AMONG ARGENTINE JUNTA MEMBERS, 1978/01/27, a CIA document. The junta split. The files keep it safe. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
cia-06709338: A Peruvian incident drew the agency's eye here. The file records what happened. The Andean file, declassified. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. This file preserves that CIA paper. The library keeps the document safe. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
cia-06752238: THE SITUATION IN VIETNAM - 27 DECEMBER 1967, a CIA assessment. The December briefing. This file preserves that declassified paper. Future scholars will discover it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
cymbeline-pg1538: Exile, slander, and a princess hiding in boy's clothes fill this edition of Shakespeare's late romance. Imogen suffers every trial with grace while villains scheme and long-lost kin draw near. A joyful tangle of reunions crowns the most elaborate happy ending he ever wrote.
dick-celestial-scenery-1838:
Thomas Dick was a Scots writer who made star science plain to all. His Celestial Scenery came out in 1838 and sold in huge runs. The full title shows the wonders of the planets, one by one. Dick held that all those worlds teem with life.

He walks the reader past the Moon, the planets, and the fixed stars. Great scale and bright scenes fill his text, with faith mixed in. Dick thought vast worlds must serve vast hosts of beings. The book put the claim of lived-in worlds in front of a mass crowd.
dickens-oliver-twist-1838:
Charles Dickens published Oliver Twist in 1838, a novel of the workhouse and London crime. The book attacked the New Poor Law and its cruel parish workhouse regime. Dickens knew London's slums well and wrote with anger and close knowledge of them.

Oliver, a workhouse orphan, asks for more food and is sold off in disgrace. He falls in with Fagin's gang of child thieves in the London underworld. Kind Mr. Brownlow and Rose Maylie fight to save him from that dark life. Bill Sikes and Nancy give the crime plot its terror and its pathos. The tale mixes outrage at cruelty with hope for one child's rescue.
doe-osti-3684124-scoping-study-report-fo: IR-26LL01020638 got scoping-reported, and this DOE study covers the scoping report. The pages detail the scoping findings. The researchers get their data. The report was study. The data were researcher. The IR-26LL01020638 were report. The scoping were study.
dupotet-introduction-animal-magnetism-18:
Baron Jules Dupotet de Sennevoy led the French school of animal magnetism for decades. His Introduction to the Study of Animal Magnetism reached English readers in 1838. The translation systematizes magnetic practice as the French school taught it. Passes, rapport, and the handling of subjects receive careful rules.

An appendix adds reports from British practitioners who tried his methods. The book thus bridges the French and English mesmeric movements in one volume. Dupotet writes with the authority of a master of the art. His Paris salon drew students from across Europe. English mesmerists treated the work as a handbook. It shows the practice at its most formal.
eriugena-de-divisione-naturae-1838:
Johannes Scottus Eriugena, an Irish scholar at the court of Charles the Bald, wrote the Periphyseon, On the Division of Nature, in the ninth century. It is the first great system of thought in the Latin Middle Ages. The text here is the Latin edition of C. B. Schlüter, from 1838, with the thirteen hymns of Eriugena to his king.

Five books sort all things into nature that creates and is not created, nature created and creating, nature created, and nature that neither creates nor is created. God and the world fold into one vast circle of going out and coming back. No English version in the public domain exists. The book stood alone for centuries in its daring.
europmc-pmc10227038:
Abanades and colleagues present ImmuneBuilder, deep learning models that predict the structures of immune proteins, in a 2023 paper. Antibodies and T cell receptors guard the body by binding to specific targets. Knowing their shape is key to grasping that binding. Shape also guides the design of new immune-based drugs.

The models were trained to predict shapes for antibodies and related proteins quickly. The team tested accuracy against known structures. Fast shape prediction helps researchers screen drug candidates on a computer. That saves costly lab work. The models are free for other labs to use and build on.
europmc-pmc10514338:
Sun and co-authors reviewed in 2023 how a form of cell death could be turned into treatment. The death is ferroptosis, which needs iron and fails when fat damage in cells runs unchecked. Proof now ties it to cancer, brain decline, organ injury, and infection. Its control web is still only partly mapped.

Drugs can push this death or hold it back, Sun reports. Pushers may kill cancer cells that shrug off other drugs. Blockers may shield organs after injury or a cut in blood flow. The review sorts the chemical tools built so far for each aim. It also flags the gaps that block use in patients, from dose to safety.
europmc-pmc10551038:
Liu and co-authors reviewed autophagy in 2023, the cell's self-eating system, and its part in cell death. Cells use autophagy to break down and recycle worn proteins and parts. That upkeep guards cell health in normal times. Too much of it, or a broken flow, can tip a cell into death.

The review sorts six death modes that hinge on this system. Liu gives close study to two: excess eating of the cell's protein factory, and eating of power units that feeds ferroptosis. Those two show how fuel shifts drive the fatal turn. Boosting the system may treat some diseases, the authors note. Shifts between death modes may serve cancer care in new ways.
europmc-pmc10561438:
Chehelgerdi and a large team reviewed nanotechnology for targeted cancer care in 2023. Tiny carriers can ferry drugs straight to tumour cells. Fresh work in protein design and materials has spawned new ways to aim them. Hope runs high among patients and labs alike.

Yet the path to clinics is steep, Chehelgerdi reports. Many carriers won approval for human trials, but only a few gained full clearance for use. The review lists the cleared products and the hurdles each one cleared. Hurdles span body safety, factory scale-up, and weak gains in real patients. The authors back more work to close the lab-to-clinic gap.
europmc-pmc10628838:
Belloy and co-authors ran a gene study in 2023 on APOE and Alzheimer disease risk. APOE is a gene that comes in forms which raise or lower the risk of this memory disease. The best-known risk form is called epsilon 4. Past work hints that its effect is not the same in each group of people.

The study tests the gene's links to risk across age bands and sex. It also splits people by race and ethnicity, and by global population ancestry. Those splits matter, since the gene's forms vary in frequency and force across ancestries. Belloy aims to show where the risk holds firm and where it shifts. Such maps can guide fair risk checks for each group.
europmc-pmc10689838:
Koh and co-authors reviewed CD8 T cell subsets in 2023, a branch of killer immune cells. These cells hunt infected or cancerous cells and kill them. After they meet a target, plain CD8 cells gain skills to strike. The classic view held one main killer subset.

Fresh proof splits the killers into distinct subsets, Koh reports. Each subset has its own mix of attack signals and toxic parcels. Each also plays a distinct part in infection, cancer, and other diseases. That split may explain why some immune drugs help one patient and miss the next. Drugs tuned to one subset could sharpen care, the authors argue. The review maps each subset and its known jobs.
europmc-pmc11023938:
Lu and colleagues show that pain-sensing nerves help wounds heal by steering immune cells in this 2024 study. Tissue healing depends heavily on the immune system, and healing falters in diabetes and old age. Nociceptors are sensory nerve cells that detect harm. Their role in repair after sudden injury was unclear.

Removing a key pain nerve channel in mice impaired skin wound repair and muscle regrowth, the team found. Nerve endings grew into the injured tissue and released a signal called CGRP. That signal acted on neutrophils and macrophages, two immune cell types, to cut recruitment and speed cell clean-up. It pushed macrophages toward a repair form. Giving an engineered form of the signal sped healing in mice lacking the nerves and in diabetic mice.
europmc-pmc11115438:
Cossarizza and a very large panel present the third edition of flow cytometry guidelines in this 2021 document. Flow cytometry runs cells past lasers to read their traits one by one, and cell sorting then separates chosen cells. It is a core method in immunology, the study of the immune system. The guidelines state what to consider when planning such experiments.

Sections describe the traits and functional tests for all major human and mouse immune cell subsets. Tables flag where human and mouse cells differ, a common source of error. Clinical samples get full treatment, with examples from autoimmune diseases, cancers, and acute and chronic infections. A section on tips, tricks, and pitfalls collects practical warnings. All parts were written and peer-reviewed by leading experts, the authors note.
europmc-pmc11223838:
Letunic and Bork present version 6 of a web tool for drawing and annotating family trees of species in this 2024 paper. Phylogenetic trees show how species relate through evolution. The Interactive Tree Of Life, or iTOL, is a free online tool to manage, display, and annotate such trees. It is open to everyone.

Version 6 brings a modernised, fully rewritten interface, the authors report. A new dataset type shows coloured and labelled ranges along branches. Templates can now assign notes to many nodes at once using text matching, including full pattern expressions. Node metadata gained new display and export options and can be edited in bulk. Labels support several font styles at once with precise placement. Automatic taxonomy assignment, which names nodes from a reference, was extended.
europmc-pmc11701638:
Dyer and a very large team present Ensembl 2025, the annual update of a genome data platform, in this paper. Ensembl integrates public genomics data from across the tree of life, focusing on species tied to human health, agriculture, and biodiversity. Expansion continued this year, with more than 4,800 eukaryotic and over 31,300 prokaryotic genomes on offer.

The new Ensembl site, still in beta, now holds over 2,700 eukaryotic genome assemblies. It provides views of genomes, genes, transcripts, variation, and homology, meaning comparisons of genes across species. It will replace the current rapid release site as a step toward a single integrated site. Regulatory annotation improved for human, mouse, and agricultural species. The Variant Effect Predictor tool, which forecasts what a DNA change does, was expanded. Training and documentation programmes accompany the release.
europmc-pmc12535838:
GBD 2023 Causes of Death Collaborators catalogued causes of death worldwide in 2025. Timely death data by age, sex, and place shape health policy. The analysis spans 204 countries and territories. It also covers 660 subnational locations from 1990 to 2023.

Estimates cover 292 causes of death for each year. A modeling ensemble produced most cause-specific death rates. Years of life lost were computed from death counts per cause. New measures add the chance of dying before age 70. GBD 2023 Causes of Death Collaborators also report mean age at death by cause. Most death rates came from a model ensemble the team calls CODEm.
europmc-pmc1273638:
Monticelli and colleagues profiled microRNAs across mouse blood cells in 2005. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that dial down gene output. Their patterns in the blood-forming system were unmapped. The study gives the first systematic profile for those cells.

Profiles differed sharply between blood cell types. Beyond guiding which lineage a cell joins, patterns marked cell identity. The authors suggest microRNAs help lock in differentiation states. Monticelli supplies a baseline atlas for blood development studies. Later work can compare disease states against this map. It appeared in Genome Biology in 2005. Mature microRNAs run just 19 to 22 letters long and recur across many species.
europmc-pmc1440938:
Garlic mustard, a plant from Europe, now spreads through North American woods. Stinson and co-authors asked in 2006 how it beats local trees. They found the invader leaks fungus-fighting compounds into the soil. Those compounds break the bond between young trees and root fungi that help them feed.

Such fungi, called arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, trade soil nutrients for plant sugars. With the bond cut, native seedlings grew poorly. Stinson argues this hidden attack may explain why garlic mustard thrives in calm, undisturbed woods. The study shows an invader can harm locals without touching them, by cutting the links they rely on.
europmc-pmc1464138:
Naming a small molecule from its mass alone is harder than it sounds. Kind and Fiehn made that point in 2006 for metabolomics, the study of all small molecules in a sample. Even with mass errors under one part per million, many formulas fit a single reading at higher masses.

The pair showed with math that a second clue fixes the problem. The pattern of isotopes, heavier forms of the same atoms, rules out over 95 percent of false formulas. Kind compared eight chemical databases for the task. Their scripts, shared free online, can shrink thousands of candidate formulas to a short list.
europmc-pmc1764438:
Algorithms can learn gene regulation from expression data, but genome-scale proof was missing. Faith and co-authors supplied it in 2007 for E. coli, using 445 expression arrays and 3,216 known regulatory links. They tested four algorithm classes and added their own, CLR.

CLR beat the next best method by 36 percent in average precision. At a setting catching 60 percent of true links, it proposed 1,079 interactions, 741 of them novel. Lab tests confirmed 21 new links for three regulators. One found link ties iron transport to central metabolism, confirmed by gene measurements. Faith offers the data set as a benchmark for the field.
europmc-pmc1887538:
Swindell, Huebner and Weber profiled in 2007 how a plant's heat shock system answers many stresses besides heat. In Arabidopsis, the heat response runs through four families of heat shock proteins and a set of 21 known transcription factors. Those same proteins also react to other hardships, but the overlap map was missing.

The team measured gene activity for all those factors and proteins across ten treatments: heat, cold, salt, drought, osmotic stress, DNA damage, ultraviolet light, oxidative stress, wounding, and infection. Samples covered both shoots and roots. Every treatment touched the heat pathways to some degree, showing wide cross-talk. Heat, cold, salt, and osmotic stress switched the system on most strongly. Other stresses gave narrower replies that varied by protein family and tissue. The heat network doubles as a general stress hub.
europmc-pmc1929138:
Herschkowitz, Perou and co-authors compared in 2007 the gene activity patterns of mouse mammary tumors with human breast cancers. Human breast tumors fall into at least three major subtypes with different outcomes, plus a normal-like group. Mouse models are used to study and test treatments for these subtypes, but only if they truly match.

The team profiled tumors from thirteen mouse models on microarrays and set them beside human tumor data. Many defining traits of the human subtypes were conserved in the mouse models. The hormone receptor negative subtypes, one marked by high HER2 levels and one resembling basal cells, had mouse counterparts. So did the receptor positive luminal subtype, which splits into better and worse outcome groups. The match validates specific mouse models for specific human diseases, rather than breast cancer in general.
europmc-pmc2022638:
Roberts and co-workers studied in 2007 whether living near farm pesticide spraying during pregnancy links to autism. They identified 465 children with autism spectrum disorders born in 1996 to 1998 in California's Central Valley. Controls were 6,975 healthy term infants matched on timing. Official spray records and land maps showed how close mothers lived to applications during pregnancy.

Out of 249 hypotheses tested, four survived strict checks against false positives. All involved organochlorine pesticides, mainly dicofol and endosulfan, sprayed during weeks one to eight of pregnancy. That is when the central nervous system first forms. Mothers within 500 metres of the heaviest spraying had an odds ratio of 6.1, and risk rose with amount sprayed. The authors call for further study.
europmc-pmc2125538: A medical paper on Spirochaeta morsus muris, the cause of rat-bite fever, second paper. The rat-bite germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128338: Part of a streptococcus culture went soft in this study, losing its power to burst red blood cells. The researchers tracked the fading hemolysis. The weakened strain's story, recorded. The article preserves that bacteriology research.
europmc-pmc2128538: A medical paper on fat metabolism in nephritis. The kidney's fat. This article preserves that nephrology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2130938: A medical paper on microbic virulence and host susceptibility in paratyphoid infection. The germ's strength again. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131138: A medical paper on normal and pathological fragmentation of red blood cells. The broken cells. This article preserves that hematology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131438: A medical paper on effect of formalin on the virus of vesicular stomatitis of horses. The pickled virus. This article preserves that virology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2131638: A medical paper with studies of tissue maintenance, persisting bloodlessness after functional changes. The bloodless tissue again. This article preserves that physiology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2134938:
Miska and a large team deleted most microRNA genes in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans in 2007 to test their importance. MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that repress gene expression after copying. The team created deletions in 87 microRNA genes. Together with earlier mutants, that covered 95 genes, or 83 percent of known worm microRNAs. Each mutant was checked for survival and visible development defects.

The majority of microRNAs proved individually non-essential for viability or development. Most deletions caused no grossly abnormal traits at all. That pattern fits the idea of redundancy, where microRNAs or their pathways back each other up. Losing one is then buffered by others. The study is the first comprehensive genetic analysis of microRNA function in any organism. The mutant set forms a permanent resource for systematic study.
europmc-pmc2140338: A biology paper on the effect of various acids on the digestion of proteins by pepsin. The acidic digestion. This article preserves that biochemistry. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2140638: A biology paper on hydrogen ion concentrations within the alimentary tract of insects. The bugs' gut acid. This article preserves that entomology. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
europmc-pmc2180238: A medical paper on the effect of pulmonary congestion on the ventilation of the lungs. The congested breath. This article preserves that pulmonology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2254638:
Hoogewijs and co-workers validated reference genes in 2008 for gene expression studies of antioxidant sod genes in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Accurate measurement needs normalisation against genes whose expression stays constant. No validated set existed for this worm, a key model for insulin signalling, lifespan and stress research. The team tested twelve candidate reference genes by quantitative PCR across wild-type worms, three insulin-pathway mutants, dormant dauer larvae and third-stage larvae.

Three genes, pmp-3, Y45F10D.4 and cdc-42, showed the most stable expression and were used for normalisation. With them, sod-1 and sod-3 levels differed significantly in daf-2 mutants versus normal worms. In dauer larvae, four sod genes differed from third-stage larvae. The authors stress that stable reference genes are essential for reliable quantification, and that their method transfers to other worm studies.
europmc-pmc2323238:
Tomancak and colleagues mapped gene activity across fruit fly embryos in this 2007 atlas study. Drosophila melanogaster is the fruit fly used in much genetics research. Knowing where and when each gene is switched on helps explain how an embryo builds tissues.

The team documented activity patterns for 6,003 genes, which is 44% of the 13,659 protein-coding genes in the fly genome. They used a staining method that shows gene activity in place, inside the whole embryo. About 40% of the genes they recorded were active only in certain tissues, not throughout the body. The rest were active more broadly. The atlas gave researchers a shared reference for comparing embryo development across genes.
europmc-pmc2446438:
Horvath and Dong gave gene network analysis a geometric reading in 2008. Coexpression networks link genes whose activity rises and falls together across samples. Biologists borrowed the network language but used only a thin slice of it, while statisticians analysing the same data spoke a different dialect.

The authors built a rough dictionary between the two fields. The bridge is geometry: correlations between genes behave like angles between arrows, so network ideas such as connectivity get precise visual meanings. They showed when a network's link matrix splits neatly into per-gene contributions, a property they call approximate factorizability. Hub genes, the most connected ones, can then be read against sample traits, and a gene's connectivity inside its module doubles as a fuzzy membership score. Examples came from human, mouse, and yeast data sets.
europmc-pmc2447538:
Mostafavi and colleagues built a gene function predictor fast enough to run live in 2008. Most genes still have no known job, and computer methods guess jobs by merging many data sets linking genes that work together. The most accurate methods took so long that their predictions sat in ageing static databases.

Their algorithm, GeneMANIA, blends several association networks with a fast method derived from ridge regression, a standard statistical fit. It then spreads known labels across a process-specific network. On a mouse benchmark and a new yeast benchmark it matched or beat the leading methods. It also shrugged off redundant or irrelevant input data. Each prediction took under ten seconds on average in their tests. A prototype web server let users query it in real time rather than downloading frozen results.
europmc-pmc2529338:
Tao, Fang, Alroy, and Sahagian improved a mouse model of late-stage breast cancer in this 2008 paper. The 4T1 tumour line is valued because it spreads to the same organs as human breast cancer, but tracking it inside living animals was hard. The team engineered two versions of the line to glow with firefly luciferase, a light-producing enzyme, so cameras could follow them.

Tumours grew in two phases, and spread appeared in the second phase, five to six weeks after implantation. A mid-course shrinkage coincided with tissue death and a rush of immune cells, and it vanished in mice lacking adaptive immunity, showing the immune system caused it. Gene analysis linked the spreading behaviour to secreted factors that build blood vessels, reshape tissue, and recruit immune cells. Blood-forming activity in spleen and liver also rose steadily.
europmc-pmc2575538:
Wirapati and colleagues performed in 2008 the largest meta-analysis then done of gene activity signatures in breast cancer, pooling 2,833 tumours. Many published signatures claimed to predict patient outcome, yet they shared almost no genes, which puzzled the field. The team organised genes by three biological processes: cell proliferation, estrogen receptor signalling, and HER2 signalling.

All nine prognostic signatures they tested performed about equally well. Their power came mostly from detecting proliferation, how fast tumour cells divide. The known tumour subtypes mapped cleanly onto the three process modules, from basal-like to HER2-like to the two luminal types. Being estrogen-receptor negative or HER2 positive predicted poor outcome mainly because those tumours proliferate more. Tumour size and lymph node status still added information of their own, beyond the genes.
europmc-pmc2684638:
Sella and co-authors reviewed in 2009 growing proof that natural selection shapes far more of the fruit fly genome than textbooks assumed. The classic view held that most DNA change is neutral drift, with adaptation rare and the functional share of the genome small. New data from comparing variation within fly species and differences between them told a busier story.

Much of the fly genome, they report, sits under purifying selection, selection that weeds out damage, which means it does something that matters. A large share of the differences between species, in coding and noncoding DNA alike, look adaptive rather than accidental. Selection may be so common that neutral changes ride or fall with adaptive neighbors they happen to sit beside. The shift reaches beyond flies: conservation work and genome analysis alike must reckon with a genome largely under selection's hand.
europmc-pmc2774338:
Gregory and co-authors reported in 2009 genomic and epigenetic evidence tying the oxytocin receptor gene, OXTR, to autism. Autism is strongly heritable, yet single-gene causes explain under a tenth of cases. They scanned one hundred nineteen people from families with several autistic members. They hunted for deleted or duplicated DNA stretches. Then they studied how the gene is switched off by methylation, a chemical tag on DNA.

One autistic child carried a deletion removing OXTR, shared with his mother, who had obsessive-compulsive symptoms. His affected sibling lacked the deletion. Instead, that sibling showed abnormal silencing of the gene by methylation. Across separate blood and brain samples, autistic people showed higher methylation at several sites in the gene's control island. Brain tissue from autistic donors also made less OXTR message. Both loss and silencing of this receptor, they argue, can feed into autism.
europmc-pmc2788538:
Shankar and Walsh reviewed in 2009 synaptic dysfunction and the amyloid beta protein in Alzheimer's disease. Loss of synapses, the junctions between brain cells, is an early and constant feature of the disease. Its extent tracks the severity of dementia closely. That link suggests synapse failure drives the early memory loss, and that lasting disruption of plasticity may later kill cells outright.

Wide-ranging research implicates amyloid beta in causing the disease. The harmful forms, on the evidence, are not the stiff fibers of plaques but small soluble clusters that float between cells. These non-fibrillar forms appear to compromise synapses directly. The review gathers the evidence for that case and walks through possible mechanisms of this synaptotoxicity, how the clusters might jam signaling and weaken connections. It ends with points where drugs might intervene against the process.
europmc-pmc2792038:
Lin and colleagues asked how a vaccine can protect mice against two very unlike bloodstream invaders at once: the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus and the fungus Candida albicans. Their 2009 vaccine used a piece of a Candida surface protein, called rAls3p-N, mixed with a standard booster chemical.

Protection needed two signals from helper T cells, named IFN-gamma and IL-17A, plus working eater cells that destroy germs. Vaccinated mice made three T-cell types that released these signals, drew more eater cells into infected tissue, and cleared both germs faster. Blocking the IL-17A signal likewise left ordinary mice open to both infections. Mice lacking IFN-gamma stayed prone to both infections, showing one shared defense covers both.
europmc-pmc2820538:
Coppé and colleagues found in 2010 that mouse cells only mimic the human aging-cell secretions when grown at body-like oxygen levels. Senescent cells, which have stopped dividing for good, release a cocktail of signals called the SASP that changes how neighbors behave. Mouse cells grown at standard lab oxygen, twenty percent, arrested but secreted almost none of it.

Grown at three percent oxygen, which matches body tissue, and pushed into senescence by radiation, mouse cells produced a robust human-like cocktail. Both species raised tissue-cutting enzymes from one shared gene cluster. A single factor, CXCL-1, did most of the work of making nearby precancer cells grow, and only low-oxygen mouse cells fed tumor growth in animals.
europmc-pmc2867938:
De Santa and colleagues reported in 2010 that much of the genome's activity outside genes happens exactly at its control switches. Mammalian DNA is copied into RNA in many places beyond known genes, and some of that RNA comes from enhancers, stretches that boost gene activity. The team mapped where the copying enzyme RNA polymerase II sits across the genome in immune cells.

A large share of the outside-gene copying sites landed precisely on enhancers, and the enhancers themselves were being transcribed. That copying rose when the cells were stimulated, tying it to active gene control rather than stray noise. The finding suggests the short RNAs made at enhancers deserve study as part of how genes are switched on, and it helps annotate what the vast non-gene genome is doing.
europmc-pmc2998438:
Yang and Hekimi reported in 2010 that a burst of a reactive oxygen signal from mitochondria can lengthen life in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans. Mitochondrial oxidants are usually cast as ageing toxins, yet several long-lived worm mutants carry faulty mitochondria.

Reviewing that mutant evidence, they argue the oxidant superoxide works as a stress signal that switches on defences, rather than only as damage. Mutations that mildly impair the power chain raise the signal and extend lifespan, while stronger faults shorten it. The reframing helps explain why some antioxidant treatments fail to slow ageing and why mild stress can protect.
europmc-pmc3017038:
Ferrer-Vaquer and colleagues engineered a mouse strain that lights up wherever a key development signal, Wnt, is active, in a 2010 study. Watching embryos develop live needs reporters bright and sharp enough to resolve single cells, and existing Wnt reporters fell short.

They placed six signal-responsive switches ahead of a glowing protein fused to a nuclear anchor, so active cells shine as bright dots. In embryos and adults the glow appeared exactly at known Wnt sites, discretely and specifically. The strain gives developmental biologists a crisp live readout for filming how signals guide shaping of the body.
europmc-pmc3035538:
Sulaiman and coauthors asked in 2003 whether a gut parasite found in animals can also infect people. The parasite, Giardia duodenalis, causes diarrhea worldwide and looks the same under the microscope whether it comes from a person, a dog, or a cow. The team read one gene from parasites taken from people and from several animal hosts to sort them into family groups.

Most host types carried their own distinct parasite lines. One large group, however, mixed most human samples with those from muskrats and beavers, plus a rabbit sample. That mixing shows parasites from some animals can plausibly reach people through water or contact. The gene test also gives health workers a way to tell parasite types apart. Such typing can trace outbreak sources and sharpen the classification of this messy parasite group.
europmc-pmc3069738:
Winn and many coauthors gave in 2011 an overview of CCP4, the shared software suite that structural biologists use to solve molecular structures from X ray crystal data. The project, run as a community collaboration since the nineteen nineties, gathers around two hundred programs from many labs into one package with common file formats. It serves academic and commercial researchers alike.

The overview traces how the suite grew, what it can do today, and what is planned for its next generation. Shared libraries and a graphical interface let separate programs hand results to each other smoothly. A user can go from raw diffraction images to a finished structure in one environment. Training and education are part of the mission. The paper serves as the standard reference for citing the suite as a whole.
europmc-pmc3084838:
Masliah and coauthors showed in 2011 that antibody treatment can ease brain disease in a mouse model of Lewy body disorders, which include Parkinson disease and a common dementia. Both involve clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein in neurons. The team gave model mice a lab made antibody aimed at the protein's tail end, by passive immunization rather than vaccination.

Treated mice performed better in a water maze that tests memory and navigation. Their brains held less of a harmful cut form of the protein in axons and synapses, and the related nerve damage was reduced. Tracking studies showed the antibody entered the brain, latched onto cells carrying the clumps, and routed the protein to the cell's disposal system. The authors argue the approach deserves development for patients. Antibodies against this protein have since become a major drug strategy.
europmc-pmc3185738:
Patrick Woo and colleagues surveyed coronavirus genomes with computer analysis in a 2010 paper in Viruses. A surge of newly found coronaviruses in animals and people, including the SARS virus, finally allowed family-wide comparison. These viruses carry the largest genomes of any RNA virus, and their base composition varies widely between members.

The family sorts into three established genera, with a fourth emerging from bird viruses. Dating analysis placed the shared ancestor of SARS-related viruses only a few years before the outbreak, evolving at a brisk clip. Genome shuffling between strains proved common, even across species, and letter-usage bias bore the marks of two distinct pressures. The review maps the family's structure and habits for future outbreak science.
europmc-pmc3219338:
Herbert Schöchl and colleagues compared two strategies for controlling bleeding in badly injured patients, in this 2011 analysis in Critical Care. One group, treated in Salzburg, received clotting-factor concentrates guided by a bedside test of clot strength, and no fresh frozen plasma. The other, drawn from a German trauma registry, received plasma-based care.

The groups had similar injury severity. Patients on the concentrate strategy needed far fewer donor blood products. Red-cell transfusion was avoided in nearly three in ten of them, against almost none in the plasma group. Platelet transfusion was avoided in the great majority. Death rates were similar between the strategies. The authors conclude that test-guided concentrates reduce exposure to donated blood products without harming survival.
europmc-pmc3220038:
Yan Zhang and colleagues tested blocking the immune checkpoint PD-L1 as a treatment for sepsis, in this 2010 mouse study in Critical Care. Sepsis can paralyze the immune system, partly through death of lymphocytes and failure of monocytes. The team induced sepsis in mice by puncturing the gut and measured checkpoint expression on immune cells a day later.

Septic mice carried more PD-1 and PD-L1 on their T cells, B cells, and monocytes than healthy controls. Giving an antibody that blocks PD-L1 significantly improved survival. Treated mice kept more of their lymphocytes, produced more of some inflammatory signals and less of a suppressive one, and cleared bacteria better. The authors propose PD-L1 blockade as a promising strategy against sepsis-driven immune suppression.
europmc-pmc3257638:
Asa Hakansson and Goran Molin reviewed the resident microbes of the human gut in relation to inflammation, in this 2011 article in Nutrients. The gut's microbial community can aggravate or calm inflammation, both locally and across the body, and probiotic products aim to tilt that balance. The authors restricted their evidence to human trials rather than cell or animal experiments.

They describe the dominant groups of organisms in the gastrointestinal tract and their inflammatory potential. Then they work through probiotic applications one by one. The list runs from whole-body immune modulation and liver injury to the metabolic syndrome, colorectal cancer, and inflammatory bowel disease. Radiation damage to the gut is covered too. A recurring caution concerns how much probiotic species and strains differ in their genes. The body can therefore respond very differently to each one. That point is often neglected when trial results are discussed.
europmc-pmc3376738:
Kondapalli and a large team reported in 2012 how the protein PINK1 switches on its partner Parkin, a process broken in some inherited Parkinson's disease. Faulty PINK1 genes cause a recessive, early form of the disease. The team tested whether PINK1 directly tags Parkin or fifteen other disease-linked proteins.

Only Parkin was tagged, at a single conserved spot, serine 65. Human PINK1 woke up when the voltage across mitochondrial membranes collapsed, and the tag it placed strongly boosted Parkin's enzyme activity. Blocking the spot or disabling PINK1 stopped the boost. Watching those tags could give the first readouts of this pathway in living tissue.
europmc-pmc3420138:
Deavall, Martin, Horner, and Roberts examined in 2012 how drugs can injure the body through oxidative stress. Reactive oxygen species arise from normal metabolism and double as signals, but cells must keep them leashed. When production outruns the antioxidant defenses, the overflow attacks DNA, proteins, and fats.

The review explains the kinds of damage these species inflict on key cell targets. It then gathers evidence tying them to real drug side effects: heart damage from the cancer drug doxorubicin, muscle wasting from an HIV drug, and hearing loss from cisplatin. Understanding which drugs tip the balance, the authors argue, should help design safer medicines and protect patients during treatment.
europmc-pmc3476838:
Vucenik and Stains reviewed the evidence linking obesity with cancer in a 2012 issue of the Annals journal of the New York Academy of Sciences. Obesity had already been tied to diabetes, heart disease, and high blood pressure. Population studies also link it to higher risk of several cancers, from colon and breast to liver and kidney, along with worse survival after diagnosis.

The authors survey how fat tissue might drive cancer: through growth signals, shifting energy balance, and steady low-level inflammation. One signaling cascade inside cells draws special attention as a shared hub and drug target. Vucenik and Stains close with practical advice. Keeping a healthy weight across life, they argue, ranks among the strongest steps a person can take against cancer.

fludd-philosophia-moysaica-1638:
Robert Fludd sums up his occult philosophy in Philosophia Moysaica, in Latin from 1638. Man mirrors the universe, the small world answering the great one in part by part. Moses himself is read as the first true philosopher of nature, whose words hide the secrets of creation for those with eyes to read them.

Weather, disease, and the elements all fall under Fludd's vast scheme. His famous engravings map soul, body, and cosmos in bold figures. Critics like Kepler and Gassendi crossed pens with him for years. The book forms the most elaborate summing up of Renaissance magic ever bound, a grand system built just as the new science rose.
frus-1861-d138:
Writing from Paris on 22 July 1861, William Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a last calm report. The dispatch is document 138 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton wrote the day after Bull Run, but the news had not yet reached Paris. His letter keeps the old mood for one more page. In the file it stands at the edge of a change that the next mails would bring in full. The mails that followed would bring the Bull Run tale in full and grim color. Grim color, when it came, would test the calm of every post in Europe.
frus-1861-d238:
News and judgment from James Shepherd Pike reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 14 June 1861. It was printed as Document 238 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d38:
Thomas Corwin wrote from Mexico City to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 June 1861. The dispatch is document 38 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Corwin spent 1861 trying to keep Mexico steady and friendly to the Union. Money, loans, and border fears filled his talks there. His end of June report shows an envoy working a hard post with few tools but his name and his voice. His post lacked money and troops, so words carried nearly the whole weight of his mission. Words, in Corwin's hands, had swayed crowds before; now they served a state.
frus-1862-d138:
Writing on 5 September 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 138 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d238:
William Stuart wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 September 1862, and the letter is printed as Document 238 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart was running the British legation while Lord Lyons was absent.

Stuart wrote four days before Antietam, in the last stretch of the Maryland campaign's approach. The legation's letters home in this window helped London judge whether the invasion proved Southern staying power. This letter's date gives it its weight: it is a dispatch from the edge of the war's bloodiest day, written in ignorance of it. The British legation stood a short walk from the State Department, and messengers passed between them daily.
frus-1862-d338:
A Dayton report dated 23 October 1862 stands as Document 338 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

By late October, informed men in Paris could see the truce scheme failing for want of British support. Dayton's task shifted from warning to watching: would France act alone, or turn back to Mexico? His report that week belongs to the file's closing account of the autumn crisis, written as the tension drained away. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d38:
Writing on 27 March 1862, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent his report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 38 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d438:
On 17 September 1862, the very day of the battle of Antietam, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Gabriel García Tassara. It is Document 438 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Business at the State Department went on even as the armies fought in Maryland, and notes to resident ministers were part of that day's work. Seward's dealings with Spain's minister covered the standing file between the two nations, from maritime questions to Mexico.
