Within days, Antietam and the emancipation order would change the tone of every foreign conversation in Washington. The note catches the Spanish exchange at the edge of that change, still in the forms of ordinary wartime routine.
frus-1862-d538:
Three days after the Dutch minister's note, on 22 July 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward replied to Roest van Limburg. The letter is Document 538 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Seward's July answers to resident ministers had to carry conviction in a discouraging month, and his Dutch reply was no exception. The substance between the governments remained the law and practice of the blockade as it touched Dutch trade. Van Limburg's legation was one of the steadiest in Washington. The correspondence shows no rupture. It shows only the friction natural between a blockading belligerent and a carrying neutral. The letter is a fair sample of that managed friction in the war's second summer.
frus-1862-d638:
On 2 July 1861 Townsend Harris dispatched this letter from Japan to the Secretary of State. It is Document 638 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Harris wrote days before the first battle of Bull Run, in ignorance of it that would last for months. His Japan letters in this period report the grinding detail of a new treaty relationship. They cover audiences and disputes over the ports. They also cover the shogun's government's own troubles with foreigners. The contrast inside the volume is striking. Ministers in Europe reported a war for the Union's life. Harris, at the far end of the earth, reported whether the treaty of 1858 would hold. Both were the same government's business.
frus-1863p1-d138:
A month-end pair for London opens with this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 31 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 138 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's month-end pair closed his March file for London. The brief he fed Adams had not changed its heart all spring: hold Britain fair, stop the ships, keep the tone firm but cool. This letter opens the pair of 31 March. It is the kind of sheet that kept the long game in play, one steamer at a time.
frus-1863p1-d238:
Reporting on 16 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 238 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d338:
On 12 December 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 338 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d38: Marked private and confidential, this paper is dated 11 September 1862. It is printed as document 38 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It sits among the Confederate letters in that part of the volume. The evidence gives its mark and date but no writer and no name addressed, so this note claims no more than that.
frus-1863p1-d438:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 2 April 1863 letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d538:
In the flow of wartime mail, Lord Lyons wrote to William H. Seward on 27 May 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d638:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London sent an official note to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State on 16 October 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d138: Kirk wrote to the Secretary of State again on November 18, 1943, his second Cairo dispatch in two days in this series. It is Document 138 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The quickening pace of the host's reports matches the nearness of the conference, which opened on November 22. The record gives the parties and the date and no subject. The dispatch rests in the Foreign Relations volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d238:
Minutes record President Roosevelt's second meeting with the Joint Chiefs of Staff aboard the Iowa, on 19 November 1943 in the admiral's cabin. At some thirty-five thousand characters, the record is long, and its printed opening turns on the fight over a single commander for the war in Europe.

Roosevelt says he likes proposal A, the unified command plan, dislikes proposal B. He will take the matter up with Churchill at the first chance, though a compromise may follow. Admiral King calls A plain logic; General Marshall attacks committee command, citing a year and a half of failure in the Middle East. The chiefs then count forces: some eleven million Americans and four and a half million British in uniform by January, with American strength in England already matching the British.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d338:
Secretary of War Henry Stimson sent John McCloy an eyes-only telegram from Washington on 28 November 1943, numbered 1124. It answers McCloy's reports from Cairo on the civil affairs negotiation with Foreign Secretary Eden.

Stimson says he and Secretary Hull agree with the key suggestion. The European Advisory Commission's draft recommendations should go to the Combined Chiefs of Staff for comment. That step should come before any final submission to governments. Both men welcome Eden's tentative agreement to drop the pressure for moving the Combined Civil Affairs Committee to London. The State Department, he adds, thinks the proposed British-American commission on the French political situation should sit in London. Stimson closes by congratulating McCloy heartily on working out so satisfactory a solution.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d38: A second message from Churchill to Roosevelt is also dated October 5, 1943, and it follows as Document 38 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The prime minister often split his business into separate notes rather than one long letter. Which errand this one ran, the record does not say. It is preserved in the Foreign Relations series, in the dense October traffic before the Moscow Conference opened.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d438:
December 4, 1943 was the opening day of the Second Cairo Conference, and the Combined Chiefs of Staff, the joint American-British military command, held a formal session that day. The minutes printed here come from the State Department's published record of the Cairo and Tehran conferences, where the chiefs' meetings sit alongside the talks of Roosevelt and Churchill.

A reader gets the working level of the alliance: senior officers weighing operations, shipping, and manpower, and recording the points they agreed on. Because the second Cairo meeting had to finish what Tehran started, these sessions matter. They show strategy being fixed in detail while the political leaders met in the same city.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d538:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull set out this memorandum on January 3, 1944, as the government in Washington took stock after the Tehran and Cairo conferences. Hull had not traveled to the summits, yet his department had to make their results work. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Departmental memoranda by the Secretary gathered a subject into one considered paper, rather than a hasty cable. Hull was then the administration's elder statesman of diplomacy, architect of its trade policy and a planner of the postwar order. For readers, the memorandum shows the Secretary thinking on paper at the opening of the decisive year.
frus-1944-quebec-d138:
American policy toward Hungary, as State Department planners stated it for Quebec in September 1944, began from frustration. Hungary had repeatedly said it wanted out of the war but had taken no realistic step. Budapest hoped the Anglo-Americans would protect it from Soviet Russia, and it clung to territories gained with German help.

Draft armistice terms had already gone to the European Advisory Commission. The paper rules out American troops in Hungary's occupation, but wants political representatives there after surrender. Long term, Washington favored a broadly based provisional government, land and electoral reform, and frontiers starting from the pre-Munich lines. Ethnic adjustments were possible, including a small strip of Transylvania returning to Hungary.
frus-1944-quebec-d238:
Taylor cabled urgently from Vatican City on September 11, 1944, about Italian relief shipments. His greatest concern was that material accumulated in America for the Italian relief committee would not reach Italy because of failures to ship on schedule. The first shipment should already have arrived, and failure to deliver would badly damage American prestige.

His remedy was simple and practical. Allocate one or two ships to strictly relief voyages, with standard cargoes of staples and essentials, kept constantly en route between an American port and convenient Italian ports. Dedicated ships would avoid the delays and complications of mixed cargoes of munitions and other goods. The people in distress, Taylor wrote, do not understand shipping difficulties.
frus-1944-quebec-d38:
A second Roosevelt message to Churchill is dated August 30, 1944. The State Department printed both messages that day. They appear in the pre-conference correspondence of the Quebec 1944 volume.

Paired messages before a summit usually split the business. Some points could be settled by letter. Others needed a room and a handshake. August 1944 left plenty in both piles. For readers, this companion message completes a day's preparation. The two leaders had written to each other for four years. They were about to meet again on Canadian soil. It would be their second conference there. The letters show how much business they handled in writing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d138:
Minutes of the first meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board are dated 4 February 1946. The advisory board gathered the departments' intelligence chiefs under the new director. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

First meetings matter: they seat the members, fix the habits, and test whether rivals can sit in one room under a chairman not their own. The advisory board was the January design's working level, where the services' chiefs advised the director of central intelligence. Readers can watch the experiment begin here. The men in that room had spent the autumn fighting over the system's shape. Now they had to run it together. The minutes show how the running started.
frus-1945-50-intel-d238:
A memorandum dated 11 January 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 238, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Dulles survey team was checking how well the CIA worked, and agencies across Washington were stating their views on the record.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d338:
The Secretary of Defense’s Special Assistant (McNeil) addressed a letter to Mathias F. Correa on 2 February 1948. Readers meet it as document 338 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

Senior men used letters to make requests that could not be brushed aside, since the paper itself proved the ask. Its worth now is the voice: a chief stating his case as he wished it to be read. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d38:
Harold Smith, director of the Bureau of the Budget, wrote to President Truman on 31 October 1945. Smith was the president's chief adviser on the machinery of government. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

When the budget director wrote to the president, the subject had reached decision level. Smith had strong views on how intelligence should be organized, favoring a modest central staff over a grand new agency. His memorandum put that view where it counted most. Readers should mark this paper: the plans that finally emerged in January bear the stamp of the Budget Bureau's thinking. Smith's letters to Truman are where that stamp was pressed into the record.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d138:
General Macready, head of the army side of the British Staff Mission in Washington, wrote to Assistant Secretary of War McCloy on 20 January 1945. His letter, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, is headed “Bremen Enclave.” It moves the ports dispute close to settlement.

The British Chiefs of Staff, Macready reports, are ready to accept the formula worked out at the War Department on 5 January. They ask the American chiefs to confirm their reading of one or two points. He attaches the formula with two small amendments underlined, so both sides read it the same way. One amendment pins down the role of a deputy controller, an officer who runs only his own office's agents inside another power's zone.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d238:
Persia belongs on the conference table, Churchill told Roosevelt on 15 January 1945. His top secret message, number 890, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He proposes discussion with Stalin, or between the foreign secretaries, and he quotes the pledge all three signed at Tehran.

That declaration of December 1943 records the three governments as at one with Iran in desiring her independence, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. Recent Russian conduct in Persia, Churchill argues, departs from those words. Moscow refused to accept Persia's decision to grant no concessions until after the war. Its pressure brought down a prime minister who would not grant the oil demands at once. The new premier, backed by parliament, holds the same line.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d338: Harry Hopkins coached from the sidelines at Yalta with short handwritten notes passed to the President. This one, dated February 5, 1945, concerns the breaking up of Germany. Hopkins urged Roosevelt to call the matter very important and urgent. The three foreign ministers, he wrote, should bring in a proposal the next day. It would set a method for reaching a decision on dismemberment at an early date. The slip shows the adviser feeding words to the President mid-session.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d38: Churchill opened the new year with a message to Roosevelt on 1 January 1945. It is document 38 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on Malta and Yalta, published by the Department of State. January was departure month for both delegations, so the tone of the correspondence shifted from general planning toward the practical business of travel and meeting arrangements.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d438:
What still needs settling fills this delegation checklist of February 10, 1945. Poland probably need not be discussed before the plenary, it says. The Declaration on Liberated Europe stands in the same state. On Iran, the British may propose adopting their paper, and Matthews holds a copy.

On reparations, the British had not yet agreed to the Soviet-American paper. Eden, the memo notes, wants three things: Hungarian control rules extended to Bulgaria, Bulgarian reparations for Greece, and a statement against a Russian-backed Tito-Bulgaria alliance. The paper, likely prepared by Hiss for Stettinius, is a crib sheet for the conference's penultimate day.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d138:
Ambassador Winant asked for instructions on press arrangements in an urgent telegram from London on July 13, 1945. The message is document 138 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. London correspondents had heard from their Washington offices that a meeting place would be fixed for reporters late in the conference.

The correspondents claimed they would be told a time and place where they could join the President's party, and that the embassy in London would notify them. Winant reports that the embassy has no record of any instructions on the point. He asks Washington to tell him how to handle such inquiries. The query shows the loose end left by the press ban: reporters were shut out of Potsdam, but nobody had yet told them where to wait for the end.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d238:
Ambassador Kirk reported a split in Rome's cabinet over the war declaration in a telegram dated July 9, 1945. The message is document 238 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Kirk had seen Renato Prunas, the Italian foreign ministry's secretary general, the evening before.

After Washington's approval arrived, Prunas said, the Council of Ministers met. Most ministers, including the Socialists, favored immediate and active participation against Japan. Only the Communists were cool, insisting any Italian part in the Far East war be symbolic rather than actual. With timing and degree in dispute, Rome asked Washington when the declaration should come. Kirk repeated the Department's line: the choice was Italy's, but the sooner the better. Reports from Moscow suggested the Soviets did not look favorably on the move.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d338:
Robert Murphy, the political adviser in Germany, objected on June 27, 1945, to the shape of the French occupation zone. In an extract of his cable from Hoechst, he regretted the pressure on France to accept southern Württemberg against its wishes. The grant, he said, split an old German state and might wipe it out as a political unit.

Württemberg, Murphy noted, had a long liberal history. He added that Ambassador Winant and Mr. Mosely had also objected. Forcing the division clashed, he argued, with the allied aim of breaking up the Reich by reviving its traditional states, Prussia aside. Zone lines, his cable warns, could do lasting political harm.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d38: Truman gave Hopkins his answer for Stalin in this telegram of May 28, 1945. Two of Hopkins's messages had been received. Hopkins might inform Stalin that the President saw no objection to meeting in the Berlin area. About the 15th of July appeared to be a practicable date for him. The wire, sent by Navy channels through the naval attaché in Moscow, reached Hopkins while his Kremlin talks still ran. Its lines fixed the frame of the Potsdam Conference — place and month — weeks before the leaders traveled.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d438:
Klieforth, the American chargé in Prague, cabled on June 28, 1945, that one issue towers over Czechoslovakia's reconstruction: the minority problem. Its solution, he writes, means the transfer to Germany and Hungary of about three million citizens, a fifth of the country's population. A second phase would replace them with about as many Czechoslovaks, most of them uprooted in turn.

Together, transfer and replacement would touch forty percent of the population. Prague knows the transfers need allied agreement, Klieforth reports, but the earliest possible agreement is essential, since all reconstruction is makeshift until then. He ends with a warning: delay could feed a dramatic leader, backed by radicals, seeking a solution by force.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d538:
Second-year lend-lease for Britain is anticipated in a briefing book paper dated July 6, 1945. Churchill may seek a commitment, at least in principle, it warns. The commitment would fix the amount of lend-lease for the United Kingdom and the British Commonwealth. It would cover the second year of Phase II. The existing agreement covers the first year, applied to calendar 1945.

At Quebec in 1944, the paper recalls, Churchill sought Roosevelt's agreement in principle. He obtained it: 6.5 billion dollars of lend-lease during the first year of Phase II. The American Joint Chiefs had not considered that the Pacific war's needs called for anything near that amount. No corresponding benefit to the United States was requested in return. Later Washington talks settled on 5.5 billion dollars in total.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d638:
George Wadsworth, the U.S. minister in Lebanon, sent a detailed confidential report from Beirut on June 30, 1945. It is document 638 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Its subject is the Troupes Speciales, the local forces officered by France in Syria and Lebanon.

Wadsworth gives a careful head count, checked with local ministers and British staff men. Before the May troubles the force stood near 20,000 men, some 5,000 in Lebanon and 15,000 in Syria. About 5,500 Syrians had since deserted, while the Lebanese ranks held firm. The 9,000 Syrian troops left stayed under French officers but under close British control. Wadsworth lists where they were held, from camps in the Bekaa valley to barracks at Aleppo and Mezze airport.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1038:
The European Advisory Commission sent this report to the four occupying governments on July 25, 1945. It transmits an agreement on certain additional requirements to be imposed upon Germany. The June 5 declaration on Germany's defeat had promised such added political, economic, and military demands. The commission urges the four governments to approve the agreement and pass it to the Allied representatives in Berlin.

The report attaches comments on single clauses. When conditions allow, all German research on war or war material should be flatly abolished by public order. German authorities should also hand over the plates and tools used to print money tokens for lands Germany once occupied. Further comments guard the property of other nations held in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1138:
Ambassador Winant wrote from London once more on 24 July 1945. His cables came near daily during the Potsdam weeks. Each tracked British official thinking as the summit's choices took shape in Germany.

Reports from London added texture that the conference room could not give. Winant heard party talk, press views, and Whitehall's private mood. Washington used that stream to judge its ally's stands and staying power. This dispatch keeps the embassy's close watch going into the summit's second week. It is a small part of a large, steady flow of London reporting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1238:
The Acting Secretary of State set down this memorandum on 17 July 1945, the day the conference opened. Grew's notes from Washington fixed the home office's thinking on paper. Staff memoranda did the quiet reasoning that leaders later turned into choices.

A memorandum from the man running the department carried weight beyond its length. It could frame a question, record a call, or set a line for the desks below. This one dates from the summit's first day, when Washington's part in the talks was just taking shape. It is the home office thinking aloud, in its chief's hand.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1338:
On 18 July 1945, George Allen wrote to Loy Henderson, the director of the Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs. Allen was Henderson's deputy, so the paper moved inside a single office of the State Department. It dates from the second day of the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill, and Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945.

Inside-office papers show how a bureau shaped its advice before it reached the secretary of state. Henderson's office covered a wide map, from Iran and the Arab lands to Africa, at a time when all of it was in flux. The message helps readers trace how American policy for that region was built, step by step, by the men assigned to it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-138:
State Department minutes record a meeting of July 30, 1945, as Potsdam moved toward its close. The formal minute sets give the conference its ordered skeleton. This one joined the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. It covers business done two days before the final protocol was signed.

Readers find the session's work stated cleanly: topics, speakers, outcomes. In the last days the minutes grow dense with decisions. They show the machinery of agreement running at full speed. Paired with the note-takers' drafts, the formal minutes let readers judge how the record itself was built.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-38:
One line in volume two of the Potsdam papers states that no record of a meeting's substance has been found. It is the thirty-eighth unnumbered item following document 710, sitting between the records of July 20, 1945. The meeting it concerns is not even named in the line itself.

Such notes are the editors' way of keeping the record honest. Rather than pass over a known meeting in silence, they mark the gap in print. The reader is told that the conference's paper trail breaks at this point. Whatever was said, and whatever it may have moved, cannot be recovered from the files the editors searched. The entry belongs to a family of like notes throughout this volume. Together they map how much of the Potsdam Conference was transacted off the record, in talks no secretary minuted.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d738:
A second Yost memorandum bears the date August 9, 1945, as document 738. The Central Secretariat's executive secretary had more than one thread to close. Two memos in a day mirror the secretariat's load. This one joined the post-conference papers of the second Potsdam volume.

Paired wrap-up memos show the range of loose ends. Texts, records, and duties all needed owners after the close. Yost assigned them in writing. Readers see the unglamorous labor that makes a clean archive. The document also marks how long Potsdam's shadow ran: a week on, its staff still worked its files.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d838:
Kennan wrote again from Moscow on July 18, 1945, in document 838. The chargé sent a second letter in two days to the Acting Secretary of State. His reports fed Washington while Harriman sat at Potsdam. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume beside the first.

Two letters in two days show an embassy with much to report. Moscow watched the summit and reacted in ways worth cabling. Readers follow Kennan's reading of those reactions. The document extends one of the volume's most literate threads. His dispatches from this summer are still quoted, and letters like this one show why.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d938:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled Edwin Pauley on July 26, 1945, about a British memorandum on Soviet reparation claims. The British foresaw a chance that single Soviet republics might file separate claims. They also imagined republics seeking their own seats on a reparations commission.

London's view was to resist most such claims. White Russia and the Ukraine could be heard, by the San Francisco precedent, but their shares must come out of the Soviet total. Baltic state claims should not be entertained at all. Washington's reply called any policy premature. No sign yet showed whether Moscow would raise the questions.
frus-1952-54v16-d1038: The final declaration on Indochina from the 1954 Geneva Conference in FRUS. Vietnam was temporarily divided. This entry preserves that declaration. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
frus-1969-76v10-d238: A 1969-1976 FRUS backchannel message on Vietnam. The secret channel. This document preserves that message. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298438: United Medical Systems-DE took its September 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Medical deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298838: Smiths Detection doubled its December 2006 protest — two case numbers, one detection-tech fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299338: Vaden Industries took its March 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the call on the claims. The firm challenged the award, and the ruling tests the protest in full. The bid-law hearing treats every challenger alike. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-299738: Camnetics Mfg. took its June 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The manufacturer said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the claims. Factory-floor contracts get the same fair-play ruling as high-tech deals.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-238: Drug offenders' benefit denials had limited impact in 2005, and GAO's report says various factors might limit the effects of the denial laws. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the punishment's bite deserved honest assessment. The factors had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-438: The LOCAL TV Act's admin funds looked done in 2005, and GAO's report says the money may no longer be necessary. The review gives the quiet verdict. The program's paperwork was paid up. The funds were no longer needed. The program's paperwork was paid up.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-538: Global trade talks were back on track in 2005, and GAO's report says the WTO negotiations progressed, though considerable work remained. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the ambitious goals deserved honest effort. The work had to continue.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-238: Contractors with Social Security numbers needed stronger protections in 2006, and GAO's report says safeguards were required when vendors held SSNs. The findings demand the locks. The report warns that the nine-digit keys deserved guarding. The protections had to be stronger.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-338: States' 911 wireless funds got a GAO review in 2006, and the report examines collection and use of the enhanced 911 money. The findings follow the dollars. The report warns that the emergency-call funds should save lives, not budgets. The funds had to be used right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-438: Privatized military housing needed attention in 2006, and GAO's report says management issues required focus as the program matured. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the troops' homes deserved good landlords. The issues had to be addressed. The troops deserved good landlords.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-538: The Pentagon's EEO pilot needed a better evaluation in 2006, and GAO's report says the program was underway, though the evaluation plan needed improvement. The findings balance the start and the gaps. The report warns that the fairness experiment deserved real measurement. The plan had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-638: Export controls for dual-use tech needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says Commerce's system needed improvements to protect U.S. interests. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the civilian-military tech should not leak. The system had to be tightened.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-938: The Pentagon's mobility study had holes in 2006, and GAO's report says the limitations raised questions about the capability assessment. The findings doubt the conclusions. The report warns that the lift capacity for war needed honest math. The study had to be solid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-138: The State Department's watchdog got watched in 2007, and GAO's report examines what the department's inspector general actually accomplished all year. The findings audit the auditor in careful detail, grading its cases and its reach. The report's meta-lesson stands firm: even the watchdogs need watching, and the diplomats' overseer was no exception.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-238: Health IT was racing ahead of privacy in 2007, and GAO's report says a comprehensive privacy approach was needed for the national strategy. The findings demand the safeguards. The report warns that the digital chart should not become a public record. The patients' secrets needed locks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-38: Small-business research grants needed better tracking in 2007, and GAO's report says agencies had to strengthen their data on the innovation program. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the seed money for inventors needed sunlight. The data had to be solid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-538: The Pentagon's computer buying needed grown-up rules in 2007 — GAO's report says the department had to fully spell out how it managed tech investments. The findings demand the written playbook. The report's refrain: billion-dollar systems deserve better than improvisation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1138: The Government Accountability Office dug into health Information Technology: HHS Has Taken Important Steps to Address Privacy Principles and Challenges, Although More Work Remains in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-38: Covering the 2007 tax filing season, this Government Accountability Office report finds the IRS continuing a trend of improvement in processing returns. It also urges the agency to evaluate ways to cut costs and boost voluntary tax compliance. The review balances praise for smoother operations with pressure to do more with less, as the IRS handles hundreds of millions of returns each year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-538: GAO published its findings on supply Chain Security: CBP Works with International Entities to Promote Global Customs Security Standards and Initiatives, but Challenges Remain in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
godwin-man-in-the-moone-1638:
Francis Godwin wrote The Man in the Moone in the last years of his life. The tale came out in 1638, after his death. Its hero, Domingo Gonsales, is a Spaniard who flees a duel and roams the world. In the isle of St. Helena he trains wild geese to bear him in the air.

The geese bear him up past Earth to the Moon on their yearly flight. He finds the Moon a green land of tall folk who live in peace. Their tongue is tones, not words, and he learns it in part. The tale is a root text of the trip to the Moon.
grimke-letters-equality-sexes-1838:
Sarah Grimké published Letters on the Equality of the Sexes, and the Condition of Woman in 1838 in Boston. Grimké, a South Carolina abolitionist who had left a slaveholding family, wrote the letters first for a newspaper. Speaking tours by her and her sister had drawn attacks on women who spoke in public.

Grimké answered from the Bible itself, arguing that scripture grants woman equality and that men had twisted it to rule her. She surveyed women's condition across lands and demanded equal education and rights. The letters linked the abolitionist and feminist causes at their joint birth. They stand as a founding document of American feminism, bold for their time and place.
historische-skizze-der-alchemie-besonder: Historische Skizze der Alchemie, 1838. The historical sketch. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
hutcheson-inquiry-beauty-virtue-1738:
Francis Hutcheson, an Irish-born professor at Glasgow, published his Inquiry into the Original of Our Ideas of Beauty and Virtue in 1725. The fourth edition of 1738 is the text here, holding both treatises. Hutcheson founded the moral-sense school with this book, and he aimed it squarely at Mandeville's cynical Fable of the Bees.

One treatise argues that we have an inner sense of beauty, by which harmony pleases us at once. The other argues for a moral sense that approves kindness without any thought of profit. Against Mandeville, Hutcheson holds that benevolence is natural to us, not a mask for selfishness. The Inquiry set the terms of British moral debate for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowe-august-101:
August Löwe, a Russian mathematician, gets one of the shortest entries in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The article gives no birth or death dates for him. Instead it is built almost entirely from a list of his books. Those books were written in Russian and aimed at teaching practical mathematics.

The titles show a career spent on textbooks rather than research. His best-known works cover perspective, practical geometry, surveying, and arithmetic. Several of them reached second editions between 1858 and 1872. One arithmetic book was written for girls, and another for elementary public schools. The entry cites a Russian encyclopedic dictionary as its source. For modern readers it opens a small window on math teaching in nineteenth-century Russia. It also recalls the Jewish teachers who wrote its textbooks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-macedonia-10238:
Macedonia, the land of Alexander the Great, is treated in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia for its place in Jewish sources. The country in southeastern Europe was then part of the Turkish empire. Rabbinic writings call Alexander himself the Macedonian. The Book of Daniel names the Macedonians as the Kittim, the article notes.

The entry gathers the rabbis' picture of Macedonia. In Daniel it appears as the fourth beast of prophecy, a kingdom of the end times. The rabbis equated the Hebrew Yawan, or Greece, with Macedonia. They mentioned its gold, its speech in the Greek Bible, and its weapons in Josephus. Macedonian-named cities such as Pella were founded on Palestinian soil. The article also records Paul's visits to Philippi, Thessalonica, and Beroea, where Jewish communities heard him. It closes by pointing readers to the article on Turkey for modern times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malvano-giacomo:
Giacomo Malvano, an Italian diplomat, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Turin on December 14, 1841, he entered the diplomatic service in 1862. By 1887 he had risen to envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary. Two years later he became a councilor of state. He then served as general secretary in the ministry of foreign affairs.

The article highlights his work on trade. In 1875 and 1876 he sat on a committee drafting commercial treaties. He represented Italy at the Paris monetary conference of 1879. In 1891 and 1892 he arranged commercial treaties with Austria-Hungary, Germany, and Switzerland. Malvano also served the Italian Geographical Society repeatedly as vice-president and council member. He still held the council seat in 1904. The short entry preserves a Jewish diplomat at the working center of Italy's foreign ministry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marseilles-or-1:
Marseilles, the great seaport of southern France, gets a city entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Kahn wrote it. The article counts about 5,000 Jews in a city of 420,300 people in 1896. It traces Jewish life there back to a colony in the fifth century. Exiles from Clermont found refuge in the city in 567.

From there the entry follows a long swing between welcome and pressure. Pope Gregory spoke out against forced conversion in 591. Benjamin of Tudela found 300 Jews with two synagogues around 1165. In the later Middle Ages the Jews were called citizens of the city. Yet they still wore a colored badge and faced limits on testimony, work, and baths, and they paid for the city's political troubles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-b-moses:
Menahem ben Moses Tamar, a poet and commentator of the Ottoman world, is entered by Gotthard Deutsch and H. Brody in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Probably a pupil of Mordecai Comtino of Constantinople, he flourished in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries at Adrianople or Philippopolis. He wrote commentaries on Proverbs, Ruth, and Esther. He wrote a supercommentary on Abraham ibn Ezra's Pentateuch commentary. He also wrote a Hebrew grammar, "Rashe Besamim," Heads of Spices.

His fame rests more on verse. His "Azharot" set out the commandments in poetic form, furnished with his own commentary, "Tanhumot El." The entry calls them a noteworthy gift to Hebrew poetry. He also imitated Judah ha-Levi's famous Zionide and composed a hymn for the opening of Purim. The entry ends with an honest doubt. Attempts to identify him with a liturgical poet of the Roman and Avignon prayer-books have not been proved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meter-in-the-bi:
Whether the poetry of the Old Testament follows regular meter is the open question taken up in a Jewish Encyclopedia article by Joseph Jacobs and W. H. Cobb, published in 1906. The poems at stake are chiefly Psalms, Proverbs, Job, and the prophetical books. The authors argue the answer must come from a trained ear, not the eye.

Using Psalm 54 as a test case, the article shows verses built from equal tone groups, often three plus three, and finds the same patterns in other psalms and songs. Most psalms, though, are irregular, and the writers warn against rewriting the text to force a meter. A history of the debate runs from Bellermann and Saalschütz to Sievers and Grimme.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-millaud-edouard:
Edouard Millaud, born at Tarascon on September 27, 1834, was a French barrister who rose to the Senate and the cabinet. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Trained at Lyons and called to its bar in 1856, he opposed Napoleon III's empire and became Lyons' attorney-general when it fell.

Millaud sat in the Assembly from 1871 with the Extreme Left and helped found the Republican Union, then moved to the Senate in 1880 and held his seat through two reelections. A strong speaker, he served as minister of public works in 1886 and 1887 under Freycinet and Goblet. His books range from a study of the orator Hortensius to army reorganization and the peace question of 1871.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mombach-julius-:
Julius Lazarus Mombach, born at Pfungstadt in 1813, was the choirmaster who set the sound of Anglo-Jewish worship, as Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came to London at fifteen, studied under Enoch Eliasson, and joined the Great Synagogue's choir when Simon Ascher became its reader. He directed that choir until his death in 1880.

Fifty-two years at one synagogue, the entry says, and behind them a revolution: nearly all the music used in the German synagogues of England and its colonies was Mombach's own composition. Synagogues across London and the provinces borrowed him for great occasions, and a generation of readers learned their ḥazzanut from him at Jews' College. Few single musicians have defined a community's sound so completely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moscheles-felix:
Felix Moscheles was an English artist born in London on February 8, 1833. Joseph Jacobs wrote his short Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied painting in Paris and Antwerp and first showed his pictures in those cities. Later he exhibited at the London Academy and the Grosvenor and New galleries.

The entry gives as much room to his peace work as to his art. Moscheles was very active for international arbitration and peace, and he chaired the International Peace Association. He also edited Felix Mendelssohn's letters to his father. His own books include In Bohemia with Du Maurier and The Fragments of an Autobiography, published in 1904. The sketch catches a painter who was also a public campaigner.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-saerteles:
Moses Saerteles ben Issachar ha-Levi was a Bible exegete at Prague in the first half of the seventeenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and Alexander Kisch. His odd surname is a matronymic, taken from his mother Sarah's name. He published his main work at Prague in 1605.

His Be'er Mosheh gives the Pentateuch and the Five Rolls with glosses and notes in Judeo-German. It was reprinted often and was highly esteemed by Ezekiel Landau. As a supplement he added Lekah Tob, glosses in German to the Prophets and the Hagiographa. The book brought Bible study to Jews who read the vernacular rather than rabbinic Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-niggun-11538: Niggun is a Neo-Hebraic word for tune or melody. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote its short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It comes from a verb meaning to play strings. In northern prayer books it heads hymns with a direction. The hymn is sung, that rubric says, to the tune named. The word also names a droning, formless chant. Most of all it marks the prayer motive of a service. The Sabbath Niggun is the entry's own example.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oak-and-terebin:
Oak and terebinth are two trees of the Bible lands. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote on them for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The piece sorts out a set of Hebrew words. Some of those words mean the oak. Some mean the terebinth, a like tree. Both trees are large, strong, and long lived.

In the Bible these trees mark well known spots. Men were buried beneath them in old tales. Their shade drew rites and prayer in early days. Oak wood was used for ships and for idols. Both trees stand as signs of strength and long life. The piece ends with notes on kinds found in Palestine. Three kinds of oak grow there, the piece says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheimer-sir:
Sir Charles Oppenheimer was a British consul at Frankfurt am Main. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Nastätten, in Nassau, in 1836. He died at Frankfurt on June 21, 1900. He was schooled in Frankfurt, the town of his death.

At eighteen Charles went to London to seek his way. He set up there as a merchant in goods. His firm did well for seventeen years of trade. In 1871 he gave up the firm and went home. At Frankfurt he threw his strength into good works. He helped Jewish aid groups most of all there. In 1880 Britain named him its consul for the town. Two years on, he rose to consul general there. Queen Victoria made him a knight in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-perlbach-max-12:
Max Perlbach was a German historian of the Prussian lands. He was born at Danzig on November 4, 1848. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Perlbach spent his career in great university libraries. His doctorate came from Göttingen back in 1871.

He worked at Königsberg, Greifswald, and Halle in turn. He ended as a director of the Royal Library in Berlin. His books cover medieval East and West Prussia. He edited charters, chronicles, and the statutes of the Teutonic Order. He also edited Polish sources for a national series.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pick-philipp-jo:
Philipp Joseph Pick was an Austrian skin doctor of Prague. He was born at Neustadt, in Bohemia, in 1834. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied medicine at Vienna. Skin medicine was still a young field then.

Pick took his degree in 1860 and assisted in hospitals. In 1868 he moved to Prague to teach. He rose to full professor of dermatology in 1896. With Auspitz he founded the Archiv für Dermatologie in 1869. After Auspitz died he edited the journal alone. He also founded Germany's dermatology society in 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polemon-ii-1223:
Polemon the Second was a king in Asia Minor who died in the year 74. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He ruled first over Pontus and the Bosporus. Later he held Pontus and Cilicia, then Cilicia alone.

Polemon once visited King Agrippa the First at Tiberias with other kings. He later wed Berenice, the widowed sister of Agrippa. To marry her he took up Judaism and accepted circumcision. She soon left him, and he gave up his new faith. A later Christian tale claims he became a Christian, then a pagan again. The writers treat that tale with care and doubt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-predestination-:
Predestination is the belief that God fixes each man's fate beforehand. Kaufmann Kohler and Isaac Broydé wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They are careful to split the term in two. One sense deals with wealth, health, and earthly luck. The other deals with a soul's final bliss or loss.

That second sense is held by Christian and Muslim teachers. The writers call it foreign to Judaism. Judaism holds fast to free will, they say. A man's end rests on his own good or evil deeds. No decree shuts him out from life or bliss. The article then asks what is fixed, if deeds are free.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pulpit-12438:
Pulpit means the raised stand from which the Law is read and taught. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the earliest time a post stood in place of a pulpit. From it the king spoke to the people. From it Josiah renewed the covenant of the Law.

When Ezra came back from Babylon, he used a wooden stand. It was made for the purpose, the book of Nehemiah says. He stood on it to read the Law in the street. In Talmudic and geonic times the pulpit had its set place. The article traces that place, and the stand's shape, age by age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rahem-na-alaw-1:
Rahem Na Alaw is a Sephardic dirge sung at funerals. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Singers use it during the sevenfold walk around the bier. That walk comes just before burial.

The article says the tune carries prayerful hope, not only grief. The same chant serves a hymn by Solomon ibn Gabirol. Sephardic worship uses that hymn on the Day of Atonement. The entry also lists printed collections of the melody. It gives dates and page numbers for each one. Readers learn where a funeral song also fits in holiday prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-regenbogen-bart:
Barthel Regenbogen was a German meistersinger of the late thirteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He lived as a smith at Mayence. His songs carried Christian teaching aimed at Jews.

The article stresses his intense hatred of Jews. He wove Christian dogmas into his poetry to convert them. When persuasion failed, he turned to abuse, the writers say. He often voiced a wish to see Jews wiped out. One song ends with a blunt line of hate. It says, I hate you, Jews, beyond all measure. The short entry preserves a harsh voice from medieval song. It cites Hagen's Minnesinger and Güdemann's history as sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rice-abraham-12:
Abraham Rice was an American Talmudist and rabbi born in 1800. Cyrus Adler and Harry Friedenwald wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Gagsheim near Würzburg in Bavaria. He died in Baltimore on October 29, 1862.

The article says Rabbi Abraham Bing ordained him at Würzburg. He later studied under Rabbi Wolf Hamburger. In 1840 he came to America as Baltimore's first called rabbi. He led Congregation Nidche Israel until 1849. He then resigned and became a merchant. Yet he founded a small congregation and served it freely. In 1845 he started an early Hebrew school. He stood firmly against Reform all his life. The entry shows old school learning in a new country.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenbacher-arn:
Arnold Rosenbacher was an Austrian lawyer and communal worker born in Prague on April 4, 1840. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his law degree in Prague in 1863 and kept up Hebrew study.

Rosenbacher led Prague's Jewish community as president from 1887, and later headed the Bohemian congregations' union. He fought the rule that barred Jews from a canon law doctorate. That fight failed for him, but the bar was lifted in 1870. He was also the first Jew in Austria's treasury law department. He was likewise a Hebrew scholar in his own right.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rulf-isaac-1293:
Isaac Rülf was a German rabbi and author born in Holzhausen, Hessen, on February 10, 1834. Isidore Singer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. He took his doctorate in 1865 and at thirty-one became rabbi at Memel.

Rülf served the Memel district synagogue for thirty-three years, until 1898. There he took deep interest in the plight of Jews in Russia. He edited the Memeler Dampfboot, a daily political paper, for decades. His books include Three Days in Jewish Russia, from 1882. He also built a whole system of metaphysics across several volumes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-russia-10038:
Russia, in this entry, means the Russian empire and the long Jewish presence inside it. Its six authors were Herman Rosenthal, J. G. Lipman, Vasili Rosenthal, L. Wygodsky, M. Mysh, and Abraham Galante. The article supplements other headings rather than retelling everything.

Armenian and Georgian historians place Jews there in very remote times. After the First Temple fell in 587 B.C., Nebuchadnezzar reportedly deported captives to Armenia. The Jewish Bagratuni family rose high in Armenian councils for centuries. By the late fourth century, some Armenian cities held 10,000 to 30,000 Jews. Persian invasions then brought destruction and captivity on them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salomons-13038:
Salomons is an English family descended from Solomon Salomons, a London merchant of the eighteenth century. Joseph Jacobs, Goodman Lipkind, and Isidore Harris wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It profiles the family's principal members in turn.

Levi Salomons, born in 1774, was a financier and underwriter in London. He served his synagogue as warden and sat on the Board of Deputies. His son Sir David, born in 1797, broke barrier after barrier in public life. He was the first English Jew to serve as sheriff, alderman, and Parliament member. He also became lord mayor of London, a first as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-natr:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ben Naṭronai. He was a German tosafist, a scholar who added notes to the Talmud. He lived in the second half of the twelfth century. Samuel studied under Eliezer ben Natan and married his teacher's daughter.

Later scholars often cite Samuel by the short name RaSHBaT. His father-in-law quotes him in the work Eben ha-'Ezer. Zedekiah ben Abraham also cites him in Shibbole ha-Leḳeṭ. A few of his new readings appear in notes on Maimonides. Samuel died as a martyr at Neuss in 1197. The entry shows how his learning passed into later law books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sax-julius-1323:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Julius Sax. He was an electrical engineer. Sax was born at Sugarre, in Russia, in 1824. He died in London in August 1890. He emigrated to England in 1851. There he set up a shop making fine scientific instruments.

The master of the royal mint hired Sax to build automatic balances. His bullion and chemical balances won a prize medal in 1862. The governor of Hongkong bought them for his mint. Sax then patented a string of inventions. They included a metal fire-alarm button and a magnetic telegraph. He also built electric call-bells for fire stations. His cell-call system served police stations and prisons. He won eight prize medals in all. He also served as overseer of the Western Synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schwarz-adolf-1:
Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Adolf Schwarz. He was an Austrian theologian. Schwarz was born in July 1846 at Adász-Tevel, near Papa, in Hungary. His father, a rabbi, taught him Talmud early. He studied philosophy at Vienna and at Breslau's seminary. Two prize essays on philosophy and the calendar appeared by 1872.

Schwarz served as rabbi of Carlsruhe for eighteen years. In 1893 Vienna called him to head its new theological seminary. He still holds that post in 1905. His sermons fill several volumes. His deep work treats the Tosifta, the companion to the Mishnah. He also studied the quarrels of the schools of Shammai and Hillel. Later lectures cover the women of the Bible and the Bible's storytelling art.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-serebszczyzna-s:
Serebszczyzna, the silver tax, was a land tax laid on people in Lithuania and Russia. Herman Rosenthal and George D. Rosenthal wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The tax took its name from the rule that it be paid in silver. Russia first owed it to the Tatars, then to Poland and Lithuania.

Over time the levy became a state tax across the region. Jewish communities often won release from paying it directly. That was no special favor, the entry argues. Those communities already paid their taxes each year in one lump sum. Readers see how a tax name can hide a fair, practical bargain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shela-13538:
Shela was a Babylonian teacher at the close of the tannaitic age. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He headed the school, or sidra, at Nehardea in Babylon. When Rab visited Babylon, he expounded at Shela's public lectures.

Nehardea's school took Shela's name in his honor. Its scholars were called the Debe Rabbi Shela, his household. One Mishnah reading by Shela himself survives in tractate Yoma. Sayings of his pupils appear across the Talmud as well. They surface in Pesahim, Rosh ha-Shanah, Gittin, and Kiddushin. The entry is short, but it shows a teacher remembered mainly through the school that bore his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-soldi-emile-art:
Emile-Arthur Soldi was a French engraver, sculptor, and writer on art. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Paris on May 27, 1846. His father David Soldi taught modern languages and came from Denmark. In 1869 Emile won the Grand Prix at Rome for medal engraving.

Four years later he showed a cameo and a bronze medal. The government bought both for the Luxembourg museum. He carved marble bas-reliefs and medallion portraits of noted sitters. He also modeled a gate of the citadel of Angkor-Tohm. His books dealt with Egyptian art and art methods. He was a chevalier of the Legion of Honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-simon-adl:
Simon Adler Stern was an American author, editor, and critic born in Philadelphia in 1838. Cyrus Adler and Felix N. Gerson wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. As a boy he showed real talent on the violin. He chose literature over music in the end. He died on May 2, 1904.

Stern translated prose works by Heinrich Heine into English. He also translated two novels by Berthold Auerbach. After a trip to the Far East in 1887, he published a travel book. Its title records his jottings from China and Japan. He edited the Penn Monthly and the Industrial Review. He helped lead the Jewish Publication Society of America early on. The entry blends literary work with business service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sutro-abraham-1:
Abraham Sutro was a German rabbi born near Erlangen in 1784. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Brück on July 5 of that year. He studied at the yeshivas of Fürth and Prague. He died at Münster on October 10, 1869.

In 1815 Sutro became state rabbi for Münster and Dortmund. In 1828 he added the chief rabbinate of Paderborn. He held that office until his death. His 1836 book protested against religious reforms in worship. He opposed the organ in the synagogue most strongly. At the same time he championed Jewish emancipation. He petitioned Prussia to open public office to Jews. Months before his death, an 1869 law removed those bars. The entry joins strict faith with civic courage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tannaim-and-amo:
Tannaim and amoraim are the two great ages of rabbinic teachers. Wilhelm Bacher, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, Joseph Jacobs, and Louis Ginzberg wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Tanna comes from an Aramaic verb meaning to teach. It names the sages whose words fill the Mishnah. Amoraim are the later authorities who followed them.

The tannaitic age ran about 210 years, from 10 to 220 C.E. It opens with disciples of Shammai and Hillel. It closes with the circle of Judah the Prince. Earlier teachers bear the title former elders instead. Scholars divide the age into six generations. That split shows which teachers worked side by side. Some sages spanned more than one generation. In amoraic times, tanna also meant a Mishnah expert. The entry maps the terms that order rabbinic history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-terracino-14338:
Terracino was an Italian rabbinical family with members across three centuries. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The entry names four men of the family. Each gets a short note on his post and writings.

David Mordecai Terracino served as rabbi at Asti in the nineteenth century. Hezekiah, a scholar at Lugo, pled blindness in one responsum. His answer to a legal question was left incomplete for that reason. Moses ben Menahem was rabbi at Ferrara. He wrote on a dispute at Lodi and later retracted a ruling. Solomon appears in a responsa collection by Shabbethai Bär.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tudela-ancient-:
Tudela held the oldest and most important Jewish community in Navarre. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Alfonso the Valiant took the city from the Moors in 1114. Many Jews already lived there at the conquest. Fearing for their safety, they planned to emigrate.

Alfonso begged them to stay with promised rights. His charter of 1115 granted municipal standing like Najera's. Christian hatred still made their lives hard. Sancho the Wise confirmed their rights in 1170. He gave them the fortress as a safer residence. He freed them from the merchandise tax too. A rebellion in 1235 wounded many Jews there. Shepherd attacks of 1321 began at Tudela.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vows-hebr-nedar:
Vows, in Hebrew nedarim, are promises made under religious sanction. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Talmudic law sorts vows into two chief kinds. One kind pledges a gift to a holy or charitable cause. The other kind bans the enjoyment of some thing.

The entry explains how each kind binds. A pledge of a named object need not be replaced if lost. A pledge of a set sum must still be paid. A ban vow can even be accepted by a simple Amen. A valid vow must be free and understood. The article sets out these rules with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weiller-pauline:
Pauline Weiller, born Eichberg, was a pianist of rare gift. Cyrus Adler and Henrietta Szold wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born in Stuttgart on April 22, 1839. She died at Baltimore on December 28, 1874. Her father was a cantor in Stuttgart. She played in public before age ten.

At thirteen, Pauline played for Anton Rubinstein. He brought her to Meyerbeer, who arranged her training. She finished her studies at the Leipsic Conservatorium. Her greatest triumphs came as a Chopin performer. Critics praised her flawless technique and memory. In 1859 she moved to New York as a teacher. She married Alexander Weiller of Baltimore in 1861.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-winchester-1493:
Winchester is the ancient capital of England, in Hampshire. Joseph Jacobs wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there at an early date. A pipe roll of 1160 fines a Winchester Jewess. She paid to avoid marrying a certain Jew. The Jewry stood on Shorten Street, later Jewry Street.

The synagogue stood in what is now Jail Street. Isaac of Chernigov was found at Winchester in 1182. The massacres of 1189 spared the city's Jews. A blood accusation arose there two years later. Another such charge came in 1232. One account calls Winchester the Jerusalem of the Jews. A leading Jew there served Aaron of Lincoln.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zabdai-ben-levi:
Zabdai ben Levi was a scholar of Palestine of the first rank. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the third century of this era. He was of the school group led by Hoshaiah Rabbah.

His rules of law came down by the hand of Johanan. He stood high in tale lore and in Bible sense. In both fields he oft clashed with great men of his day. He clashed with Rab, with Joshua ben Levi, and with Jose. One clash treats a verse on the cool of the day. He read it as the side of the set of the sun. Rab read it as the side of the rise of the sun. Two hymn heads for the Book of Lamentations are his. In one he sets four kings and their prayers side by side.
measure-for-measure-pg2238: The Duke of Vienna pulls the strings in this edition of Shakespeare's dark comedy: disguised as a friar, he watches Angelo's hypocrisy unfold. Justice, mercy, and the bed-trick resolve a city of license. The most probing of the problem plays, unsettling and brilliant.
on-the-functions-of-the-cerebellum-1838: Franz Josef Gall and others are named on this 1838 volume. George and Andrew Combe helped spread phrenology in Britain. The book treats the cerebellum, a part of the brain. The record lists 339 pages for the volume. The hosted sample preserves publisher lists of phrenology books. It gives no readable text of the cerebellum study itself. Those lists name works by George Combe on phrenology and education.
openalex-w1993200938:
María Fernanda Adame and co-authors measured coastal wetland carbon. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in the year 2013. Coastal wetlands can hold exceptionally large carbon stocks. Protecting them could slow climate change in a real way. Counting those stocks is required for climate plans.

The team worked in the Mexican Caribbean's karst landscape. Tropical coastal wetlands there store carbon in plants and soils. Mangroves and marshes bury carbon for very long periods. Measured stocks let planners value protection and restoration. Loss of such wetlands would release stored carbon fast. The study gives hard numbers for mitigation policy.
openalex-w2078953638:
Julia Reisser, Jeremy Shaw, Chris Wilcox and colleagues surveyed plastic pollution in waters around Australia. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Plastic makes up most human debris in the oceans. Its amounts and travel paths were poorly known there. The team sampled surface waters at many sites.

They recorded hundreds of plastic pieces in net tows. Most were small fragments from larger objects. Packaging and fishing gear were likely sources. Particle tracking models traced possible travel routes. Currents linked samples to coastal cities and overseas sources. Plastic levels resembled some overseas regions. They were lower than in the worst ocean gyres. Even small fragments can harm sea life, they note.
openalex-w2194582938:
Luca Montanarella, Daniel Pennock, Neil McKenzie, and colleagues published this report summary in SOIL in 2016. The Intergovernmental Technical Panel on Soils had just finished the world's first report on the state of its soil resources. Soils underpin food, water, and climate stability, yet they lacked any global status statement until this effort.

Soil erosion was judged the gravest threat, fouling water in rich regions and cutting harvests in poorer ones. The panel urges more fertilizer on infertile tropical soils, even while total world use should fall. Governments should set targets to stabilize or grow soil carbon stores. Better soil information is also demanded, since many regional judgments rest on decades-old studies.
openalex-w2500721338: Lead author Michele Carbone heads a long list of specialists on this consensus report from the 2015 Weinman International Conference on Mesothelioma. The metadata title reads only SPECIAL ARTICLE, while the sample itself gives the conference report title. The preserved sample contains just the title page, authors, and affiliations, with no readable abstract or recommendations. Its specific guidance on this asbestos-linked cancer therefore cannot be described from the evidence kept here.
openalex-w2762285338:
Muhammad Akram, Mehwish Iqbal, and Muhammad Daniyal, with Asmat Ullah Khan, reviewed breast cancer awareness and knowledge in Biological Research in 2017. Breast cancer is the most common tumor in the world and a leading killer of women. Better awareness and imaging have improved recognition and screening. Still, many cases are found late, especially where self-examination and clinical checks are neglected.

The review covers breast anatomy, risk factors, and how the disease develops. It walks through stages, diagnostic investigations, and the full range of treatments. Options span surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, hormone and targeted therapies, plus newer gene and stem-cell approaches. Two decades of research have produced more proficient treatments, the authors note. Their summary aims to raise awareness among women and health workers. Earlier detection remains the simplest way to cut deaths, they argue.
openalex-w2769496038:
Roger Iván Rodríguez-Vivas, Nicholas Nils Jonsson, and Chandra Bhushan reviewed cattle tick control in Parasitology Research, published online in 2017. The cattle tick Rhipicephalus microplus is the costliest pest of its kind for cattle farming in warm regions. Control has leaned on chemical sprays and related drugs for decades. Heavy use has bred tick populations that resist every major chemical class.

The authors survey other, and combined, strategies for this new reality. Options include rotating chemicals, mixing products, breeding hardy cattle, and managing pastures. Plant extracts, essential oils, vaccines, and sterile male releases also feature. Integrated tick management deliberately pairs at least two tools at once. Pairing tools lowers the pressure that creates hard-to-kill ticks. The review aims to help producers keep control working while chemical options narrow.
openalex-w4283796538:
The ATLAS collaboration presents a detailed map of Higgs boson interactions in Nature in 2022, ten years after the particle's discovery. The Higgs boson was found at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012. Theory predicts exactly how strongly it should couple, or interact, with every other particle. Those strengths rise with particle mass, and all are fixed once the masses are known.

The paper measures the Higgs couplings to force carriers, to matter particles, and to itself. Each measurement is an independent test of the standard model of particle physics. Rival theories generally predict different coupling patterns, so precision here limits them sharply. A decade of collision data turned a discovery into a detailed portrait of how the Higgs behaves.
openalex-w4387568738:
Maria del Pilar Arias López, Bradley Ong, Xavier Borrat Frigola, and colleagues review digital literacy as a new determinant of health. Their review appeared in PLOS Digital Health in 2023. Digital tools can widen access to care, from booking visits to reading test results. They can also deepen inequality for people who struggle with technology. This scoping review maps what is known about low digital health literacy.

The authors assess how the idea is defined and how far the problem reaches. They examine its effects on people's health and the programmes meant to reduce it. Their librarian-built search covered the major medical databases. Framing digital skill as a health determinant, like income or education, pushes health systems to treat access and training as care issues.
openalex-w4395112138:
Alexandre Zuntini, Tom Carruthers, Olivier Maurin, and colleagues present a new family tree of flowering plants in Nature in 2024. Flowering plants, or angiosperms, underpin most land ecosystems and human livelihoods. Earlier trees rested mainly on the small plastid genome. New methods now read hundreds of nuclear genes across nearly any plant, using a shared probe set called Angiosperms353. The team used it to build the most complete tree yet.

Their tree covers all sixty-four orders and four hundred sixteen families of flowering plants. It spans nearly eight thousand genera, a fifteen-fold jump in sampling over earlier work. Two hundred fossil dates scale the tree in time. The result lets scientists trace how flowering plants rose to dominance and rethink their classification.
openalex-w7161711938: Japan's Juntendo medical school has deep roots. This history study looked at how doctors were trained and how they worked there under its first three leaders. The team dug through archives and old papers. A medical-history piece on a school's early years.
openalex-w7166510838: Septic shock kills, and filtering bacterial toxins from blood was once a great hope. This paper revisits polymyxin B hemoperfusion guided by endotoxin tests, asking why trials failed and what biology says now. The authors separated hype from evidence. A critical-care review of a therapy seeking redemption.
openalex-w7204644738: When jawbone dies after radiation or certain drugs, the damage is severe and hard to treat. This paper studies combining vitamin E (tocopherol) with pentoxifylline as a therapy for jaw osteonecrosis. The authors review the evidence for the drug pairing. A specialized medical review of a treatment that offers hope where surgery alone falls short.
openalex-w7204993238: After keyhole surgery to clear bile duct stones, surgeons must decide how to close the duct: stitch it directly or leave a T-shaped drain. This updated systematic review, built to PRISMA standards, compares the safety and outcomes of both approaches in patients with bile duct stones. The authors weigh complication rates and recovery. A technical but consequential comparison for surgeons choosing between two established techniques.
openalex-w7212036638:
Arthur Ripper leads a team reviewing acne in adult life, a problem far past the teen years. Adult acne can last for years, come back, or start late. It is tied to oil glands, male-type hormones, scar risk, and strain on mood and social life. The team read trials, data banks, and care guides in 2026 to weigh causes, impact, and care today.

Cases past age twenty-five run to tens of millions, with women hit most. Hormone signals can drive acne even when blood tests look normal. Acne alone, though, is a weak sign of a hormone disorder. Pooled data link adult acne with both depression and anxiety. Care now pairs daily skin drugs with careful use of antibiotics, hormone options for some, and a strong drug for hard cases. The authors urge care matched to each person.
openalex-w7213368438:
Acione Leite de Souza Cremonesi and colleagues review how young children become literary readers. Their 2026 article gathers research on reading mediation in the early years of elementary school in Brazil. It follows the PRISMA method for systematic reviews and searches the SciELO Brazil collection.

Sixteen studies from 2015 to 2026 were included. The review finds debate over whether literature is an art experience or a teaching tool. Teacher mediation, shared reading, and talk about books stand out as central. School libraries and book collections also matter as basic conditions. Good formation, the authors conclude, needs access, skilled help, interaction, and respect for children's own responses.
openalex-w7214035238:
Karla Maria Cordeiro Cabral and Maria Emília Camargo return to telework, now centred on worker health and human rights. Their 2026 library and study reviews scientific work, labour law, and related papers. Telework grew with information and communication technology, letting work leave the employer's premises.

Flexibility, autonomy, and fewer commutes are real gains, they find. Intensified work, constant connection, and blurred home-work limits are the counterweight. Ergonomic risk, physical and mental overload, and endless availability appear among the harms. Health protection must follow the worker wherever work happens, balanced with privacy. The right to disconnect is named a key protection in digital labour.
openalex-w7214157138:
Rosineia Oliveira dos Santos analyses the Instagram profile of a Santa Maria tragedy families' association as a living archive. Her single-author 2026 qualitative study concerns the 2013 Kiss nightclub fire.
