Two 2023 posts are examined closely: a clarification note about a television series, and a post on a Brasília act demanding accountability.

Content and visual analysis sort the posts by discourse, imagery, memory marks, and political reach. The first post intervenes in how the tragedy is publicly represented, she finds. The second turns collective grief into denunciation and a claim for justice. The profile does not merely store records, Santos concludes. It updates meanings, organizes feeling, and calls the public to take part.
openalex-w7215109138:
Maria Isadora Andrade Ferreira led a 2026 review on demand-side public policy and innovation ecosystems. Innovation ecosystems join companies, universities, government, and society in creating and spreading new solutions. Traditional policy works from the supply side, funding research and granting tax incentives. Demand-side policy instead steers effort toward society's needs, using public procurement, technology orders, and regulation as its levers.

Such instruments, the review finds, widen the links between government, firms, and research bodies, favor new markets, and put knowledge into practical use. Bureaucracy, weak joint work among actors, and institutional limits hinder implementation. The authors conclude that combining supply and demand policies is the way to build more dynamic and sustainable ecosystems. The state should act to reduce uncertainty and direct effort toward real problems.
phrenological-observations-on-the-skull-: Phrenological Observations on the Skull of Eugene Aram, 1838. The murderer's skull. This book preserves that work. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
phrenology-vindicated-and-antiphrenology: Phrenology Vindicated, and Antiphrenology Unmasked, 1838. The vindication. This book preserves that work. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
plos-pone-0000038:
Rafal Farjo, Jeff Skaggs, Alexander Quiambao, and co-authors delivered genes to the eye without using a virus in work published in 2006. Gene therapy for eye disease often rides on viruses, which carry risks. The alternative tested here was compacted DNA nanoparticles: the therapeutic DNA squeezed into tiny particles that cells can absorb.

The team reported efficient non-viral transfer into eye tissue. Efficiency is the hurdle for nanoparticle methods, so clearing it in the eye, an accessible and well-contained organ, was a meaningful step. Success there points toward repeatable, safer gene treatments for inherited blindness and other eye disorders, where a viral carrier's one-shot limits are a real problem.
plos-pone-0000138:
Hanoch Kaphzan, Kenneth J. O'Riordan, Kile P. Mangan, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It works on the hippocampus, a region central to memory, in mature animals. The team examines how two chemical signals, NMDA receptor activity and dopamine, meet at the NMDA receptor itself.

Together, the authors report, the two signals switch on the ERK pathway and produce synaptic depression, a lasting weakening of connections between neurons. That weakening is one way the brain stores and updates information. The paper helps explain how reward-related dopamine and memory circuits interact at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0000238:
Hyemyung Seo, Kai-Christian Sonntag, Woori Kim, and colleagues published this Huntington's disease study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Huntington's is caused by a faulty protein that builds up in brain cells. The authors test a proteasome activator, a compound that boosts the cell's protein-shredding machinery, in neuronal model cells of the disease.

The title reports enhanced survival of the model cells with the activator. Helping cells clear toxic protein is one of the main strategies against Huntington's and similar diseases. The study gives that strategy a concrete test, showing boosted cleanup can keep sick neurons alive longer in the dish.
plos-pone-0000338:
David M. Gamm, Shaomei Wang, Bin Lu, and colleagues published this eye therapy study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Human neural progenitors are immature cells that can support or replace retinal cells. In a rat model of retinal disease, the authors report that these progenitors protect visual functions, preserving sight in the treated animals.

Cell treatments that protect rather than rebuild are nearer to clinical use. The authors measure preserved vision in the model, not just surviving cells. The study supports developing progenitor transplants for retinal diseases that currently end in blindness.
plos-pone-0000438:
Ripan S. Malhi and colleagues built a genetics resource for the rhesus macaque, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Macaques are among the most used animals in medical research because their biology closely matches ours. The team catalogued SNPs, single-letter DNA differences, in Macaca mulatta, giving the resource the name Mamu SNP.

A shared catalogue of genetic differences lets researchers compare animals properly, check breeding colonies, and link genes to traits and diseases. Without it, each lab rediscovers the same variants. Resources like this rarely make headlines, but they quietly raise the quality of every primate study that uses them.
plos-pone-0000538:
Michelle L. Hastings and colleagues showed how two general splicing factors steer the editing of gene messages, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Splicing cuts introns out of pre-mRNA and joins the rest; it is controlled by factors including PUF60 and U2AF65. The team examined how these general factors control pre-mRNA splicing decisions.

General factors touch thousands of messages, so their control logic shapes the whole proteome. Mis-splicing underlies many genetic diseases and cancers. Detailing how PUF60 and U2AF65 choose splice sites gives drug developers something concrete. These choice points can, in principle, be nudged. The goal would be to correct a patient's faulty message.
plos-pone-0000638:
Jeffrey A. Johnson, Jin-Fen Li, Xierong Wei and co-authors presented simpler tests for HIV drug resistance in PLOS ONE in 2007. Antiretroviral therapy fails when HIV-1 becomes resistant to the drugs. Standard bulk sequencing finds resistance only when resistant virus is fairly common. Clinicians also needed to judge the low-frequency resistant variants hiding below that detection limit.

Their PCR assays, aimed at HIV-1 subtype B, raise the sensitivity of resistance testing. The title adds a second gain: the assays can link resistance mutations together on the same virus. Knowing which mutations travel together changes how a treatment plan reads a test result.
plos-pone-0000738:
Ann-Brit Eg Hansen, Nicolai Lohse, Jan Gerstoft and colleagues examined deaths among siblings of patients carrying both HIV and hepatitis C. Their 2007 PLOS ONE finding is stark. Co-infection is linked with three- to four-fold higher mortality among the patients' siblings. The comparison groups were siblings of HIV-only patients and population controls. Dead siblings never caught the patients' viruses, so something else must be shared.

The authors break the excess down by cause of death. Their reading is that risk factors shared by family members partly explain the pattern. Families share habits, environments, and sometimes drug use or poverty. This study turns an individual infection into a family-level warning sign.
plos-pone-0000838:
Bonnie R. Pedersen, Deborah Kamwendo, Melinda Blood and colleagues studied whether a mother's HIV-related genes affect transmission to her child, in Malawi. Variants in the CCR5 and CCR2 genes have been associated with protection against HIV transmission in adults and with delayed progression to AIDS. The CCR5 delta-32 deletion and another variant are associated with reduced expression of the CCR5 protein, the doorway HIV uses to enter cells.

The team investigated associations between CCR5 haplotypes, combinations of variants inherited together, and mother-to-child transmission. If a child's or mother's gene pattern lowers CCR5, transmission odds may fall. Such knowledge could sharpen prevention for the highest-risk pairs.
plos-pone-0000938:
Wilfried Thuiller, Jasper Slingsby, Sean Privett and colleagues studied how plant species replace each other in a fire prone region, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The Cape Floristic Region of South Africa is one of the richest plant areas on Earth. Keeping so many species side by side needs explaining.

Using a long term data set, the team test whether chance turnover of species can sit alongside stable coexistence. Fire resets the stage there at intervals, and species must return or yield. Their analysis works at both local and wider scales. The results matter for managers who must keep this hotspot diverse under a changing climate.
plos-pone-0001038:
Malcolm Semple, Hinke Dankert, Bahram Ebrahimi and colleagues compared airway chemistry in infants with severe RSV illness, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Respiratory syncytial virus causes bronchiolitis, a swelling of the small airways, and some previously well infants become severely ill. Differences in the first immune response may explain why.

The team tested whether two airway factors differ with severity: interferon gamma, an antiviral signal, and substance P, a nerve related chemical. Their title reports both are reduced in severe cases. A weaker early response in the airway itself could let the virus do more damage. The measures may also help flag infants at risk.
plos-pone-0001138:
Ovarian cancer often responds well to first chemotherapy, then returns in a drug-resistant form. Marianne Tuefferd and a multicenter French group, GINECO, examined a possible drug target in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The target is HER2, a growth signal protein already used to guide treatment in breast cancer.

The study measured HER2 status in ovarian cancers from 320 patients. Targeted drugs such as trastuzumab exist for HER2-driven tumors, so knowing how often ovarian cancers carry the marker matters for trial design. The paper gives a large, multi-center count of how common HER2 positivity is in this disease.
plos-pone-0001238:
When the lungs fail, fluid floods the airspaces and gas exchange collapses. Arturo Briva and colleagues studied how high carbon dioxide levels affect the lung's lining cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Those levels build up in patients whose lungs are failing. Mechanical ventilation maintains gas exchange but can itself injure the lung.

The authors report that high CO2 levels impair alveolar epithelial function independently of pH. The harm comes from the CO2 itself, not just the acidity it creates. That distinction matters for ventilator strategies that tolerate high CO2 to protect the lung. Their result says tolerance may carry its own cost.
plos-pone-0001338:
New blood vessels in tumors grow with the help of endothelial progenitor cells from the bone marrow. Alessia Ciarrocchi and colleagues studied a regulator of those cells, Id1, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Loss of Id1 in the bone marrow severely impairs tumor angiogenesis and significantly inhibits tumor growth, a phenotype tied to missing circulating progenitor cells.

The authors report that Id1 restrains p21 expression to control endothelial progenitor cell formation. p21 is a brake on cell division; Id1 keeps it in check so progenitors can be produced. The pathway offers targets for starving tumors of their blood supply.
plos-pone-0001438:
Tara Mangal, Steve Paterson, and Andrew Fenton published a 2008 PLOS ONE model of a worm disease spread by water snails. Many such ills are passed by cold blooded hosts whose numbers shift with heat. If the world warms, disease rates may shift too. The team built a step by step model of the disease, called schistosomiasis.

Their model links heat to snail numbers, worm growth, and human cases. It then tests how control steps would fare as heat changes. Models like this help health teams plan years ahead, not just for one season. They also flag where field data are most needed to firm up forecasts.
plos-pone-0001538:
Tiago Dos Vultos and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the family tree of the TB germ. TB germ strains look near alike, with 99.9 percent of their code the same. Tracing the past of such a uniform germ is a hard task. The team used single letter changes across many strains to build the tree.

Their tree sorts the main TB lines and their order of split. Even a near uniform germ holds a readable past in rare changes. That past helps track how strains spread and gain drug resistance. It also frames why some lines thrive in set regions.
plos-pone-0001638:
Matthew G. Cottingham, Rikke F. Andersen, Alexandra J. Spencer, and their co-authors built a new genetic tool for working with a vaccine virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The virus is modified vaccinia virus Ankara, or MVA, a weakened poxvirus used as a base for vaccines. The team engineered a bacterial artificial chromosome clone of MVA so the viral genome could be handled like a plasmid in bacteria.

Using recombination-based engineering, often called recombineering, they could add expression units or change genes in the viral genome far faster than with older methods. The full text gives the build steps, the checks that the clone still worked as a virus, and examples of changes they made. A faster build cycle helps vaccine teams test new designs without long delays.
plos-pone-0001738:
Katsuhiko Hayashi and co-authors showed that mice need microRNA production to make germ cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. MicroRNAs are small RNAs that fine-tune gene activity during development in many organisms. Mouse germ cells also express piwi-interacting RNAs, another small RNA class.

The team blocked microRNA biogenesis, the process that builds microRNAs, and examined primordial germ cells and sperm production. Both were impaired, per the paper's title. The full text gives the mouse model, the germ cell counts, and the fertility effects. The result separates what microRNAs do in the germ line from what other small RNAs do, a step toward understanding infertility.
plos-pone-0001838:
Daniel J. Kliebenstein examined how gene duplication shapes plant metabolism in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Most plant and animal genomes have been through whole genome doublings during their history. Studies had shown doubled genes can part from the parent gene by gaining new functions or splitting old ones within one plant.

Kliebenstein adds another process: natural variation of gene expression between plants and groups as a driver of how plant chemistry evolves. The full text lays out the evidence and the argument across plant pathways. Metabolism is where genes meet the environment, so how doubled copies diversify helps explain the chemistry that lets plants make medicines, poisons, and flavors.
plos-pone-0001938:
Antonin Lamaziere and co-authors studied a peptide that can cross cell walls, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The peptide is penetratin, drawn from a homeodomain protein, a class of gene switches. Such crossing peptides drew great interest, since a carrier that slips through the cell wall could ferry drugs inside cells.

How they cross was still debated. The team tested penetratin on fluid membrane domains, the soft films that mimic a cell wall, and watched the shape of the film. They report that the peptide induces curvature in the film. A bend in the wall may be the first step by which such peptides get in.
plos-pone-0002038:
Alejo Rodriguez-Cattaneo and co-authors compared the electric signals of weakly electric fish, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. These fish make small pulses with an electric organ to sense the world and signal kin. The pulse is a fixed motor pattern, the same each time, yet it varies by species.

That mix of sameness within a species and variety across species makes the pulse a fine model for how brains evolve motor output. The team charted species-specific diversity in the fish Gymnotus and its kin. Comparing known patterns can reveal how neural circuits change as species split.
plos-pone-0002138:
Silvia Parajes, Celsa Quinteiro, Fernando Domínguez, and co-authors examined a gene tied to a hormone disorder, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The gene, CYP21A2, can fail and cause congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a condition where the adrenal glands cannot make key hormones. The failure is most often due to a lack of the enzyme 21-hydroxylase.

Human genomes differ between people not only in single letters of DNA but also in how many copies of a gene each person carries. The authors found that copy changes and sequence variants are both common at this gene. That finding matters for genetic testing, since a test that misses copy changes can give families the wrong answer.
plos-pone-0002238:
Maria Silvia Giretti and co-authors studied how estrogen helps breast cancer cells move and invade, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Estrogen is well known to fuel the growth of breast cancer. Less was known about its effect on the later stages, when cancer spreads within the breast or beyond it.

The team examined how estrogen receptor signaling, acting outside the cell nucleus, reshapes the cell's inner skeleton of actin fibers. That reshaping drives cell movement and invasion into nearby tissue. Blocking the spread signals, not just growth, could matter for keeping early breast cancers from becoming lethal ones.
plos-pone-0002338:
Ewan Ross and co-authors uncovered a role for a surface protein in steering blood-forming stem cells. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. PECAM-1, also called CD31, sits on blood vessel and blood cells inside the bone marrow. Its presence in that niche was known, but its physiological role there was unexplored.

The team shows that PECAM-1 influences how haematopoietic progenitor cells are divided between the blood and the bone marrow at steady state. These progenitors replenish all blood cell types. A protein that helps set their address could matter for stem cell transplants, where getting cells to home to marrow is half the battle.
plos-pone-0002438:
Work from Maitra and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Radhashree Maitra, Cristina C. Clement, Giovanna M. Crisi, and others. Its subject is immunogenecity of Modified Alkane Polymers Is Mediated through TLR1/2 Activation. With the advancement of biomedical technology, artificial materials have been developed to replace diseased, damaged or nonfunctional body parts.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002538:
In 2008, Doering and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Clinton J. Doering, Renata Rehak, Stephan Bonfield, and others. Its subject is modified Ca v 1.4 Expression in the Cacna1f nob2 Mouse Due to Alternative Splicing. The rest of the title points to an ETn Inserted in Exon 2. The Cacna1f nob2 mouse is reported to be a naturally occurring null mutation for the Ca v 1.4 calcium channel gene.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002638:
Natacha Arede led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was modified Whole-Mount in situ hybridization protocol for the detection of transgene expression in electroporated chick embryos. The catalog record names Natacha Arede first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. In vivo electroporation has been extensively used as an effective means of DNA transfer for analyzing gene function as well as gene regulation in. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002738:
Scott E. Solomon led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was paleodistributions and comparative molecular phylogeography of leafcutter ants ( atta spp.) provide new insight into the origins of amazonian diversity. Authorship is credited in the record to Scott E. Solomon and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The evolutionary basis for high species diversity in tropical regions of the world remains unresolved. The summary also notes a further point. Much research has focused on the biogeography of speciation in the Amazon Basin, which harbors the greatest diversity of terrestrial life. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002838:
Edward W. Maibach led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was climate change and local public health in the united states: preparedness, programs and perceptions of local public health department directors. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Edward W. Maibach, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. While climate change is inherently a global problem, its public health impacts will be experienced most acutely at the local and regional level. The summary also notes a further point. The public health infrastructure in the U.S. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002938:
Vincent Doublet, Catherine Souty-Grosset, Didier Bouchon and co-authors reported a case of mixed mitochondrial DNA lasting some thirty million years in 2008. Mitochondrial DNA passes mainly through mothers, and new variants usually sort out fast in the female germline. Mixed types, called heteroplasmy, are generally short-lived.

An inherited heteroplasmy persisting that long breaks the usual expectation. The PLOS ONE paper sets out the evidence and asks how such a mixture survived. Geneticists get a rare natural case that tests basic rules about how mitochondrial lineages are passed down. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003038:
Claire Grills, Nyree Crawford, Alex Chacko and co-authors modeled activation of the death protein BAK in 2008. How BAK switches on at mitochondria during apoptosis was highly controversial. One model said it needs activating BH3-only proteins; another proposed a different trigger, and the two seemed to conflict.

A dynamical systems analysis of BAK activation kinetics predicted resistance to BH3 domains, per the title. Modeling lets the rivals be tested for what each predicts over time. Published in PLOS ONE, the result guides lab work on a core step in planned cell death and cancer therapy.
plos-pone-0003138:
Yoshihiro Matsuoka, Shigeo Takumi and Taihachi Kawahara study flowering time in wild wheat in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. When a plant flowers has a strong effect on its fitness. While lab work on the molecular steps of flowering has moved fast, few field studies had asked how flowering time varies and spreads in wild populations.

Their subject is Aegilops tauschii, a wild wheat from central Eurasia, studied through both family history and ecology. Readers learn how flowering time diversified as this grass dispersed. The work links gene history to real habitats, which matters for wheat breeding and crop adaptation.
plos-pone-0003238:
Dael Geft, Shmuel Schwartzenberg, Ori Rogowsky and colleagues count dying progenitor cells in heart failure in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Circulating CD34+ endothelial progenitor cells are capable of differentiating into mature endothelial cells to assist in new vessel growth. The team sought to quantify the numbers of apoptotic progenitors in patients with congestive heart failure, using peripheral blood samples.

Readers learn how many of these repair cells are already dying in heart failure patients. Low or dying progenitor counts could help explain poor vessel repair in the failing heart. Such counts might also serve as a marker of disease severity.
plos-pone-0003338:
Stéphane Brunet, Julien Dumont, Karen W. Lee and colleagues study a spindle protein in mouse eggs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Formation of female gametes requires acentriolar spindle assembly during meiosis. Mitotic spindles organize from centrosomes and via local activation of the RanGTPase on chromosomes. Vertebrate oocytes present a RanGTP gradient centred on chromatin at all stages of meiotic maturation.

The title reports that meiotic regulation of TPX2 protein levels governs cell cycle progression in mouse oocytes. Readers learn how egg cells control division without the usual organizing centres. Errors in this process are a major cause of embryo chromosome problems.
plos-pone-0003438:
Jana Anja Eccard and Thilo Liesenjohann tested foraging choices under even risk in this 2008 paper. Animals must balance food gains against danger while they feed. Most choice models assume danger varies from place to place. The authors studied settings where risk stays the same everywhere.

Even with uniform risk, foragers still face real decisions about where to feed. Their tests checked how classic risk models hold up in that case. The results refine ideas about how animals weigh gain and safety. Field biologists can use them when danger is spread evenly across a habitat.
plos-pone-0003538:
Everett A. Roark and Kasturi Haldar studied Salmonella's home inside host cells in this 2008 paper. Salmonella is a germ that lives and multiplies inside cells. It grows within a membrane-bound bubble called a vacuole. Two lysosomal membrane proteins, LAMP-1 and LAMP-2, gather on that bubble.

The team depleted those proteins and watched the vacuole's fate. Attached filaments linked to the germ also involve these proteins. What changes without them shows how Salmonella exploits host compartments. Such details may expose weak points in its hiding strategy. Salmonella also causes common food poisoning, so its tricks matter widely.
plos-pone-0003638:
Oliver Thompson, Iivari Kleino, Luca Crimaldi, and colleagues published this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It looks at podosomes, small foot-like structures that help young muscle cells grip and move. The team studied three proteins thought to build them: dystroglycan, Tks5, and Src.

Dystroglycan is best known as part of the complex that fails in some muscle diseases. Here it worked with Tks5 and Src to assemble podosomes in myoblasts, the cells that form muscle. The findings show how muscle cells anchor themselves, a basic step in building and repairing tissue.
plos-pone-0003738:
Christine B. Jensen, Malgorzata S. Martin-Gronert, Heidi Storgaard, and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Babies born with low birth weight face a higher risk of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes as adults. The molecular reasons were poorly understood. The team studied young men born small.

They found altered PI3-kinase and Akt signaling in the skeletal muscle of these men. That pathway carries insulin's signal inside cells, and the group had seen lower levels of one of its parts before. The finding traces part of adult diabetes risk back to before birth.
plos-pone-0003838:
Sylvia Cremer, Line V. Ugelvig, Falko P. Drijfhout, and colleagues published this ant study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Some species become successful invaders while close relatives fail. Whether success rests on traits already present at home or on new traits evolved after arrival was unclear. Ants include some of the worst invasive pests.

Working with garden ants of the genus Lasius, the team traced how invasiveness evolved. They compared invasive and non-invasive relatives to see which traits came first. The study probes the roots of conquest in six-legged colonizers that now trouble ecosystems worldwide.
plos-pone-0003938:
Marta Gómez-Nuñez, Kurtis J. Haro, Tao Dao, and co-authors used altered building blocks to probe immune pairing in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns the Wilms tumor protein, WT1. That protein appears at high levels in leukemias and other cancers. Trials were testing altered WT1 pieces as cancer vaccines.

The team built peptides with non-natural, light-reactive amino acids. Those altered pieces let them study how peptides bind MHC proteins. MHC binding decides which pieces immune cells get shown. Better probes of that step can sharpen cancer vaccine design. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004038:
Steven J. Swoap and David Weinshenker studied torpor control in mice in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Some mammals enter torpor, a deep energy-saving state, when food runs short. The hormone leptin can soften those torpor bouts. Mice lacking norepinephrine fail to lower leptin when fasting.

The authors report norepinephrine controls both entry into and exit from torpor. Distinct mechanisms govern each direction of the switch. Separating the two helps explain how animals time their energy saving. It also links brain chemicals to survival during food shortage. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004138:
Marianne Peters, Leigh Simmons, and Gillian Rhodes published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Earlier studies found that women prefer more masculine male faces during the fertile phase of the menstrual cycle. Evidence for a matching shift in taste for symmetry, even features on both sides, was much less clear.

Past work asked women to choose between slightly altered computer images of men. The title signals that this study used photographs of real male faces and bodies instead. The authors tracked how choices changed across the cycle, testing whether both masculinity and symmetry tastes rise near fertility. The work checks whether a widely cited pattern holds up with more natural images.
plos-pone-0004238:
Sonja Langmesser and colleagues published this sleep study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many effects of nitric oxide run through an enzyme cascade that produces the messenger cGMP. That messenger activates cGMP-dependent protein kinases, placing them downstream of a major signalling route.

The team studied mice with altered cGMP-dependent protein kinase type I and tracked their sleep and wakefulness. They report that this kinase is implicated in regulating both the timing and the quality of sleep. A single enzyme in the chain thus helps set when animals sleep and how well.
plos-pone-0004338:
Joshua Milstein and colleagues published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The local field potential, the summed electrical activity recorded from brain tissue, is a workhorse signal in neuroscience. The team demonstrate that human recordings from intracranial electrodes show a ubiquitous 1/f2 scaling in the power spectrum. The recordings came from a variety of brain regions, and the pattern is a Brownian one.

They develop a quantitative model treating the signal's generation as neuronal shot noise, the sum of many tiny random events. Explaining a universal pattern in brain recordings matters for every study that reads them.
plos-pone-0004438:
Bacillus bacteria matter for farming, medicine, and even defense, yet telling their strains apart is tricky, as Shalini Porwal, Sadhana Lal, Simrita Cheema, and co-authors explain in PLOS ONE in 2009. The usual method reads one gene, called 16S rRNA, but it can only sort bacteria to the species level. It also leaves some Bacillus subtilis strains grouped in ways that do not fit.

The authors turn to family trees built from more data to sort out the confusion. Better family trees can reveal new microbial lineages hiding inside known groups. For a genus used in products and watched as a possible weapon risk, clear identity is not a small thing. The study offers a sharper way to name, track, and understand these widespread bacteria.
plos-pone-0004638:
Seeing a speaker's lips helps most when noise is moderate, not extreme, a Bayesian model by Wei Ji Ma, Xiang Zhou, Lars Ross, and co-authors explains in PLOS ONE in 2009. Watching a speaker's facial movements can dramatically enhance our ability to comprehend words, especially in noisy environments. A general doctrine of combining senses predicts the benefit should be biggest when hearing is worst.

Reality is different: lip-reading aids word recognition most in moderate noise. The authors explain that peak using a Bayesian model with a high-dimensional feature space. The brain, on this account, weighs each sense by its reliability in a way that produces the hump. The result refines theories of multisensory integration used in hearing aids and speech technology.
plos-pone-0004738:
Shajahan, Nayak, and Pandit studied spiral wave chaos in heart tissue and how to control it, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Normal electric waves sweep the heart in a steady rhythm and drive each beat. When those waves break into spirals, the heart can fall into fast, disordered rhythms that endanger life.

The team used four math models of heart tissue with uneven patches. They asked how spiral chaos starts and how it might be tamed. Ways to calm spiral waves could improve devices that reset the heart. The models let them test ideas safely before animal work.
plos-pone-0004838:
Michael Coble and colleagues solved the identification of the two missing Romanov children using DNA analysis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. One of the greatest mysteries of the twentieth century was the fate of the Romanov family, the last Russian monarchy. Following abdication of Tsar Nicholas II, he, his wife Alexandra, and their five children were exiled to Yekaterinburg, and Murdered, but two bodies were missing from the main grave.

DNA matched remains to the missing children. No survivor escaped, the evidence shows. Historic forensic genetics closed the case. Methods also serve modern identification work. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up.
plos-pone-0004938:
The windpipe keeps itself clean with rows of tiny beating hairs. These hairs, called cilia, sweep mucus and trapped particles upward. Known nerve chemicals such as acetylcholine speed up that beating. Peter König and colleagues added a new name to the list. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They showed serotonin also boosts cilia-driven transport in the mouse trachea.

Serotonin had been suspected of exciting cilia. Its route of action was unclear, though. The team showed it raises particle transport directly. The effect does not depend on acetylcholine. The finding adds a separate control knob to the lung's self-cleaning system. It may matter for airway disease.
plos-pone-0005038:
Cells normally trash misfolded proteins. Quality control tags them for destruction. Michael Lewis and Hugh Pelham tested that system on membrane proteins. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They focused on thermosensitive proteins. These proteins unfold when the temperature rises. The test site was the plasma membrane.

Quality control handled these surface proteins poorly. Heat-damaged proteins lingered instead of being degraded. For soluble proteins, the proteasome does the cleanup. Membrane proteins follow a different, less efficient route. The gap exposes a weak spot in the cell's cleanup crew. It may matter in diseases where misfolded surface proteins accumulate.
plos-pone-0005138:
Malaria in pregnancy threatens mother and child alike. Drug resistance in Africa is spreading. Theonest Mutabingwa and colleagues ran a randomized trial in Tanzania. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They compared several antimalarial drug combinations in pregnant women. Safety and efficacy were both measured. Drugs carry greater risks in pregnancy, so the evidence was badly needed.

The trial pitted artesunate plus amodiaquine against three rival regimens. Head-to-head results guide treatment choice. Pregnant women are often excluded from trials. That leaves doctors guessing for the patients who need care most. This study fills a dangerous gap. Its evidence comes from the population actually at risk. Malaria programs in Africa can set policy from it.
plos-pone-0005238:
Dopamine is a brain signal that can lift focus and drive reward, but too much for too long is tied to mental illness. Dzirasa and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 on what lasting high dopamine does to brain rhythms in the hippocampus.

Theta oscillations are steady rhythms that support attention and memory. Persistent high dopamine lowered the peak frequency of those rhythms during quiet waking and during REM sleep. Slower rhythms may help explain the attention and memory problems seen when dopamine signaling stays high. Slow brain waves are a sign of a brain at rest, so a shift in their speed is a clear sign that the drug state has left a mark.
plos-pone-0005338:
Mouse embryonic stem cells can be coaxed into germ cells, the precursors of eggs and sperm, in a dish. Primate stem cells can also start that path, but the markers and culture needs were little known. Yamauchi and colleagues worked with cynomolgus monkey cells in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their in vitro system drove monkey embryonic stem cells toward germ cell differentiation. A primate model sits much closer to human biology than mouse cells do. Progress here supports research on fertility, inherited disease, and the earliest steps of reproduction. Germ cells made in a dish could one day help men and women who make none of their own,. The monkey work shows how far that road still has to go.
plos-pone-0005438:
Tommy Noh and co-authors studied bone loss in special mice for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. A gene called Lef1 passes on signals from the Wnt pathway, which helps build and keep bone. The team asked what happens to bone when mice carry only one working copy of the gene.

Scans of young mice showed less spongy bone in the mice with one copy. The effect differed between males and females and changed with age. Even a half loss of this signal can weaken bone. That may help explain some forms of low bone mass in people.
plos-pone-0005538:
Rogier Bodewes and co-authors raised a caution about flu vaccines in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Yearly flu shots are advised for people at high risk from seasonal flu. Many countries also began advising shots for all healthy children.

In their animal study, a shot against a seasonal strain blocked the building of wider immunity against a lethal bird flu strain. Immunity gained from catching flu itself covered more strains than vaccine immunity did. The finding urges care in weighing child flu shot policies against the risk of a pandemic strain. Bird flu strains remain a pandemic threat, so any policy that trades away broad immunity deserves careful weighing.
plos-pone-0005638:
Fonnet Bleeker and co-authors looked for a mutation in brain tumours and did not find it, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Glioblastoma is the most aggressive common brain tumour. A growth pathway that is often switched on in it runs through a protein called AKT1.

A mutation in AKT1 had been reported in other cancers, so the team screened glioblastomas for it. They found none. A clear negative result saves other labs wasted effort and steers the search for this pathway's fault elsewhere in the tumour. Publishing a clear negative result is part of what keeps a fast field honest about its leads.
plos-pone-0005738:
Daniele Fanelli pulled together survey data in 2009 to ask how many scientists fake or bend their results. Surveys have long asked researchers, in confidence, whether they or people they know have cheated. The answers varied widely from survey to survey.

Fanelli combined them in a systematic review and meta-analysis, a method that pools many studies into one estimate. The pooled picture separates outright fabrication from softer bad practice. Both rates matter for how much trust science can claim. The paper became a reference point for debates on honesty in research and how to police it.
plos-pone-0005838:
Douglas Hayden, Peter Lazar, and David Schoenfeld offered in 2009 a simpler way to judge whether gene-chip results are real. Microarray studies compare thousands of genes between groups, a setup ripe for false alarms. Their test uses the overall distance between chips as the unit of evidence.

By permuting labels, the method checks whether two groups truly differ in expression pattern, spread, or both. Using whole chips avoids cherry-picking single genes. The approach suits small studies where fancy models overfit. It gives labs a sturdy first check before chasing individual genes from a chip experiment.
plos-pone-0005938:
The plague bacterium usually takes care not to kill the host cells it invades. Ayelet Zauberman, Avital Tidhar, Yinon Levy and colleagues flipped that trait in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They gave Yersinia pestis stronger cell-killing power, then tested the changed germ in a bubonic plague model.

The stronger killer turned out harmless as a plague agent, the title reports, yet it sparked fast protection against the lung form of plague. A germ that has lost its punch but still trains the immune system is just what a vaccine needs. The work points to a fresh route toward guarding people against a feared disease.
plos-pone-0006038:
The lamprey is a jawless fish whose line split from ours very early. Michael Baker, David Chang and Charlie Chandsawangbhuwana used it in 2009 to study the roots of hormone receptors. Their PLOS ONE paper builds a 3D model of the lamprey estrogen receptor holding estradiol, and also holding an unusual lamprey hormone form with an added oxygen.

Lampreys make 15-alpha-hydroxy steroids as their main sex hormones, a puzzle for receptor science. A model of the receptor's grip shows how one pocket can hold both forms. The work opens a window on the first steps of vertebrate hormone signaling, written in an animal that keeps many ancient traits alive today.
plos-pone-0006138:
The QT interval on a heart tracing times how the heart resets after each beat, and a slow reset invites dangerous rhythms. Ilja Nolte, Chris Wallace, Stephen Newhouse and colleagues pooled three genome-wide studies in 2009. Their PLOS ONE meta-analysis, covering three thousand five hundred fifty-eight people, hunts loci that set the QT interval and thus the risk of sudden cardiac death.

Common variation near the phospholamban gene tracks with cardiac repolarisation, the title reports. Phospholamban governs calcium in heart muscle, so the neighbor makes biological sense. A pooled analysis of this size can catch small effects, and each confirmed locus sharpens the genetics of a rhythm trait tied to sudden death.
plos-pone-0006238:
Shiga toxin, made by some gut bacteria, enters cells by an unusual route that skips the usual entry machinery. Barbara Windschiegl and colleagues watched the toxin's binding part cluster on flat model membranes, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The B-subunit binds a fatty molecule called Gb3 in the cell membrane.

Clustering of the toxin went together with a reorganisation of membrane lipids. The authors discuss how protein clusters and lipid sorting may drive entry. Understanding this first step could suggest ways to block the toxin before it harms cells. Shiga toxin causes severe gut and kidney disease, so entry blockers matter.
plos-pone-0006338:
Yaws, a disfiguring skin and bone infection, was nearly wiped out by mass treatment decades ago. Sibylle Gerstl and colleagues surveyed its return in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper followed fresh case reports in 2005. They used lot quality assurance sampling to estimate village-level prevalence.

That sampling method classifies areas as high or low prevalence from small samples. It suits neglected diseases where full surveys are unaffordable. Finding where yaws persists is the first step to new treatment campaigns. The survey shows an old disease exploiting gaps in attention.
plos-pone-0006438:
Raheem Peerani and colleagues built artificial stem cell niches for a 2009 PLOS ONE study. In the body, a stem cell's fate depends on its local niche. Soluble factors, the matrix around cells, and contact with other cells all play a part. That mix is so complex that single factors are hard to test in real tissue.

The team varied signal levels in their engineered niches in a controlled way. From the responses they drew design criteria for screens of pluripotent stem cells. Such screens test how stem cells react to many conditions at once. Clear design rules make those screens more reliable and easier to interpret.
plos-pone-0006538:
Nathalie Daude, Serene Wohlgemuth, Ekaterina Rogaeva, and colleagues surveyed variation in a sheep prion-related gene for PLOS ONE in 2009. The cellular prion protein is encoded by the Prnp gene. It is expressed in the central nervous system and serves as precursor to the misfolded form in prion disease. A related gene, encoding the Shadoo protein, was their focus.

They found frequent missense and insertion/deletion polymorphisms in the ovine Shadoo gene. The pattern parallels species-specific variation seen in the prion gene itself. Cataloguing natural variation helps judge which changes might affect prion disease risk. Sheep are a classic model for these disorders.
plos-pone-0006638:
Yi Feng, Julia Johansson, Ruijin Shao, and colleagues studied brain reproductive control in a rat model of PCOS in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adult female rats continuously exposed to androgens from prepuberty have reproductive and metabolic features of polycystic ovary syndrome. The team investigated whether such exposure alters hypothalamic neuroendocrine functions. The hypothalamus is the brain's hormone command center.

PCOS is common in women and poorly understood. Effects at the hypothalamus would place part of the disorder in the brain, not just the ovary. Their model lets them probe that level directly. Results shape how the syndrome's many features are connected.
plos-pone-0006738:
Victoria Megan Arbour calculated the hitting power of dinosaur tail clubs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ankylosaurid dinosaurs carried heavy clubs at the tail's end. The club combines interlocking vertebrae as a handle and a bony knob. People long assumed the club swung as a weapon. Whether that behavior was physically feasible had not been tested in detail.

Arbour estimated the impact forces a tail club strike could deliver. Her calculations drew on the club's anatomy and mechanics. The results judge whether strikes could injure predators or rivals. A feasible weapon supports the classic picture of ankylosaur defense. The study shows how engineering math can test dinosaur behavior claims.
plos-pone-0006838:
Jennifer Carpenter and her team read how fruit fly genes react to a virus in PLOS ONE in 2009. Germs such as bacteria and fungi rouse a strong defense in the fly Drosophila melanogaster. If a virus rouses its own defense was not clear. The virus here is the sigma virus, kin to the rabies virus group. It lives in flies in the wild.

The team used gene chips to track gene use after the virus struck. The shifts showed which paths the fly turns on to fight a virus. A set anti-virus plan would match the anti-germ plans flies are famed for. The work fills a gap in what we know of bug immunity. The fly stands as a model for virus defense in far larger beasts.
plos-pone-0006938:
Gauri Patwardhan, Qian-Jin Zhang, Dongmei Yin, and colleagues tested a new cancer drug aid in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many tumors resist chemotherapy, and an enzyme called glucosylceramide synthase helps them do it. The enzyme boosts a process that limits drugs such as doxorubicin. The team built a mixed-backbone oligonucleotide aimed at that enzyme.

Their short synthetic strand was designed to lower the enzyme's activity. They tested it on multidrug-resistant tumors. The treatment made resistant cells more likely to die by apoptosis. Blocking this enzyme could restore the power of standard cancer drugs in tumors that no longer respond.
plos-pone-0007038:
Thomas Kelly, Kevin Wilson, and Steven Heymsfield published body composition reference values in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their source was NHANES, a national health survey of the United States. The survey's whole body DXA scans were gathered in fifteen counties between 1999 and 2004. They were collected with modern fan beam scanners.

DXA scanning measures fat, muscle, and bone across the body. Reference values tell clinicians what is typical for a person's age and sex. The authors turned the national dataset into those yardsticks. Doctors and researchers can now judge individual scans against a solid population standard.
plos-pone-0007138:
Francisco O'Valle, Raimundo Del Moral, María Benítez, and colleagues studied transplant kidney injury in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cold storage time strongly affects outcomes for expanded-criteria donor kidneys. Restoring blood flow after cold ischemia triggers injury. Excess activation of the enzyme PARP-1 is part of that injury. The team tested whether PARP-1 levels in tubules predict trouble.

They linked PARP-1 expression to cold ischemia, acute tubular necrosis, and delayed kidney function. A marker readable at transplant time could warn surgeons early. It might also point to drugs that protect donated kidneys during storage.
plos-pone-0007238:
Walid Fayad, Mårten Fryknäs, Slavica Brnjic, and colleagues searched natural products for a new cancer drug lead in 2009. Natural products have wide chemical diversity. They are attractive starting points for drug discovery, especially in oncology, where several treatments began as natural compounds.

Some cancer cells resist drugs by pumping them out through efflux transporters. The authors screen a natural product library for topoisomerase inhibitors. Topoisomerases manage DNA tangles during cell division. They identify a new inhibitor that stays effective in cells overexpressing drug efflux transporters. That property addresses a common cause of treatment failure.
plos-pone-0007338:
James D. Fessenden measured structural changes in a calcium channel using a new labeling method in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The ryanodine receptor type 1 releases calcium inside muscle cells. Its static structure had been determined by cryo electron microscopy, but changes during channel opening were little known.

Fessenden applies Förster resonance energy transfer, a distance-sensitive light method. A novel site-specific labeling method places probes at chosen spots on the receptor. Measurements reveal structural movements that accompany channel gating. Understanding those movements helps explain muscle disorders linked to this channel.
plos-pone-0007438:
Xu Shi-wen and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on fibrosis, the excess scar tissue laid down by cells called fibroblasts. Fibrotic diseases form one of the largest groups of conditions with no effective therapy. In scleroderma, patient fibroblasts contract tissue too strongly and produce too much of a muscle-like protein. The team looked for a way to calm those cells.

They targeted a protein called Rac, which helps control cell shape and movement. Blocking Rac reversed the abnormal behavior of the fibrotic fibroblasts in the lab. The cells eased their grip on surrounding matrix and cut their excess protein output. Because no therapy exists for this disease family, a compound that resets scar-forming cells would be significant. The study names Rac as a candidate worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0007538:
Kankan Wang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how a cancer drug pushes tumor cells to die. Fenretinide disturbs the redox balance of cancer cells, creating oxidative stress. Such stress can end in apoptosis, orderly cell death. How the stress signal becomes a death order was unclear. The team followed two stress-responsive regulators, HSF1 and NRF2, in treated cancer cells.

Those regulators convert the redox disturbance into apoptotic activity. They translate a chemical imbalance into the machinery of self-destruction. Mapping that conversion matters for a new generation of targeted cancer therapies. Many drugs aim to tip cancer's fragile redox balance. Knowing the middlemen tells developers where the tipping actually happens. The study links two famous stress sensors to a drug's killing power.
plos-pone-0007638:
Johannes Brettschneider and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on predicting the course of multiple sclerosis. MS features a broad antibody response against common viruses: measles, rubella, and varicella zoster. That pattern, measurable in spinal fluid, is called the MRZ reaction. The team asked whether it predicts what happens after a first neurological episode, known as clinically isolated syndrome. Many such patients later convert to definite MS; some do not.

Antibodies against the three viruses did predict conversion. A patient carrying the signature was more likely to develop full MS. An early warning test helps doctors counsel patients and start treatment sooner. It also helps trials recruit those most likely to progress. The study turns a curious antibody pattern into a prognostic tool. Prediction, in a disease of uncertain course, is itself a kind of care.
plos-pone-0007738:
Kwangmi Kim and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests how blocking mitochondria affects the earliest signals in mouse T cells. T cells are immune cells that recognize targets through a receptor on their surface. Their first signals start close to that receptor, at the membrane.

The authors applied mitochondrial antagonists, drugs that jam the cell's energy centers. The blockade quickly dampened the early receptor signals. That link between energy supply and immune signaling was not obvious before. It suggests that a cell's power state can tune how strongly it answers a threat.
plos-pone-0007838:
Gallen Triana-Baltzer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a flu drug against viruses that already resist standard therapy. Many seasonal H1N1 isolates carried a mutation, H274Y, that defeats the drug oseltamivir. The new pandemic H1N1 raised fears of more resistance to come.

The candidate drug, DAS181, works in a different way. As a sialidase fusion protein, it strips the docking sites flu needs from airway cells. The team showed it inhibits neuraminidase inhibitor-resistant influenza virus. Host-targeted drugs give doctors a fallback when viral resistance spreads.
plos-pone-0007938:
Cherry Kingsley and colleagues looked at immune effects of unprotected sex in PLOS ONE in 2009. During sex, partners meet each other's cells, and the immune system can learn to react to them. Past work had hinted that such responses may affect the spread of HIV.

Partners in the study, both mixed-sex and same-sex couples, showed signs of immunity against a partner's cell types. A smaller share showed tolerance, a calming of response, instead. The mix of push and calm may help explain odd patterns in how HIV passes between people, a question with clear weight for prevention work.
plos-pone-0008138:
Sheetij Dutta and colleagues set the antibody bar for a malaria vaccine in monkeys in PLOS ONE in 2009. The vaccine targets AMA1, a protein the parasite uses to enter red blood cells. An earlier human trial slowed parasite growth but did not fully protect anyone.

In the Aotus monkey model, only animals with high antibody levels against the protein gained real protection. Low levels, however promising in a dish, did not suffice. That bar tells vaccine makers how strong a recipe must be before human trials are worth their cost and risk.
plos-pone-0008238:
Joshua O. Goh, Jiat Chow Tan, and Denise C. Park studied culture and eye movements in PLOS ONE in 2009. When viewing complex scenes, East Asians tend to watch the context more. Westerners tend to focus more on the objects themselves. These habits reflect holistic and analytic styles of visual processing. The team asked how culture shapes responses to visual novelty.

Using eye tracking, they recorded where people looked at new elements in scenes. Culture modulated those movements in measurable ways. The study pinpoints a specific mechanism behind broad cultural differences. It connects everyday perception to the culture a person grows up in.
plos-pone-0008338:
Emmanuel Dias-Neto and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about a lab tool called phage display. For twenty years this tool has helped find which proteins stick to each other. It sifts huge sets of test proteins on the shell of a virus. Some steps in the work are slow, and one slow step is the count of picked phages. That count caps how much can be done in a day.

The team joined and weighed all the tools at hand to build a next step for the field. Their aim was fast, large-scale tests at a cost labs can bear. More speed means more protein pairs found in each study. The piece serves labs that map how proteins meet.
plos-pone-0008438:
Xiaoqing Liu and co-authors study eye disease in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Some gene flaws cause the light-sensing cells of the eye to die. In one group, an enzyme stays too active in the dark. That keeps channels open and lets calcium build up to toxic levels. One such flaw is called Y99C.

The authors test if more light can help. Light can close those channels and lower calcium in the cells. They check if that slows the loss of the light-sensing cells. The work points to a simple factor that may ease one form of this decay. It may guide care for like gene flaws.
plos-pone-0008538:
Sandesh Subramanya and co-authors study iron uptake in parasites in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The parasites are trypanosomatids, a group that includes the sleeping sickness germ. How small lipids control their cells is little studied. In one species, a lipid called DAG boosts uptake of transferrin. Transferrin is the protein that carries iron in blood. The team ask if other species in the group respond the same way.

They find the boost needs enzymes called tyrosine kinases to be active. When those enzymes are blocked, the lipid no longer works. Iron uptake in these parasites thus rests on a signal step. That step could be a drug target.
plos-pone-0008638:
Keren Byrne and co-authors study an imprinted gene in sheep in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. PEG11, also called RTL1, is a retrotransposon-like gene. Members of its family are rare in mammalian genomes. They retain a gag-pol-like structure characteristic of retroviruses but lost jumping ability. The callipyge mutation in sheep causes extreme muscle growth. PEG11 lies in the imprinted region behind that trait. The team test if PEG11 is expressed as a full-length protein in callipyge muscle.

They find it is expressed as a full-length protein in skeletal muscle. That expression supports a direct role in the callipyge phenotype. An ancient retroviral gene thus shapes modern livestock muscle. The finding aids understanding of genomic imprinting.
plos-pone-0008738:
Karen Lloyd, Daniel Albert, Jennifer Biddle, and colleagues mapped microbes under a sulfur mat at the seafloor. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study comes from a hydrocarbon seep in the Gulf of Mexico. Fluids rising there feed microbes that cycle methane and sulfur. White Beggiatoa mats carpet the most active patches. Seep ground is patchy, mixing busy and quiet sediments side by side.

The team sampled across the mat and its edges. Microbe communities changed sharply over short distances. Activity measures matched the patchwork of seep flow. The map shows how seep life organizes itself around uneven fuel supplies.
plos-pone-0008838:
Yong-Yi Shen, Jie Liu, David Irwin, and colleagues read the night-vision gene in many kinds of bats. Their evolution study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rhodopsin, made by the gene RH1, detects very dim light. Bats are night animals living in poor light. Fruit bats rely on big, well-developed eyes. Insect-eating microbats lean more on echolocation, hearing echoes instead.

Comparing RH1 across bat lineages showed parallel and convergent changes. Unrelated lineages arrived at similar gene tweaks. Vision clearly still matters even to echo-guided bats. Shared tweaks reveal how dim habitats shape the same gene repeatedly.
plos-pone-0008938:
Valerie Storms and co-authors worked on finding the short DNA patterns that switch genes on, in PLOS ONE in 2010. These patterns, called regulatory motifs, are where proteins bind to control a gene. Computers can hunt for them, but the search often turns up false leads. Two kinds of clues can help: matching genes across species, and genes that act together.

The team tested how each clue, and both together, changed the hunt's accuracy. Genes inherited from a shared ancestor carry similar switches, which narrows the search. Genes switched on together also tend to share the same patterns. Combining both clues gave cleaner results than either clue on its own.
plos-pone-0009038:
Hongjun Dong and co-authors opened a locked door in the genetics of Clostridium bacteria, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Clostridium species matter in medicine and in industry, making fuels and chemicals. Yet they resist genetic tinkering because they destroy foreign DNA. Their restriction-modification systems chew up DNA that lacks the right chemical marks.

The team mapped that defence system in Clostridium acetobutylicum, a model species. They then engineered the strain to accept bare, unmethylated DNA. Genes can now be delivered far more easily for experiments. Easier engineering speeds work on these useful but stubborn bacteria.
plos-pone-0009138:
C. Scott Mahan and co-authors treated tuberculosis in Ugandans living with HIV and tracked their immune systems, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Both infections keep the immune system in a state of alarm. In HIV, that chronic activation predicts progression to AIDS. Earlier studies in advanced HIV saw no calming from TB therapy alone.

The patients here still had CD4 counts above 350. TB treatment lowered markers of immune activation in them. HIV levels and CD4 counts stayed unchanged during the same period. Treating TB early may quiet harmful inflammation even before HIV therapy.
plos-pone-0009238:
Ali Bouamrani and co-authors published this brain tumor study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Meningiomas are tumors that grow from the membranes around the brain. Most stay put, but a subset invades nearby tissue and carries a poor outlook. Telling the two kinds apart early guides how aggressively doctors treat them.

The team compared the full protein content of infiltrative and noninfiltrative tumors. They looked for marker proteins that separate the groups cleanly. One protein stood out: vimentin carried extra phosphate tags in the noninfiltrative tumors. A measurable difference like this could become a lab test for sorting meningiomas before treatment begins.
plos-pone-0009338:
Illia Tchernikov and Mazyar Fallah published this vision study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The eyes send color and motion down partly separate brain pathways. Color flows through the ventral stream, motion through the dorsal stream. When several objects compete for attention, the brain must pick a target fast.

The authors propose a color hierarchy for automatic target selection. Some colors, in their scheme, win attention over others without conscious choice. A built-in ranking would help the visual system break ties instantly. The idea gives testable rules for why certain colored objects seem to jump out at us.
plos-pone-0009438:
Clara Menendez and colleagues reported a trial from Mozambique in PLOS ONE in 2010. Malaria in pregnancy can harm both mother and child. Pregnant women can be given preventive doses of malaria drugs, a plan known as IPTp. The trial asked whether that care also helps babies live through their first weeks.

Newborn deaths were lower when mothers got the preventive treatment. The study came from a randomized trial, so the link is strong. It gives direct proof that guarding mothers from malaria saves newborn lives too. Health programs can use the result to support wide use of the treatment where malaria is common.
plos-pone-0009538:
Elena Losina and colleagues studied HIV care in Durban, South Africa, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Treatment for HIV works only if patients stay in care. Much attention goes to people who drop out after starting drugs. Less is known about those lost before treatment even begins. The team tracked newly diagnosed people at two program sites.

They measured how many never came back to start care after a positive test. That pre treatment loss proved to be a large leak in the system. Finding it matters, because a diagnosis that leads nowhere saves no one. Programs can use the numbers to build stronger links from testing to treatment.
plos-pone-0009638:
Po-Jang Hsieh and Peter Tse scanned brains during a visual fading trick in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stare fixedly at one point, and a still object nearby can vanish from awareness. The object still casts light on the eye, yet it is not seen. The team used brain imaging to watch activity in the visual cortex as objects faded. They looked at cortex maps for both the same side and the opposite side of the brain.

Signals in both sets of maps rose and fell with the fading. So the loss of awareness has a clear neural echo on both sides. The study ties a strange quirk of consciousness to measurable activity. It helps pin down where seeing becomes conscious seeing.
plos-pone-0009738:
William C. Hines and co-authors published a cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks whether a gene called BORIS is switched on in breast cancer. BORIS is kin to a gene control protein called CTCF, and some work had linked it to tumor growth.

Using careful counting assays, the team found no sign of BORIS messages at levels that could be detected in most breast cancer cells or tissues. A drug could force the gene on in one cell line, but on its own it stayed off. The authors conclude that BORIS is unlikely to drive most human breast cancers.
plos-pone-0009838:
Ordinary body cells can be reset to a stem-cell state, a trick called reprogramming. Mi-Yoon Chang and colleagues achieved that reset in rat cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. They worked with two starting types: neural precursor cells and fibroblasts.

Pluripotent stem cells can become nearly any cell type in the body. Direct reprogramming turns a mature cell back without passing through an embryo stage. Rats are a major lab animal, so rat pluripotent cells widen research options. The work extends reprogramming beyond the mouse and human cells shown before.
plos-pone-0009938:
Fruit fly embryos build their outer skin layer cell by cell, guided by landmark proteins. Wei Shao and colleagues screened for genes that interact with one such landmark. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Drosophila is the fruit fly of genetics fame.

The landmark is Bazooka, also called PAR-3, a protein that marks cell tops. A modifier screen hunts for genes that strengthen or weaken another gene's effect. The screen ran in the Drosophila embryo epithelium, the embryo's outer sheet. Partners found this way reveal how cells keep their orientation.
plos-pone-0010038:
The authors were Rolf Fendel, Christian Brandts, Annika Rudat, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered severe anemia caused by falciparum malaria in Gabon. One in four hospital patients there had this dangerous low blood state. The parasite destroys red blood cells, a process called hemolysis.

The team linked hemolysis to a low reticulocyte production index. That index shows how fast the body makes new red blood cells. They also found it predicts who will need a blood transfusion. Such a marker can help doctors plan scarce blood supplies for the sickest patients.
plos-pone-0010138:
The authors were Malin Inghammar, Anders Ekbom, Gunnar Engström, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study followed a whole population to link two lung diseases. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, and tuberculosis both strike the lungs. Both rank among the world's major causes of illness and death, and they share risk factors like smoking.

In a population-based cohort, the team measured how much COPD raises TB risk. Shared poverty and weakened lung defenses may explain part of any link. A clear risk figure helps doctors decide which COPD patients need TB checks.
plos-pone-0010238:
The authors were Caroline Montaudouin, Laurent Boucontet, Marie-Pierre Mailhé-Lembezat, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used special mice that are standard tools in immune research. These mice lack RAG genes and carry one fixed T cell receptor. Labs use them as a source of T cells that are all the same.

After moving those T cells into other hosts, the team found cells with new receptors. Strong activation in the body had uncovered new gene shuffling in cells thought to be fixed. That surprise warns labs that such T cell groups may not stay uniform in use.
plos-pone-0010338:
Kalpana Ghoshal, Tasneem Motiwala, Rainer Claus and colleagues studied a gene that may hold back colon cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cancer cells often add too many methyl marks to certain DNA stretches, silencing useful genes. That excess is thought to come from enzymes that place the marks. One such enzyme is DNMT3B. The team searched for which genes it targets in colon tumors.

They found that HOXB13 is one of those targets. In early colon tumors, a marked stretch near the gene is methylated, switching it down. Tests suggested HOXB13 normally acts like a brake on tumor growth. Losing that brake could help a tumor start. The work names both a culprit enzyme and a silenced guard gene.
plos-pone-0010438:
Sergei Danilov and colleagues traced a single mutation's damage to a blood-pressure enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, ACE, trims several small hormones and helps control blood pressure and vessel change. Total absence of ACE in humans causes severe kidney problems before birth. The team studied one change in the gene, swapping a single building block in the enzyme. They followed how that swap harmed the protein.

The altered enzyme failed to reach the cell surface properly. One of its two working domains then unfolded selectively. A tiny change thus wrecked both delivery and structure. Such case studies explain how rare mutations cause disease. They also refine knowledge of an enzyme targeted by common blood-pressure drugs.
plos-pone-0010538:
Ian Lanza and co-workers used two lab methods to confirm disturbed body chemistry in diabetes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Insulin steers how the body handles sugar, fat, and protein after meals. Without it, type 1 diabetes brings sweeping faults: high blood sugar and rapid fat burning among them. The team measured many small molecules in samples at once. They paired two methods so that each caught what the other missed.

The combined profile confirmed which pathways go off track in diabetes. Such maps guide both drug design and the care of patients. Confirming old beliefs with full data is valuable, not a repeat chore. It shows exactly where body chemistry bends, molecule by molecule. Two tools agreeing also makes the map harder to doubt.
plos-pone-0010638:
Sandor Dudas and colleagues characterized mad cow disease cases found in Canada, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bovine spongiform encephalopathy, or BSE, is a fatal brain disease of cattle caused by prions. Cases come in one classic type and two rarer atypical types.

The team tested Canadian samples with molecular, biochemical, and genetic methods. The tests separated classic cases from atypical ones and detailed each type's fingerprint. Knowing which type appears matters, because the types may arise in different ways. Clear typing also guides food safety rules and trade decisions that depend on BSE status.
plos-pone-0010738:
Martin Wikelski and colleagues fitted orchid bees with tiny radio tags, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Male orchid bees in Central and South American forests gather scents from flowers. They were thought to patrol huge routes, visiting scattered blooms. If true, they could pollinate rare plants separated by long distances.

The tags showed bees covering far larger ranges than trackers expected. Some flights spanned many kilometers of forest in a day. Long routes explain how isolated orchids still set seed. They also mean forest fragments stay connected by bee traffic, as long as the corridors in between remain flyable.
plos-pone-0010838:
Marta Rizzi, Rolf Knoth, Christiane Hampe and colleagues reported this case study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stiff person syndrome is a rare nerve disorder that causes sudden cramps and spasms. Most patients carry high levels of antibodies against GAD65, an enzyme the body needs to make a calming brain chemical, which points to an immune attack.

The team followed identical twins with the syndrome who were treated with rituximab, a drug that wipes out one class of immune cell. Part of the antibody response faded fast after treatment, yet a stubborn share remained and kept blocking the enzyme. Rizzi and colleagues trace that lasting share to long-lived plasma cells and hardy memory cells. Their results help explain why antibody levels can persist even after strong immune therapy.
plos-pone-0010938:
Enno Wildschut, Matthijs de Hoog, Maurice Ahsman and co-authors published this drug study in PLOS ONE in 2010. During the 2009 flu pandemic, some children with severe influenza were kept alive by ECMO, a machine that oxygenates blood outside the body. Doctors worried the machine's large circuit might dilute the antiviral drug oseltamivir, so doses were doubled as a precaution.

The team measured drug levels over half a day in three children on ECMO, aged from early childhood to mid-teens. In two children, levels of the active drug form ran higher than in patients off ECMO, tracking the doubled dose and reduced kidney function. One child showed lower levels. Wildschut and colleagues show that circuit dilution is not the whole story, and that kidney function can dominate dosing in these fragile patients.
plos-pone-0011038:
Dawn Thompson, Lene Martini and Jennifer Whistler published this cocaine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Addictive drugs raise brain dopamine, and chronic use selectively lowers the D2 dopamine receptor, tipping the balance of signaling toward the D1 receptor. What removes D2 receptors in the living brain was unknown, so the authors studied mice lacking a sorting protein called GASP-1.

Comparing normal and knockout mice during cocaine sensitization, the process where repeated doses produce growing responses, they tied the D2 loss to receptor sorting after activation. Lowering D2 or raising D1 signaling each shifted the receptor ratio the same way chronic cocaine does. Thompson and colleagues identify a molecular route by which repeated drug exposure rewires dopamine balance. That route is a candidate target for treatments aimed at the receptor loss itself, not just dopamine levels.
plos-pone-0011138:
Senapathy, Bhasi, Mattox and colleagues presented a gene reading method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reading a whole genome costs time and money, and much of the DNA does not code for proteins. The authors described a way to pull out only the useful regions before sequencing.

Their targeted method enriches the parts of the genome most likely to matter for function. That focus makes gene reading cheaper and sharper for many studies. Labs hunting disease genes could screen more people for the same cost. The approach helps turn raw sequence data into findings that can be used.
plos-pone-0011238:
Glauche, Herberg and Roeder modeled stem cell variation in PLOS ONE in 2010. Embryonic stem cells vary in levels of a protein called Nanog, which helps keep them able to become any cell type. The authors used a math model to ask how that wavering affects the cell population.

The model shows noise in one protein can keep a population flexible rather than locked in. Some cells drift toward change while others stay ready to revert. That insight helps labs control stem cells for regenerative medicine. It reframes randomness not as a flaw but as part of how stem cells keep their options open.
plos-pone-0011338:
Ivan Laponogov and co-authors reported in 2010 on enzymes that cut and reseal DNA. These enzymes untangle DNA by slicing both strands of one segment, letting another segment pass through the gap, then sealing the break. The cycle is vital for copying and reading DNA, and many cancer and infection drugs target it.

Using detailed structural work, the team captured how the enzyme holds the cut segment and how the break is made and then closed. The pictures explain how the enzyme keeps a dangerous break under tight control instead of letting broken DNA loose in the cell. That control is exactly what some drugs exploit to kill cancer cells. A clearer structure helps chemists design drugs that jam the enzyme at the right moment.
plos-pone-0011438:
Abdel-Majid Khatib and co-authors followed a growth factor during zebrafish fin regrowth in 2010. Zebrafish regrow amputated fins quickly, and the factor VEGF-C helps guide that rebuilding. The factor is first made as a longer raw form that must be cut to become active, and the team tracked both forms during regeneration.

They found the uncut raw form does not merely wait its turn; it actively blocks regeneration. The same molecule thus promotes growth in one form and brakes it in another. That built-in brake may keep regrowth orderly, preventing the fin from overshooting its proper shape. For regenerative medicine, the lesson is that delivering a growth factor is not enough. Its processing state decides whether it helps or hinders, a subtlety any future therapy must respect.
plos-pone-0011538:
Thomas Chertemps and co-authors showed in 2010 that one mosquito protein shapes malaria parasite development at two separate checkpoints. To spread, Plasmodium parasites must cross the mosquito's gut wall and later invade its salivary glands, the two tightest squeezes of their journey. The team studied a protein of the mosquito Anopheles gambiae called PRS1 and its effect at both steps.

Modulating PRS1 changed how well parasites developed at the midgut step and again at the salivary gland step. A single mosquito-side handle on both bottlenecks is a valuable find, since most control ideas target only one stage. Blocking the parasite inside the mosquito stops transmission before any human is bitten. Such transmission-blocking strategies are a growing hope for malaria control, and a double checkpoint protein is exactly the kind of target they need.
plos-pone-0011638:
Silvio Brugger and colleagues tracked pneumococcal bacteria in children's noses around a vaccine launch, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Children often carry more than one strain of Streptococcus pneumoniae at once. Such mixed carriage lets strains swap genes, which can change their capsules and spread drug resistance.

The team compared mixed carriage before and after the seven-strain conjugate vaccine arrived. Their tracking shows how vaccination reshaped the whole carried community, not just the targeted strains. That fuller picture helps officials anticipate replacement strains early and keep vaccine programmes effective over time.
plos-pone-0011738:
Kristin Stieler and Nicole Fischer tested a human defence protein against the retrovirus XMRV, in PLOS ONE in 2010. At the time, XMRV was thought to play a part in two human illnesses, prostate cancer and chronic fatigue syndrome.
